Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verses 1–5:

(p-561) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat al-Kahf

This surah is Meccan according to the consensus of the exegetes. It is also reported from a group that the beginning of the surah was revealed in Medina, up to His saying, "barren ground" (juruzan). The first view is more sound.

It is among the best surahs of the Qur'an. It is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of a surah whose magnitude fills what is between the heavens and the earth, and whoever brings it will have a reward like that?" They said: "What surah is it, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Surat al-Kahf. Whoever recites it on Friday will be forgiven for what is between that Friday and the next Friday, and three extra days in the narration of Anas. And whoever recites it will be given a light between the heaven and the earth, and will be protected by it from the trial of the grave."

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has sent down to His servant the Book and has not made therein any crookedness﴾ ﴿[but has made it] straight, to warn of severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward﴾ ﴿in which they will remain forever﴾ ﴿and to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾ ﴿They have no knowledge of it, nor did their fathers. Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths; they speak not except a lie.﴾

Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, would pause briefly at His saying "'iwajan" (crookedness), and at "marqadina" (our resting-place) in Ya-Sin. The reason for this beginning in this surah is that when the Quraysh asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the three matters—the Spirit, the Cave and Dhu'l-Qarnayn, as the Jews had instructed them concerning them—the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "Tomorrow I will inform you of the answer to your question," and he did not say, "If Allah wills." So Allah rebuked him by withholding revelation from him for fifteen days. The idolaters of Quraysh spread rumours about him and said: "Muhammad has been abandoned by his companion who used to come to him from the jinn," and some of them said: "He has become unable to produce his falsehoods," and other such things. This grieved the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and affected him greatly. Then, when the matter that Allah intended—the rebuke of Muhammad (ﷺ) concerning it—had been carried out, revelation came from Allah with the answer to the questions and other matters. The revelation was opened with "Praise be to Allah, who has sent down to His servant the Book," meaning: according to your claim, O Quraysh, just as you would say to a man who wishes you ill but sees nothing except your blessing: "Praise be to Allah who has blessed me and done such-and-such for me," in the sense of a favour bestowed upon him. "The Book" is the Qur'an.

His saying, "and has not made therein any crookedness," means: He has not turned it away from the path of uprightness. "'Iwaj" (crookedness) is the absence of straightness; it is with a kasra on the 'ayn for matters, paths and things not perceived as standing bodies, whereas "'awaj" with a fatha on the 'ayn is for physical things such as a staff, a wall and the like. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "He has not made it created."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

His saying, "and has not made therein any crookedness," encompasses this and all that has been mentioned: that there is no contradiction in it, and that there is no defect or disagreement in it.

His saying, "qayyiman" (upright), is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the Book." It has the sense of being placed first though it is delayed in wording; that is, He sent down the Book as upright. The phrase "and has not made therein any crookedness" intervenes between the circumstantial clause and its referent. Al-Tabari transmitted this interpretation from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also possible that it is accusative by a hidden verb whose estimate is: "He sent it down," or "He made it upright." In some codices of the Companions: "and has not made therein any crookedness, but has made it upright" (wa lam yaj'al lahu 'iwajan lakin ja'alahu qayyiman), reported by Qatada. The meaning of "qiyam" is "straight." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak. It was also said that its meaning is that it is a guardian (qayyim) over the other books by directing them. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

(p-563) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is possible, but it is not part of straightness. It is also possible that the meaning of "qiyam" is its standing by the command of Allah, blessed and exalted, over the world, and this meaning is supported by what follows of warning and good tidings, which encompass the world. "Severe punishment" is the punishment of the Hereafter; it is possible that the punishment of this world, at Badr and other occasions, is included with it in the warning. Its accusative form is as the second object, and the meaning is: that it may warn the world. His saying, "from Him" (min ladunhu), means: from Him and from before Him, and the pronoun refers to Allah, exalted. The majority read "min ladunhu" with a damma on the dal, sukun on the nun and damma on the ha'. 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read "min ladnihi" with sukun on the dal, a suggestion of damma (ishmam) in it, and kasra on the nun and the ha'. There are several dialectal forms of "ladun": it is said "ladun" like "sabu'," "ladn" with sukun on the dal, "ludn" with damma on the lam, and "ladan" with fatha on the lam and the dal. It is a word built on sukun, and the nun is dropped when it is followed by a genitive construction. 'Abdullah and Talha read "wa yabshura" with a fatha on the ya', sukun on the ba' and damma on the shin. His saying, "that for them is a good reward," is to be estimated as "with the fact that for them is a good reward." "The good reward" is the bliss of Paradise, and worldly good precedes it. "Forever" (makithina) is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "lahum," and "abadan" is an adverb of time, because it indicates an endless period.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

We have already indicated in the explanation of this verse the matter of the Jews instructing the Quraysh to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the three matters, and it is fitting that we state explicitly how that happened.

Ibn Ishaq related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, with a chain of narration that he said: The Quraysh sent al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'it to the rabbis of the Jews in Medina, and said to them: "Ask them about Muhammad, peace be upon him, and describe his attributes to them, for they are the people of the first Book, and they have knowledge of the prophets which we do not have." So the two set out until they reached Medina, and they asked the rabbis of the Jews about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The rabbis of the Jews said to them: "Ask him about three things. If he informs you of them, then he is a sent prophet; and if he does not do so, then the man is a fabricator, so decide your opinion about him. Ask him about the youths who went forth in the ancient age, and what their affair was, for they had a wondrous story. And ask him about a wandering man who reached the easts and wests of the earth, what his account was. And ask him about the Spirit." Then al-Nadr and 'Uqba came to Mecca and asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about that, and the matter was as we have mentioned.

(p-564) His saying, "and to warn those who say, 'Allah has taken a son'," to the end of the verse. The people of this statement are some of the Jews regarding 'Uzayr, the Christians regarding the Messiah, and some of the Arabs regarding the angels. The pronoun in "bihi" (of it) may refer to the saying implied by the preceding "qalu" (they said), and the clause "they have no knowledge of it" would then be in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: they said it in ignorance. It may also refer to "the son," meaning: they have no knowledge of this son which they claimed, in which case the clause would be a qualifier of "a son." This was said by al-Mahdawi, but it is objectionable, because only the speaker describes it, and they did not intend to describe it. My view is that it is a fresh negation, by which Allah, exalted, informs of their ignorance concerning that, so the clause has no place in the grammatical structure. It may also refer to Allah, exalted, and this interpretation is more condemnatory of them and more decisive in ascribing complete ignorance to them. This is the view of al-Tabari.

His saying, "nor did their fathers," means: those from whom these people took this statement.

Al-Jumhur read "kabura kalimatan" with the accusative on "kalimatin," as one says: "ni'ma rajulan Zaydun" (what a fine man Zayd is). The description of the word by its coming out of their mouths explains it. Some said its accusative is by way of explanation (tafsir), in the manner of the accusative in His saying: "and how evil a resting place" (wa sa'at murtafaqan) [al-Kahf: 29]. A group said its accusative is circumstantial, and the estimate is: "their slander is great" (or something similar), "a word." These statements were called a single "word" inasmuch as they are one utterance, just as they say of a poem: "kalima."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This statement exists in the soul as one meaning, so it is fitting to call it a "word." Al-Hasan, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Ibn Mahisin, and al-Qawwas on the authority of Ibn Kathir read "kalimatun" with a damma, as its subject with "kabura." His saying, "they speak not except a lie" means: they do not say except a lie, and so "in" is negative.

(p-561) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths; they speak not except a lie.﴾

This grieved the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and affected him greatly. Then, when the matter that Allah intended—the rebuke of Muhammad (ﷺ) concerning it—had been carried out, revelation came from Allah with the answer to the questions and other matters. The revelation was opened with "Praise be to Allah, who has sent down to His servant the Book," meaning: according to your claim, O Quraysh, just as you would say to a man who wishes you ill but sees nothing except your blessing: "Praise be to Allah who has blessed me and done such-and-such for me," in the sense of a favour bestowed upon him. "The Book" is the Qur'an.

His saying, "and has not made therein any crookedness," means: He has not turned it away from the path of uprightness. "'Iwaj" (crookedness) is the absence of straightness; it is with a kasra on the 'ayn for matters, paths and things not perceived as standing bodies, whereas "'awaj" with a fatha on the 'ayn is for physical things such as a staff, a wall and the like. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "He has not made it created."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

His saying, "and has not made therein any crookedness," encompasses this and all that has been mentioned: that there is no contradiction in it, and that there is no defect or disagreement in it.

His saying, "qayyiman" (upright), is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the Book." It has the sense of being placed first though it is delayed in wording; that is, He sent down the Book as upright. The phrase "and has not made therein any crookedness" intervenes between the circumstantial clause and its referent. Al-Tabari transmitted this interpretation from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also possible that it is accusative by a hidden verb whose estimate is: "He sent it down," or "He made it upright." In some codices of the Companions: "and has not made therein any crookedness, but has made it upright" (wa lam yaj'al lahu 'iwajan lakin ja'alahu qayyiman), reported by Qatada. The meaning of "qiyam" is "straight." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak. It was also said that its meaning is that it is a guardian (qayyim) over the other books by directing them. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

(p-563) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is possible, but it is not part of straightness. It is also possible that the meaning of "qiyam" is its standing by the command of Allah, blessed and exalted, over the world, and this meaning is supported by what follows of warning and good tidings, which encompass the world. "Severe punishment" is the punishment of the Hereafter; it is possible that the punishment of this world, at Badr and other occasions, is included with it in the warning. Its accusative form is as the second object, and the meaning is: that it may warn the world. His saying, "from Him" (min ladunhu), means: from Him and from before Him, and the pronoun refers to Allah, exalted. The majority read "min ladunhu" with a damma on the dal, sukun on the nun and damma on the ha'. 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read "min ladnihi" with sukun on the dal, a suggestion of damma (ishmam) in it, and kasra on the nun and the ha'. It is a word built on sukun, and the nun is dropped when it is followed by a genitive construction. 'Abdullah and Talha read "wa yabshura" with a fatha on the ya', sukun on the ba' and damma on the shin. "Forever" (makithina) is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "lahum," and "abadan" is an adverb of time, because it indicates an endless period.

If he informs you of them, then he is a sent prophet; and if he does not do so, then the man is a fabricator, so decide your opinion about him. Ask him about the youths who went forth in the ancient age, and what their affair was, for they had a wondrous story. And ask him about a wandering man who reached the easts and wests of the earth, what his account was. And ask him about the Spirit." Then al-Nadr and 'Uqba came to Mecca and asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about that, and the matter was as we have mentioned.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verse 6–9:

(p-565) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Then perhaps you would consume yourself with grief over their footsteps if they do not believe in this discourse, [in sorrow].﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have made that which is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them [as to] which of them is best in deed.﴾ ﴿And indeed, We will make that which is upon it a barren wasteland.﴾ ﴿Or do you think that the companions of the cave and the inscription were among Our signs a wonder?﴾

This is a verse of consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ). His saying, Exalted is He, "Then perhaps," is a rebuke and a reproach in the sense of disapproval toward him, i.e., do not be like that. "The one who consumes himself" (al-bakhi'u nafsahu) is the one who destroys it through grief and sorrow over some matter. From this is the saying of the poet:

Ala ayyuhadha al-bakhi'u al-wajdu nafsahu / li-shay'in nahathathu 'an yadayhi al-muqadiru

He means: "nahhathathu" (carved it), and he lightened it.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿over their footsteps﴾, is an eloquent metaphor, in that they turn away and distance themselves from faith and turn aside from the Law; so it is as if, through the extremity of their turning away, they have gone far, and he grieves over them in their footsteps. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿this discourse﴾, means: the Qur'an which We narrate to you. "Asafan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). Al-Zajjaj said: al-asaf is exaggeration in sorrow or anger.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Al-asaf in this place is sorrow, because it is directed at one who is not under his control and not under the hand of the one who feels asaf. If asaf came from one capable toward one who is in his grip and possession, it would be anger, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When they angered Us﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 55], i.e., made us angry. If you reflect on this in the speech of the Arabs, it holds consistently. Mundhir ibn Sa'id mentioned it. Qatadah said here: "asafan": angry. Mujahid said: "asafan": distressed. Qatadah also said: grieved. From this word is the saying of al-A'sha:

Ara rajulan minkum asifan ka'annama / yadummu ila kashhayhi kaffan mukhaddaban

(p-566) He means: grieved, as if his hand were cut off.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, We have made that which is on the earth an adornment for it﴾ and the verse that follows is an expansion of the consolation, i.e., do not concern yourself with the world and its people, for its affair and theirs is of little importance because of its passing and perishing. Indeed, We have only made what is on the earth an adornment and a trial and a test.

There is disagreement about what is meant by it. Ibn Jubayr reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he meant men; Mujahid also said this. 'Ikrimah reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the adornment is the caliphs, the scholars and the rulers. Another group said: it means blessings, garments, fruits, greenery, water and the like, of which there is adornment; the solid mountains and everything without adornment, such as snakes and scorpions, are not included in this. Another group said: it means everything on the earth, and there is nothing that does not have adornment in terms of its creation, its craftsmanship and its perfection. The meaning of this verse is conveyed by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The world is sweet and green, and Allah will make you successors in it, and He will see how you act. So beware of the world, and beware of women." And "zinatan" is a second object, or an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi) according to the meaning of "ja'ala".

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿that We may test them [as to] which of them is best in deed﴾ means: that We may examine them, and in this there is a kind of warning. Sufyan al-Thawri said: "the best of them in deed" is the one most detached from it. Abu 'Asim al-'Asqalani said: "the best in deed" is the one who leaves it most.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

My father, may Allah have mercy on him, used to say: The best deed is taking by right, spending in right with faith, performing the obligations, avoiding the prohibitions, and increasing in what is recommended.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And indeed, We will make that which is upon it a barren wasteland﴾, means: all of that will return to dust, not adorned with plants or the like. "Juruz" is the land in which there is nothing of cultivation or adornment; it is a barren waste. This is the state of the land that is populated with adornment, and it must come to this in the world part by part of the land, and then that will encompass all of it at the Resurrection. It is said: the land became juruz by drought, locusts or the like, when its vegetation has gone and nothing remains in it and no benefit. And the lands are ajrez. Al-Zajjaj said: al-juruz is the land that does not grow.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What he should have said is: the land that has not grown. "Sa'id" is the surface of the earth; it is said: sa'id is dust specifically; it is said: sa'id is good land; it is said: sa'id is the high ground as opposed to the low ground.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Or do you think﴾ to the end of the verse. The position of Sibawayh regarding "am" when it comes before an alif of interrogation (that it precedes it) is that it has the meaning of "bal" (rather), and the alif of interrogation: as if he said: "Rather, do you think?" turning away from the first statement and asking about the second. Some grammarians said: it has the status of the alif of interrogation. As for the meaning of the speech, al-Tabari said: it is an affirmation to the Prophet (ﷺ) of his reckoning that the companions of the cave came as a wonder, meaning a denial of that to him, i.e., do not magnify that according to how the disbelieving questioners magnified it to you, for all of Allah's other signs are greater than their story and more striking. This is the saying of Ibn (p-568) 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Ishaq. Al-Zahrawi mentioned that the verse may bear another meaning, namely that it is a question to him: did he know that the companions of the cave were a wonder? meaning the affirmation that they are a wonder; and the benefit of this affirmation is the gathering of himself for the matter, since his answer would be to say: I did not reckon that nor did I know it, and then it would be said to him: their description at that point. The figurative usage in this interpretation lies in the word "hasibta", so consider it.

"Al-kahf" is a wide opening in a mountain; what is not wide is a ghar (cave). Al-Nahhas reported from Anas ibn Malik that he said: "al-kahf" is the mountain; this is not well known in the language. People differed about "al-raqim". Ka'b said: al-Raqim is the village that was opposite the cave. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: al-Raqim is the valley that was opposite it, which is a valley between 'Asaban and Ayla, short of Palestine. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is the mountain in which the cave is. Al-Suddi said: al-Raqim is the rock that was over the cave. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: al-Raqim is a written book that was with them, containing the law they held to from the religion of 'Isa, peace be upon him; and it is said: from a religion before 'Isa, peace be upon him. Ibn Zayd said: it is a book whose matter Allah has concealed from us and did not explain its story to us. Another group said: al-Raqim is a writing on a copper tablet. Ibn 'Abbas said: on two tablets of lead in which the disbelieving people from whom the youths fled wrote their story, and made it a record for them, mentioning the time of their disappearance, how many they were, and whose sons they were. Al-Naqqash reported from Qatadah: "al-Raqim": their silver coins. Anas ibn Malik and al-Sha'bi said: "al-Raqim": the dog. 'Ikrimah said: "al-Raqim": the inkwell. Another group said: al-Raqim belonged to other youths in al-Sarah, for whom happened what happened to the companions of the cave. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: I do not know what al-Raqim is: is it a book or a building? It is also narrated that he said: I know the whole Qur'an except: al-Hanan, al-Awwah, and al-Raqim.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verse 10–12:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿When the youths took refuge in the cave and said, "Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself and prepare for us right guidance in our affair."﴾ ﴿So We struck upon their ears in the cave for a number of years.﴾ ﴿Then We awakened them that We might know which of the two parties was more precise in computing the term of their stay.﴾

"Al-Fityah" (the youths), as is related, were a group of sons of the nobles of the city of Daqyus (Daqyanus) the disbelieving king. It is also said Daqlayus, and said Daqyanus. It is related that they were adorned with collars and bracelets of gold, that they were from the Romans, and that they followed the religion of 'Isa (peace be upon him). It is also said that they were before 'Isa. As for their names, they are non-Arabic, and the chain of transmission for knowing them is weak. However, the names that al-Tabari mentioned are these: Maksaylamina, who was the eldest and the spokesman for them; Majsaylaminiya; and Tamlikha.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He is the one who went with the silver to the city when they were raised from their sleep. And (the others are) Marutus, Kushutuqush, Bayrunus, Dinamus, and Yutunus.

The narrators differed regarding the stories of these youths, and how their gathering and their going out to (p-570) the cave came about. The historians elaborated on this at length, but we will abridge their account, mention what the verse cannot do without, and mention the essentials of the disagreement, by Allah's power.

Mujahid related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that these youths were in the religion of a king who worshipped idols, slaughtered for them, and disbelieved in Allah, glorified and exalted is He. The people of the city followed him in this. Knowledge reached the youths from some of the Disciples (al-Hawariyyun) — as al-Naqqash mentioned — or from some of the believers of the nations before them, according to the disagreement we have mentioned. So they believed in Allah, and saw with their insight the ugliness of the people's deed, and they bound themselves to adhering to the religion and worshipping Allah, exalted is He. Their matter was raised to the king, and it was said to him: "They have left your religion, scorned your gods, and disbelieved in them." The king summoned them to his assembly, ordered them to follow his religion and slaughter to his gods, and threatened them with death for abandoning that. They said to him, as is related: "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth" [al-Kahf: 14], to the end of the verse, up to His saying, Exalted is He: "And when you withdraw from them" [al-Kahf: 16].

It is related that they said words similar to this, but not exactly this. The king said to them: "You are young and inexperienced, with no sense. I will not hasten against you, but will give you time. Go to your homes, arrange your affair, and return to my command." He set a term for them in this. Then he traveled during the term. The youths consulted about fleeing with their religion. One of them said: "I know a cave in such-and-such a mountain, where my father used to bring in his sheep. Let us go to it, and hide in it until Allah opens (a way) for us." So they went out — as is related — playing with the polo stick and the ball, rolling the ball ahead of them along their path, so that people would not notice them. It is also said that they were skilled in such play, and when a festival came they went out for it and rode among the crowd, then began playing with the polo stick until they got clear through that.

A group related that the matter of the People of the Cave was that they were sons of the nobles. A festival came for the people of the city, and the youths saw what the people did at that festival of disbelief, worship of idols, and slaughter for them. Faith entered their hearts, and they resolved to separate from the people so that punishment would not befall them along with them. So they withdrew from the people and went to the cave.

Wahb ibn Munabbih related that their matter was that a disciple of 'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon him, came to the city of the People of the Cave wanting to enter it. He hired himself out to the owner of the bathhouse and worked for him there. The owner of the bathhouse saw great blessing in his work, so he entrusted him with every matter. Some youths of the people of the city came to know that man (p-571), so he spread faith among them and made Allah known to them. They believed and followed him in his religion, and their association with him became known. One day the son of the king came to that bathhouse with a prostitute, wanting to be alone with her. The disciple forbade him, and he desisted. Then he came a second time, and the disciple forbade him and reviled him, but he carried out his intention of entering the bathhouse with the prostitute. They entered, and both died there together. The disciple and his companions were accused of killing him, so they all fled until they entered the cave.

'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: The People of the Cave were youths from the sons of the great, adorned with collars and bracelets, with locks of hair, and faith had entered them one by one. Each of them resolved to flee with his religion from the land of disbelief. Allah brought them out on one day, for what He intended for them. One of them went out and sat in the shade of a tree at a distance from the city. A second came out, and when he saw the one sitting, he sat beside him. Then the third, then the rest, until all of them were gathered in the shade of the tree. Allah cast into their souls that their aim was one. They questioned one another, some were alarmed by others, and they kept it secret. Then they agreed upon two men among them and said: "Let the two of you go off alone and make a covenant, and let each of you reveal his secret to his companion. If you agree, we will be with you." So the two went off to a distance and declared their faith and their flight with their religion. They returned and disclosed the matter, and the others followed them, and they set off to the cave.

As for the dog: it is related that it was a hunting dog belonging to one of them. It is also related that they found on their way a shepherd who had a dog, and the shepherd followed them in their opinion, and the dog went with them. The name of the dog is Hamran, and it is said Qitmir. They entered the cave according to all these sayings.

A group related that Allah, exalted is He, then struck upon their ears, because of what He intended of concealing them, and their place became hidden from the people of the kingdom. The people were amazed at the strangeness of their disappearance, so they wrote this down on two tablets of lead or copper, placed them at the gate of the city, containing their names, their fathers' names, mention of their nobility, and that they disappeared in such-and-such a form at such-and-such a time. It is also said that the one who wrote this and undertook it was two judges, believers, who concealed their faith from the household of the kingdom. They kept this hidden, and buried the two tablets with them. It is also said, according to one report, that the king came to the mouth of the cave, and that the two of them buried that in the king's building over the cave.

A group related that when the youths departed, the king ordered their traces to be followed, and that the tracking led those who followed them to the mouth of the cave (p-572). The king was informed, so he rode with his soldiers until he stood at it, and ordered them to enter upon them. The men feared that, so one of his viziers said to him: "Are you not, O king, if you bring them out, going to kill them?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then what killing is more severe than hunger and thirst? Wall up the mouth of the cave over them and leave them to die in it." He did so. Allah, exalted is He, had struck upon their ears before that, for what He intended of securing them. The people dated their affair on the two tablets, or the two men dated it, according to the disagreement. The name of one of the two men, as al-Tabari mentioned, was Nidrus, and the name of the other was Ruqqas.

It is related that this king from whose religion the youths fled was one whom Allah had tested the believers with, since he sensed them: he killed them and hung their bodies and heads on the walls of his city, and he wanted to make them abandon — as was mentioned — the religion of 'Isa, peace be upon him. He and his people were of the Romans.

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed about the youths that when they took refuge in the cave, that is, they entered it and made it a shelter for themselves and a place of seclusion, they called upon Allah, exalted is He, to grant them mercy from Him, which is provision, according to what the exegetes mentioned, and to prepare for them right guidance in their affair, that is, a good outcome. Al-Jumhur read "rashadan" with fatha on the ra and the shin. Abu Raja' read "rushdan" with damma on the ra and sukun on the shin. The first is more preferred, due to its resemblance to the verse endings before and after it. This supplication from them concerned the affair of their worldly life, and its wording implies that, though they were confident of the guidance and mercy of the Hereafter.

It is fitting for every believer to make his supplication regarding the affair of his worldly life this verse alone, for it suffices. The mention of mercy may mean matters of the Hereafter. I have abridged this account, and I have not neglected any of its essential points, according to my effort. And Allah is the Helper by His mercy.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: "So We struck upon their ears" — the verse — it is an expression for Allah, exalted is He, casting sleep upon them. This and similar expressions are phrased as "striking" so that the strength of direct action and the intensity of adherence to the matter spoken of and its imposition may become clear. From it comes the striking of humiliation and poverty, and from it the striking of the sending forth (ba'th). And from it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"The spider struck upon you with its web, and the revealed Book decreed against you with it."

This is used for compelling, eloquent necessity.

As for specifying the ears by mention: it is because they are the organ by which sleep is most seriously disrupted; the sleep of a sleeper rarely ends except through his ear, and sleep is not firmly established except with the hearing being inactive. From the mention of the ear in sleep is his saying ﷺ: "That is a man whom Satan urinated into his ear," (ﷺ) indicating a man who slept long and did not rise at night.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: "'adadan" — it is an attribute of "al-sinin" (years), and the intent by it is an expression of multiplicity, meaning: they require a number, and they have a number. Al-Zajjaj said: It is also permissible that the accusative of "'adadan" be a verbal noun (masdar).

"Al-ba'th" means moving after stillness, and this is consistent with the word ba'th wherever it occurs. The stillness may be in the person, or in the matter sent forth, even if the person is moving. His saying, Exalted is He: "li-na'lam" (that We might know) is an expression for that thing coming into existence, and this is in the manner of Arabic speech, meaning: that We might know it existing; otherwise Allah, exalted is He, already knew which of the two parties computed the term. Al-Zuhri read "liya'lam" with ya. "Al-hizbani" means the two groups; the apparent meaning of the verse is that one party is the youths, when they assumed their stay was short, and the second party is the people of the city whom the youths were raised among, at the time when they had the history of the youths' affair. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes. A group said: they are two parties of disbelievers who differed about the duration of the People of the Cave's sleep.

A group said: they are two parties of believers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is not connected to the wording of the verse.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: "ahsa" — the apparent and sound reading is that it is a past-tense verb, and "amadan" is its object in the accusative. "Al-amad" means the limit, and it may be used as an expression for a duration, insofar as a duration has a limit that is its amad in reality. Al-Zajjaj said: "ahsa" is an af'al form, and "amadan" on this view is accusative as a specification. This view is flawed, because af'al does not come from a quadriliteral verb except in rare cases, and "ahsa" is a quadriliteral verb. Abu Ishaq's view is supported by the fact that the af'al form of the quadriliteral is masculine, as in your saying: "ma a'taahu lil-mal and ata-hu lil-khayr," and the Prophet ﷺ said describing Jahannam: "It is blacker than tar," and he said describing his Basin (ﷺ): "whiter than milk," and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "So it is more wasted for other than it." All of these are af'al forms of quadriliteral verbs. Mujahid said: "amadan" means: a limit.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an explanation by meaning, in an approximating way. Al-Tabari said: "amadan" is accusative by "labithu" (they remained), and this is not sound.

So they went out — as is related — playing with the polo stick and the ball, rolling the ball ahead of them along their path, so that people would not notice them. It is also said that they were skilled in such play, and when a festival came they went out for it and rode among the crowd, then began playing with the polo stick until they got clear through that.

A group related that the matter of the People of the Cave was that they were sons of the nobles. A festival came for the people of the city, and the youths saw what the people did at that festival of disbelief, worship of idols, and slaughter for them. Faith entered their hearts, and they resolved to separate from the people so that punishment would not befall them along with them. So they withdrew from the people and went to the cave.

Wahb ibn Munabbih related that their matter was that a disciple of 'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon him, came to the city of the People of the Cave wanting to enter it. He hired himself out to the owner of the bathhouse and worked for him there. The owner of the bathhouse saw great blessing in his work, so he entrusted him with every matter. Some youths of the people of the city came to know that man (p-571), so he spread faith among them and made Allah known to them. They believed and followed him in his religion, and their association with him became known. One day the son of the king came to that bathhouse with a prostitute, wanting to be alone with her. The disciple forbade him, and he desisted. Then he came a second time, and the disciple forbade him and reviled him, but he carried out his intention of entering the bathhouse with the prostitute. They entered, and both died there together. The disciple and his companions were accused of killing him, so they all fled until they entered the cave.

'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: The People of the Cave were youths from the sons of the great, adorned with collars and bracelets, with locks of hair, and faith had entered them one by one. Each of them resolved to flee with his religion from the land of disbelief. Allah brought them out on one day, for what He intended for them. One of them went out and sat in the shade of a tree at a distance from the city. A second came out, and when he saw the one sitting, he sat beside him. Then the third, then the rest, until all of them were gathered in the shade of the tree. Allah cast into their souls that their aim was one. They questioned one another, some were alarmed by others, and they kept it secret. Then they agreed upon two men among them and said: "Let the two of you go off alone and make a covenant, and let each of you reveal his secret to his companion. If you agree, we will be with you." So the two went off to a distance and declared their faith and their flight with their religion. They returned and disclosed the matter, and the others followed them, and they set off to the cave.

As for the dog: it is related that it was a hunting dog belonging to one of them. It is also related that they found on their way a shepherd who had a dog, and the shepherd followed them in their opinion, and the dog went with them. The name of the dog is Hamran, and it is said Qitmir. They entered the cave according to all these sayings.

A group related that Allah, exalted is He, then struck upon their ears, because of what He intended of concealing them, and their place became hidden from the people of the kingdom. The people were amazed at the strangeness of their disappearance, so they wrote this down on two tablets of lead or copper, placed them at the gate of the city, containing their names, their fathers' names, mention of their nobility, and that they disappeared in such-and-such a form at such-and-such a time. It is also said that the one who wrote this and undertook it was two judges, believers, who concealed their faith from the household of the kingdom. They kept this hidden, and buried the two tablets with them. It is also said, according to one report, that the king came to the mouth of the cave, and that the two of them buried that in the king's building over the cave.

A group related that when the youths departed, the king ordered their traces to be followed, and that the tracking led those who followed them to the mouth of the cave (p-572). The king was informed, so he rode with his soldiers until he stood at it, and ordered them to enter upon them. The men feared that, so one of his viziers said to him: "Are you not, O king, if you bring them out, going to kill them?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then what killing is more severe than hunger and thirst? Wall up the mouth of the cave over them and leave them to die in it." He did so. Allah, exalted is He, had struck upon their ears before that, for what He intended of securing them. The people dated their affair on the two tablets, or the two men dated it, according to the disagreement. The name of one of the two men, as al-Tabari mentioned, was Nidrus, and the name of the other was Ruqqas.

It is related that this king from whose religion the youths fled was one whom Allah had tested the believers with, since he sensed them: he killed them and hung their bodies and heads on the walls of his city, and he wanted to make them abandon — as was mentioned — the religion of 'Isa, peace be upon him. He and his people were of the Romans.

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed about the youths that when they took refuge in the cave, that is, they entered it and made it a shelter for themselves and a place of seclusion, they called upon Allah, exalted is He, to grant them mercy from Him, which is provision, according to what the exegetes mentioned, and to prepare for them right guidance in their affair, that is, a good outcome. Al-Jumhur read "rashadan" with fatha on the ra and the shin. Abu Raja' read "rushdan" with damma on the ra and sukun on the shin. The first is more preferred, due to its resemblance to the verse endings before and after it. This supplication from them concerned the affair of their worldly life, and its wording implies that, though they were confident of the guidance and mercy of the Hereafter.

It is fitting for every believer to make his supplication regarding the affair of his worldly life this verse alone, for it suffices. The mention of mercy may mean matters of the Hereafter. I have abridged this account, and I have not neglected any of its essential points, according to my effort. And Allah is the Helper by His mercy.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: "So We struck upon their ears" — the verse — it is an expression for Allah, exalted is He, casting sleep upon them. This and similar expressions are phrased as "striking" so that the strength of direct action and the intensity of adherence to the matter spoken of and its imposition may become clear. From it comes the striking of humiliation and poverty, and from it the striking of the sending forth (ba'th). And from it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"The spider struck upon you with its web, and the revealed Book decreed against you with it."

This is used for compelling, eloquent necessity.

As for specifying the ears by mention: it is because they are the organ by which sleep is most seriously disrupted; the sleep of a sleeper rarely ends except through his ear, and sleep is not firmly established except with the hearing being inactive. From the mention of the ear in sleep is his saying ﷺ: "That is a man whom Satan urinated into his ear," (ﷺ) indicating a man who slept long and did not rise at night.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: "'adadan" — it is an attribute of "al-sinin" (years), and the intent by it is an expression of multiplicity, meaning: they require a number, and they have a number. Al-Zajjaj said: It is also permissible that the accusative of "'adadan" be a verbal noun (masdar).

"Al-ba'th" means moving after stillness, and this is consistent with the word ba'th wherever it occurs. The stillness may be in the person, or in the matter sent forth, even if the person is moving. His saying, Exalted is He: "li-na'lam" (that We might know) is an expression for that thing coming into existence, and this is in the manner of Arabic speech, meaning: that We might know it existing; otherwise Allah, exalted is He, already knew which of the two parties computed the term. Al-Zuhri read "liya'lam" with ya. "Al-hizbani" means the two groups; the apparent meaning of the verse is that one party is the youths, when they assumed their stay was short, and the second party is the people of the city whom the youths were raised among, at the time when they had the history of the youths' affair. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes. A group said: they are two parties of disbelievers who differed about the duration of the People of the Cave's sleep.

A group said: they are two parties of believers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is not connected to the wording of the verse.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: "ahsa" — the apparent and sound reading is that it is a past-tense verb, and "amadan" is its object in the accusative. "Al-amad" means the limit, and it may be used as an expression for a duration, insofar as a duration has a limit that is its amad in reality. Al-Zajjaj said: "ahsa" is an af'al form, and "amadan" on this view is accusative as a specification. This view is flawed, because af'al does not come from a quadriliteral verb except in rare cases, and "ahsa" is a quadriliteral verb. Abu Ishaq's view is supported by the fact that the af'al form of the quadriliteral is masculine, as in your saying: "ma a'taahu lil-mal and ata-hu lil-khayr," and the Prophet ﷺ said describing Jahannam: "It is blacker than tar," and he said describing his Basin (ﷺ): "whiter than milk," and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "So it is more wasted for other than it." All of these are af'al forms of quadriliteral verbs. Mujahid said: "amadan" means: a limit.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an explanation by meaning, in an approximating way. Al-Tabari said: "amadan" is accusative by "labithu" (they remained), and this is not sound.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verses 13–16:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿We relate to you their story with truth. Indeed, they were youths who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance.﴾ ﴿And We fortified their hearts when they stood up and said: "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We will never invoke any god besides Him; we would have certainly uttered an outrageous lie.﴾ ﴿These, our people, have taken besides Him gods. Why do they not bring for them a clear authority? So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾ ﴿And when you have withdrawn from them and that which they worship other than Allah, then take refuge in the cave; your Lord will spread for you of His mercy and will prepare for you from your affair a provision.﴾

When the saying of the Exalted, ﴿That We may know which of the two parties is most accurate in computing what time they remained﴾ [al-Kahf: 12], required a disagreement that occurred concerning the affair of the youths, He followed it with the report that He, the Exalted and Majestic, knows their affair with the truth that occurred. In the totality of these verses is the answer of the Quraysh to their question, which the Children of Israel had instructed them to ask. And "al-qass" (narration): the reporting of a matter (p-575) that is recounted in sequence, not a speech related piece by piece, because that address was not a narrative. The saying of the Exalted, ﴿And We increased them in guidance﴾, means: We facilitated for them good deeds, devotion to Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, distancing themselves from people, and asceticism in this world. These are increases upon faith.

The saying of the Exalted, ﴿And We fortified their hearts﴾, is an expression for the intensity of resolve and the strength of patience which Allah bestowed upon them. Since fear and the weakening of the soul resemble, by analogy, dissolution, it is fitting that firmness of the soul and strength of resolve be likened to binding (rabt). From this one says: "So-and-so is steadfast of heart (rabit al-ja'sh)" when his soul does not waver in dread, in war, or otherwise. From this is "the binding upon the heart of the mother of Musa." The saying of the Exalted, ﴿when they stood up and said﴾, may bear two meanings. The first is that this describes their standing before the disbelieving king, for it is a station that requires the binding of the heart, since they were summoned before him, opposed his religion, and disregarded his awe for the sake of Allah. The second meaning is that "standing" expresses their rising with resolve to flee to Allah, the Exalted, and to separate from people, just as you say: "So-and-so stood up to such-and-such a matter" when he resolved upon it with utmost earnestness. And with these words, ﴿they stood up and said﴾, the Sufis have held on to the notion of standing (qiyam) and speech (qawl). Al-A'mash recited: "idh qamu qiyaman fa-qalu" (when they stood up a standing and said).

Their saying, ﴿We would have certainly uttered an outrageous lie﴾, meaning: if we were to invoke a god besides our Lord. "Al-shatat" means injustice, transgression of limits, and excess according to the particular matter; from it: "the man exceeded the bounds in bargaining" when he demanded for his goods more than their value; from it: the remoteness and distance of a place; and from it the saying of the poet:

Ah, O my people, my blamers have exceeded the bounds, / and they claim that my falsehood has destroyed my right.

(p-576) The saying of the Exalted, ﴿These, our people﴾, is a statement that may be among what they said in their station before the king, and it is also valid that it be a saying of some of them to others at the time of their standing for the matter upon which they had resolved. Their saying, ﴿Why do they not bring﴾, is an incitement with the meaning of challenge (ta'jiz), since it is an incitement to what is impossible; and if that is not possible for them, it is not necessary to pay attention to their claim. "Al-sultan" means proof, and Qatada said: the meaning is: with a clear excuse.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an expression that is far-reaching (muhallaqah).

Then they magnified the crime of those who invoke gods along with Allah and their injustice, by His saying, in the form of an affirmation: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾

The saying of the Exalted, ﴿And when you have withdrawn from them﴾, etc. If "standing" in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿when they stood up﴾ is resolve, as the single interpretation implies, and "saying" was among them in their private exchange, then this statement may be among their saying that they uttered at their standing. But if the "standing" mentioned refers to their station before the king, then this statement cannot be considered part of "their saying" before the king; rather there would be an ellipsis in the speech, whose estimate is: and some of them said to others.

By this it is preferred that the saying of the Exalted, ﴿when they stood up and said﴾, means only: when they resolved and carried out their affair.

As for the saying of the Exalted, "except Allah": if we suppose that the disbelievers from whom the People of the Cave fled did not know Allah, the Exalted, nor had any knowledge of Him, and believed in divinity only in their idols, then it is an exception that is disjunctive (munqati') and not from the first part. But if we suppose that they knew Allah, the Exalted, and revered Him as the Arabs used to do, yet they associated their idols with Him in worship, then the exception is connected (muttasil), because the withdrawal occurred from everything the disbelievers worship except in the direction of Allah, the Exalted. In the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa ma ya'buduna min dun Allah" (and what they worship besides Allah). Qatada said: this is its explanation. Harun said: in some of his codices: "wa ma ya'buduna min dunina" (and what they worship besides us).

(p-577) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

According to what Qatada said, "illa" is in the position of "ghayr" (other than), and "ma" in His saying, ﴿and what they worship﴾, is in the accusative position, conjoined to the pronoun in "i'tazaltumuhum." The implication of this verse is that some of them said to others: since we have separated from the disbelievers and become solitary with Allah, the Exalted, let us make the cave a refuge and rely upon Allah, the Exalted, for He will spread His mercy over us, unfold it upon us, and prepare for us a provision in our affair. All of this is supplication pertaining to the worldly life, and they were, in their affair of the hereafter, confident in Allah, the Exalted.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited "mirfaqan" with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the fa', which is a verbal noun like "rifq" according to what Abu Zayd related, and this is the reading of Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, and Shayba. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, al-Hasan, Talha, al-A'mash, and Ibn Abi Ishaq recited "mirfaqan" with a kasra on the mim and a fatha on the fa', and both are used for both the matter and the bodily limb, as related by al-Zajjaj. Makki reported from al-Farra' that he said: I know of no form other than kasr of the mim in the matter, in the hand, and in everything. Al-Kisa'i denied that "al-murfaq" could be the bodily limb except with fatha of the mim and kasra of the fa'; Abu Hatim disagreed and said: "al-marfaq" with a fatha on the mim is the place, like "al-masjid." Both, moreover, are dialectal forms.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verses 13–16:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿We relate to you their story with truth. Indeed, they were youths who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance.﴾ ﴿And We fortified their hearts when they stood up and said: "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We will never invoke any god besides Him; we would have certainly uttered an outrageous lie.﴾ ﴿These, our people, have taken besides Him gods. Why do they not bring for them a clear authority? So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾ ﴿And when you have withdrawn from them and that which they worship other than Allah, then take refuge in the cave; your Lord will spread for you of His mercy and will prepare for you from your affair a provision.﴾

When the saying of the Exalted, ﴿That We may know which of the two parties is most accurate in computing what time they remained﴾ [al-Kahf: 12], required a disagreement that occurred concerning the affair of the youths, He followed it with the report that He, the Exalted and Majestic, knows their affair with the truth that occurred. In the totality of these verses is the answer of the Quraysh to their question, which the Children of Israel had instructed them to ask. And "al-qass" (narration): the reporting of a matter (p-575) that is recounted in sequence, not a speech related piece by piece, because that address was not a narrative. The saying of the Exalted, ﴿And We increased them in guidance﴾, means: We facilitated for them good deeds, devotion to Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, distancing themselves from people, and asceticism in this world. These are increases upon faith.

The saying of the Exalted, ﴿And We fortified their hearts﴾, is an expression for the intensity of resolve and the strength of patience which Allah bestowed upon them. Since fear and the weakening of the soul resemble, by analogy, dissolution, it is fitting that firmness of the soul and strength of resolve be likened to binding (rabt). From this one says: "So-and-so is steadfast of heart (rabit al-ja'sh)" when his soul does not waver in dread, in war, or otherwise. From this is "the binding upon the heart of the mother of Musa." The saying of the Exalted, ﴿when they stood up and said﴾, may bear two meanings. The first is that this describes their standing before the disbelieving king, for it is a station that requires the binding of the heart, since they were summoned before him, opposed his religion, and disregarded his awe for the sake of Allah. The second meaning is that "standing" expresses their rising with resolve to flee to Allah, the Exalted, and to separate from people, just as you say: "So-and-so stood up to such-and-such a matter" when he resolved upon it with utmost earnestness. And with these words, ﴿they stood up and said﴾, the Sufis have held on to the notion of standing (qiyam) and speech (qawl). Al-A'mash recited: "idh qamu qiyaman fa-qalu" (when they stood up a standing and said).

Their saying, ﴿We would have certainly uttered an outrageous lie﴾, meaning: if we were to invoke a god besides our Lord. "Al-shatat" means injustice, transgression of limits, and excess according to the particular matter; from it: "the man exceeded the bounds in bargaining" when he demanded for his goods more than their value; from it: the remoteness and distance of a place; and from it the saying of the poet:

Ah, O my people, my blamers have exceeded the bounds, / and they claim that my falsehood has destroyed my right.

(p-576) The saying of the Exalted, ﴿These, our people﴾, is a statement that may be among what they said in their station before the king, and it is also valid that it be a saying of some of them to others at the time of their standing for the matter upon which they had resolved. Their saying, ﴿Why do they not bring﴾, is an incitement with the meaning of challenge (ta'jiz), since it is an incitement to what is impossible; and if that is not possible for them, it is not necessary to pay attention to their claim. "Al-sultan" means proof, and Qatada said: the meaning is: with a clear excuse.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an expression that is far-reaching (muhallaqah).

Then they magnified the crime of those who invoke gods along with Allah and their injustice, by His saying, in the form of an affirmation: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾

The saying of the Exalted, ﴿And when you have withdrawn from them﴾, etc. If "standing" in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿when they stood up﴾ is resolve, as the single interpretation implies, and "saying" was among them in their private exchange, then this statement may be among their saying that they uttered at their standing. But if the "standing" mentioned refers to their station before the king, then this statement cannot be considered part of "their saying" before the king; rather there would be an ellipsis in the speech, whose estimate is: and some of them said to others.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verse 17–18:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And you would see the sun, when it rose, inclining away from their cave to the right, and when it set, passing them on the left, while they were in a wide space within it. That is of the signs of Allah. Whomever Allah guides is the one guided; but for whomever He leaves astray, you will not find for him a guiding ally.﴾ ﴿And you would think them awake, while they were asleep. And We turned them to the right and to the left, while their dog stretched out its forelegs at the threshold. If you had looked at them, you would have turned away from them in flight and been filled with terror of them.﴾

Between these two verses there is an omission (iqtiḍāb) which is clarified by what preceded of the verses, and its implied meaning is: "So they took shelter, and Allah sealed their ears, and they remained thus."

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu 'Amr read "tazzāwaru" (تَزّاوَرُ) with a shaddah on the zay and idghām of the tā'. 'Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "tazāwaru" (تَزاوَرُ) with its lightening, on the assumption of "tatazāwaru," so one of the two tā's was dropped. Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Qatada read "tazwarru" (تَزْوَرُّ) in the pattern of "taḥmarru." Al-Jahdari and Abu Raja' read "tazwārru" (تَزْوارُّ) with an alif after the waw. The meaning of the word under all these forms is: it turns aside, swerves, and inclines. These are the expressions of the exegetes. As for al-Akhfash, he said: "Tazwarru" means it contracts; al-zawr is inclination, and al-azwar in the eye is one whose gaze is inclined toward a side; it is used for other than the eye, as in the saying of Ibn Abi Rabi'a:

"My side, out of fear of the people, is inclined (azwar)."

From the same root is the saying of 'Antara:

"He turned aside (fazwarra) from the impact of the spears upon his chest."

And from it is the saying of Bishr ibn Abi Hazim:

"The guides bring her toward the waters of a palm grove, and in her there is a deviation (izwirār) away from the two Abanayn."

In the hadith of the battle of Mu'ta, the Prophet (ﷺ) saw on the bed of 'Abdullah ibn Rawaha a deviation (izwirār) away from the beds of Ja'far and Zayd ibn Haritha.

The majority read "taqriḍuhum" (تَقْرِضُهُمْ) with the tā', and a group read "yaqriḍuhum" (يَقْرِضُهُمْ) with the yā', meaning the cave, as if it were from al-qarḍ, which is cutting; that is, the cave cuts them off from the sunlight with its shade. As for the majority who read with the tā', the meaning is that no sun at all would reach them, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both. They interpret "taqriḍuhum" as meaning "leaves them," that is, it is as if the sun, in relation to them, cuts off everything that does not reach it from itself. A group among those who read with the tā' interpreted that it would reach them in the evening, so that it "cuts" them, that is, separates them from what it does not reach, and they said: in its touching them in the evening there was benefit for their bodies. Al-Tabari related that the Arabs say: "I cut (qaraḍtu) the place of such-and-such," meaning I crossed it, and from it is the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"Toward caravans that cut through the open tracts of the high ground, leftward, and on their right the horsemen."

And from it: "Lend me (aqriḍnī) a dirham," meaning: cut it for me from your wealth. This attribute together with the sun requires that they had a screen on the south side and a screen on the dabur side, and they were in its corner. Al-Zajjaj and others related, saying: the entrance of the cave faced the Bananat Na'sh, and 'Abdullah ibn Muslim said this, and this is close to what we have said, except that the upper part of the cave was covered against rain. Al-Zajjaj went to the view that the action of the sun was a sign from Allah, the Exalted, without the entrance of the cave being toward a direction that would necessitate this.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿to the right﴾ ﴿and to the left﴾ may mean: to the right of the cave, by imagining the entrance of the cave as the face of a man, for the sun comes from it at the start of the day to the right, and at its end to the left. It may also mean: to the right of the sun and its left, by imagining the ray extending from it to the cave as the face of a man. The first aspect is clearer.

And "al-fajwa" is the open space; its plural is fijā'. Qatada said: "in a space from it." From it is the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to travel at a fast pace, and when he found an open space, he hastened." Ibn Jubayr said: ﴿in a space from it﴾: in a place inside.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is of the signs of Allah﴾: the reference is to the matter in its entirety, and according to al-Zajjaj's view that "the sun was turning aside and cutting without a screen," the reference is to this meaning specifically. Then it continues with the glorification of Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, and submission to Him, and what requires directing hopes to Him.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you would think them awake, while they were asleep﴾, the verse. It is a descriptive circumstance (ṣifat ḥāl) that has passed, and its verbs came in the future form as a figure of speech and expansion.

"Ayqāẓan" is the plural of yaqiẓ, like 'aḍud and a'ḍād, and it means awake. The people of tafsir said: their eyes were open while they were sleeping, so the onlooker would think them awake.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also possible that the onlooker would think that because of the strength of the preservation upon them and the scarcity of change. The usual state of sleepers is relaxation and postures that suggest sleep, but a sleeper may be in states that have not changed from the state of wakefulness, so the onlooker thinks him awake even if his eyes are closed. Had the opening of their eyes been established by a chain that removes the excuse, it would have been clearer for the onlooker to think them awake.

The majority read "wa-nuqallibuhum" (وَنُقَلِّبُهُمْ) with the plural of majesty. Al-Hasan read "wa-taqallubuhum" (وَتَقَلُّبُهُمْ) with an open tā' and a damma on the lām and the bā', and it is a verbal noun raised as subject, as said by Abu Hatim. Ibn Jinni related the reading from al-Hasan with a fatha on the tā', damma on the lām, and fatha on the bā', and said: this is in the accusative by an implied verb, as if he said: "And you see," or "you witness their turning."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Abu Hatim is more firmly established.

A group held that the turning is the reason why the onlooker thought them awake. Although turning for one who happens to see them is evidence of this, the wording of the verse did not convey it except as a new report. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, said: this turning happened twice a year. Another group said: every year once. Another group said: every seven years once. Another group said: they were turned only in the last nine, but not in the three hundred. Some exegetes mentioned that their turning was only for protection from the earth, and it is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, that he said: "If the sun had touched them, it would have burned them, and had it not been for the turning, the earth would have consumed them."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The sign of Allah, the Exalted, in their sleep for this long period and their living without nourishment is more remarkable in strangeness than their preservation alongside the touch of the sun and the adherence to the earth. But these are reports that differ and require further reflection. The apparent sense of the words of the exegetes is that the turning was by the command of Allah, the Exalted, and the action of His angels. It is possible that it was by Allah's enabling them to do so while they were in the depths of sleep, not waking, as happens to many sleepers, because these people were not dead.

His saying, the Exalted: "wa-kalbuhum." Most exegetes hold that it was a dog in the literal sense, which, as is related, was for the hunting of one of them. It was said: it belonged to a shepherd who passed by them, and accompanied them, and the dog followed him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

My father, may Allah be pleased with him, related to me, saying: I heard Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari in the mosque of Egypt saying from the pulpit of his preaching, in the year four hundred and sixty-nine: "Whoever loves the people of goodness obtains a share of their blessing. A dog loved the people of virtue and accompanied them, so Allah, the Exalted, mentioned it in His well-protected revelation." It was said: it was spotted; it was said: it was red. A group said: it was a cook for them; al-Tabari related it without naming its speaker. A group said: it was one of them, who had sat at the entrance of the cave as a lookout for them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He was named with the name of the animal that stays with that place among people, just as the star that follows al-Jawza' is called a dog, because it is to it as the dog is to the human. It is also called "the dog of the Giant" (Kalb al-Jabbar). As for the claim that this view is weakened by the mention of the stretching of the forelegs, these are in common usage an attribute of the dog in reality, and from it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Let none of you stretch his forelegs in prostration like the stretching of the dog." Abu 'Umar al-Mutarriz related in the book al-Yawaqit that it was read: "wa-kalibuhum bāsiṭun dhirā'ayhi" (وَكالِبُهم باسِطٌ ذِراعَيْهِ), so it is possible that by "al-kalib" he meant this man, according to what was related, since stretching the forelegs and lying flat on the ground while raising the face to look out is the posture of the sentry who hides himself. It is also possible that by "al-kalib" he meant the dog. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿stretching out its forelegs﴾ uses the active participle in the sense of the past, because it is a narration, and it does not intend to report the action of the dog.

"Al-waṣīd" is the threshold that is for the cave's entrance, or its place where it is not; Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Jubayr said: al-waṣīd is the courtyard. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, also said: al-waṣīd is the door; Ibn Jubayr also said: al-waṣīd is the dust. The first view is more correct, and "al-bāb al-mūṣad" is the closed door, that is: it stood at its threshold.

Then Allah, the Exalted, mentioned the terror that surrounded them and the awe that enveloped them. The majority of readers read "law iṭṭala'ta" (لَوِ اطَّلَعْتَ) with a kasra on the waw. Al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read "lawu iṭṭala'ta" (لَوُ اطَّلَعْتَ) with a damma. This has been related from Nafi', Shayba, and Abu Ja'far. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, and the people of Mecca and Medina read "lamullioat" (لَمُلِّئَتْ) with a shaddah on the lām, in the intensive doubling, meaning: it was filled and then filled again. The rest read "lamulī'at" (لَمُلِئَتْ) with the lām lightened, and the lightening is more common in the language. The heavier form occurs in the saying of al-Mukhabbal al-Sa'di:

"When al-Nu'man slew the people while in a state of sanctity, then it was filled from Ka'b ibn 'Awf with its chains."

A group said: this terror overwhelmed them because of the length of their hair and nails, mentioned by al-Mahdawi and al-Zajjaj. This view is far-fetched, for if their condition had been like this, they would not have said: ﴿We have remained a day or part of a day﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. Rather, the correct view regarding their state is that Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, preserved for them the condition in which they stood up, so that it would be a sign for them and for others concerning them. Thus no garment of theirs decayed, no attribute changed, and the one who rose to the city noticed nothing except the landmarks of the land and the buildings. Had there been in their persons a condition that would have been disapproved, it would have been of greater concern to him, and it would have been reported.

It may also mean: to the right of the sun and its left, by imagining the ray extending from it to the cave as the face of a man. The first aspect is clearer.
