His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is of the signs of Allah﴾: the reference is to the matter in its entirety, and according to al-Zajjaj's view that "the sun was turning aside and cutting without a screen," the reference is to this meaning specifically. Then it continues with the glorification of Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, and submission to Him, and what requires directing hopes to Him.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you would think them awake, while they were asleep﴾, the verse. It is a descriptive circumstance (ṣifat ḥāl) that has passed, and its verbs came in the future form as a figure of speech and expansion.

"Ayqāẓan" is the plural of yaqiẓ, like 'aḍud and a'ḍād, and it means awake. The people of tafsir said: their eyes were open while they were sleeping, so the onlooker would think them awake.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also possible that the onlooker would think that because of the strength of the preservation upon them and the scarcity of change. The usual state of sleepers is relaxation and postures that suggest sleep, but a sleeper may be in states that have not changed from the state of wakefulness, so the onlooker thinks him awake even if his eyes are closed. Had the opening of their eyes been established by a chain that removes the excuse, it would have been clearer for the onlooker to think them awake.

The majority read "wa-nuqallibuhum" (وَنُقَلِّبُهُمْ) with the plural of majesty. Al-Hasan read "wa-taqallubuhum" (وَتَقَلُّبُهُمْ) with an open tā' and a damma on the lām and the bā', and it is a verbal noun raised as subject, as said by Abu Hatim. Ibn Jinni related the reading from al-Hasan with a fatha on the tā', damma on the lām, and fatha on the bā', and said: this is in the accusative by an implied verb, as if he said: "And you see," or "you witness their turning."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Abu Hatim is more firmly established.

A group held that the turning is the reason why the onlooker thought them awake. Although turning for one who happens to see them is evidence of this, the wording of the verse did not convey it except as a new report. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, said: this turning happened twice a year. Another group said: every year once. Another group said: every seven years once. Another group said: they were turned only in the last nine, but not in the three hundred. Some exegetes mentioned that their turning was only for protection from the earth, and it is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, that he said: "If the sun had touched them, it would have burned them, and had it not been for the turning, the earth would have consumed them."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The sign of Allah, the Exalted, in their sleep for this long period and their living without nourishment is more remarkable in strangeness than their preservation alongside the touch of the sun and the adherence to the earth. But these are reports that differ and require further reflection. The apparent sense of the words of the exegetes is that the turning was by the command of Allah, the Exalted, and the action of His angels. It is possible that it was by Allah's enabling them to do so while they were in the depths of sleep, not waking, as happens to many sleepers, because these people were not dead.

His saying, the Exalted: "wa-kalbuhum." Most exegetes hold that it was a dog in the literal sense, which, as is related, was for the hunting of one of them. It was said: it belonged to a shepherd who passed by them, and accompanied them, and the dog followed him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

My father, may Allah be pleased with him, related to me, saying: I heard Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari in the mosque of Egypt saying from the pulpit of his preaching, in the year four hundred and sixty-nine: "Whoever loves the people of goodness obtains a share of their blessing. A dog loved the people of virtue and accompanied them, so Allah, the Exalted, mentioned it in His well-protected revelation." It was said: it was spotted; it was said: it was red. A group said: it was a cook for them; al-Tabari related it without naming its speaker. A group said: it was one of them, who had sat at the entrance of the cave as a lookout for them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He was named with the name of the animal that stays with that place among people, just as the star that follows al-Jawza' is called a dog, because it is to it as the dog is to the human. It is also called "the dog of the Giant" (Kalb al-Jabbar). As for the claim that this view is weakened by the mention of the stretching of the forelegs, these are in common usage an attribute of the dog in reality, and from it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Let none of you stretch his forelegs in prostration like the stretching of the dog." Abu 'Umar al-Mutarriz related in the book al-Yawaqit that it was read: "wa-kalibuhum bāsiṭun dhirā'ayhi" (وَكالِبُهم باسِطٌ ذِراعَيْهِ), so it is possible that by "al-kalib" he meant this man, according to what was related, since stretching the forelegs and lying flat on the ground while raising the face to look out is the posture of the sentry who hides himself. It is also possible that by "al-kalib" he meant the dog. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿stretching out its forelegs﴾ uses the active participle in the sense of the past, because it is a narration, and it does not intend to report the action of the dog.

"Al-waṣīd" is the threshold that is for the cave's entrance, or its place where it is not; Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Jubayr said: al-waṣīd is the courtyard. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, also said: al-waṣīd is the door; Ibn Jubayr also said: al-waṣīd is the dust. The first view is more correct, and "al-bāb al-mūṣad" is the closed door, that is: it stood at its threshold.

Then Allah, the Exalted, mentioned the terror that surrounded them and the awe that enveloped them. The majority of readers read "law iṭṭala'ta" (لَوِ اطَّلَعْتَ) with a kasra on the waw. Al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read "lawu iṭṭala'ta" (لَوُ اطَّلَعْتَ) with a damma. This has been related from Nafi', Shayba, and Abu Ja'far. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, and the people of Mecca and Medina read "lamullioat" (لَمُلِّئَتْ) with a shaddah on the lām, in the intensive doubling, meaning: it was filled and then filled again. The rest read "lamulī'at" (لَمُلِئَتْ) with the lām lightened, and the lightening is more common in the language. The heavier form occurs in the saying of al-Mukhabbal al-Sa'di:

"When al-Nu'man slew the people while in a state of sanctity, then it was filled from Ka'b ibn 'Awf with its chains."

A group said: this terror overwhelmed them because of the length of their hair and nails, mentioned by al-Mahdawi and al-Zajjaj. This view is far-fetched, for if their condition had been like this, they would not have said: ﴿We have remained a day or part of a day﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. Rather, the correct view regarding their state is that Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, preserved for them the condition in which they stood up, so that it would be a sign for them and for others concerning them. Thus no garment of theirs decayed, no attribute changed, and the one who rose to the city noticed nothing except the landmarks of the land and the buildings. Had there been in their persons a condition that would have been disapproved, it would have been of greater concern to him, and it would have been reported.

The majority read "ru'ban" (رُعْبًا) with a sukun on the 'ayn, while Abu Ja'far and 'Isa read "ru'uban" (رُعُبًا) with a damma. Abu Hatim said: both are dialects.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verse 19–20:

Allah, the Exalted, says:

﴿And thus We roused them, that they might question one another. A speaker among them said, "How long have you remained?" They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day." They said, "Your Lord knows best how long you have remained. So send one of you with this silver coin of yours to the city, and let him see which of its food is purest, and bring you provision from it. And let him be considerate, and let him not make anyone aware of you."﴾ ﴿Indeed, if they gain the upper hand over you, they will stone you or return you to their religion, and then you will never succeed.﴾

The reference of "that" (dhalika) is to the matter which Allah mentioned concerning them and the lesson that was made in them. "Al-ba'th" (rousing) means moving something out of stillness. The lam in His words, may He be blessed and exalted, "li-yatasa'alu" (that they might question one another) is the lam of consequence (lam al-sayrura), because their being roused was not for the sake of their questioning itself. The saying of the speaker, "How long have you remained?", implies that it occurred to his mind that they had slept for a long time, and he sensed that their condition had departed somewhat from the customary course. The apparent matter is that they awoke in a state of the time and the air of the season not different from that in which they had slept. As for determining the matter precisely, that is far-fetched.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read "bi-warqikum" (with the ra' vowelled with kasra). Abu 'Amr, Hamza and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "bi-warqikum" (with the ra' sukun). Both are dialectal variants. al-Zajjaj related the reading "bi-wirqikum" (with kasra on the waw and sukun on the ra', without idgham). It is related from Abu 'Amr that he used idgham, but in fact it is ikhfa' (concealment), because idgham with a sukun on the ra' is impracticable. Ibn Muhaysin made idgham of the qaf into the kaf. Abu Hatim said: that is only permissible with the ra' vowelled. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, read "bawariqikum", a collective noun like "al-ja'il" and "al-baqir". Abu Raja' read "bi-wiriqikum" with kasra on the waw and the ra' and idgham.

It is narrated that they awoke at times, and that the one sent was Tamlikha. It is also narrated that they slept one night only and sent Tamlikha on its morning.

It is narrated that the door of the cave had collapsed, the building of the unbelievers from it having been destroyed due to the length of the years. It is narrated that a shepherd demolished it in order to bring his flock into it. Tamlikha took tattered, unfamiliar garments and wore them, and went out of the cave. He denied that building which was demolished, since he did not recognise it the day before. Then he walked, beginning to recall the road and the landmarks, and being bewildered, while in that he did not fully perceive, but rather belied his assumption concerning what had changed for him, until he reached the gate of the city. He saw upon its gate the sign of Islam, and his bewilderment increased, and he said: "How is this, in the city of Daqnyus, when yesterday we were with him wherever we were?" So he went to another gate and saw something similar, until he had walked past all the gates, and his bewilderment increased, and he did not distinguish any person. He heard people swearing by the name of Jesus, so he became suspicious of himself and thought that he had gone mad and his mind had been corrupted. He remained bewildered, calling upon Allah, the Exalted. Then he went to the food seller whom he intended to buy from, and said: "O servant of Allah, sell me some of your food for this silver." He gave him dirhams like the flaps of a rabbit (ar-rab'), as it is mentioned, and the seller was amazed at them and passed them on to another out of his amazement, and people handled them and said to him: "These are dirhams of the reign of such-and-such king. From where are you? And how did you find this treasure?" So he began to be dumbfounded and amazed, and he and his young companions had been well known in the town. He said: "I know nothing except that I and my companions went out yesterday from this city." The people said: "This is a madman. Take him to the king." At that he was terrified, and he was taken until he was brought before the king. When he did not see Daqnyus the unbeliever, he was reassured. That king was a believing, virtuous man named Tayrusis. The king said to him: "Where did you find this treasure?" He said: "I and my companions only went out yesterday from this city, and we took refuge in the cave on the mountain of Anjilus." When the king heard that, he said (in some of what is related): "Perhaps Allah has sent you, O people, a sign. Let us go to the cave with him until we see his companions," and he went. It is narrated that he, or one of his companions, said: "These are the young men whose history was dated in the era of King Daqnyus and written on the copper tablet at the gate of the city." So the king went to them, and the people went with him. When they reached the cave, Tamlikha said: "Let me enter upon them, lest they be frightened." He entered upon them and informed them of the matter, and that the nation was a nation of Islam. It is narrated that they rejoiced, went out to the king, honoured him, and he honoured them. Then they returned to their cave. Most of the narrations hold that they died at the place where Tamlikha spoke to them. The people waited for them, and when their coming out was delayed, the people entered upon them, and each one who entered was terrified. Then they advanced and found them dead, and they disputed, according to what comes in the verse after this one.

In this narrative there is such variety of narrations and wordings that the pages would be too narrow for it. So I have abridged it, and mentioned the important part by which the words of this verse are explained, and I have relied upon the most sound. And Allah is the Helper by His mercy.

In this sending with the silver is the agency (wikala) and its validity. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, appointed his brother 'Aqil as agent before 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with them.

The majority read "fa-l-yanzur" with the lam of the imperative sukun. al-Hasan read "fa-li-yanzur" with kasra. "Azka" means, as mentioned by 'Ikrima, "more"; Qatada said its meaning is "better"; Muqatil said the intended meaning is "more pure"; Ibn Jubayr said the intended meaning is "more lawful."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It concerns the slaughter of unbelievers and other matters. It is narrated that he intended to buy raisins; it was also said: rather, dates.

His saying, exalted is He: "wa-l-yatalattaf," i.e., in his concealment and his stratagem. al-Hasan read "wa-liyatalattaf" with kasra on the lam.

The pronoun in "innahum" refers to the unbelievers, the family of Daqnyus. "in yazhharu" means: they will overcome you by their superiority and dominance. His saying, exalted is He: "yarjumukum" — al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: with stones.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the most sound, because he was determined to kill them if he got hold of them. Stoning, as was mentioned in earlier times, was the execution of one who opposed the religion of the people, as it is most effective in punishing the adherents of that religion, and they share in it. Hajjaj said: "yarjumukum" means verbally. The rest of the verse is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verse 21:

His the Mighty and Majestic's saying:

﴿And thus did We cause them to be found, that they might know that the promise of God is true, and that the Hour, there is no doubt about it, when they disputed among themselves their affair. And they said: Build over them a structure; their Lord knows best about them. Those who prevailed over their affair said: Indeed we will take over them a place of worship.﴾

The reference of "that" (dhalika) in His saying, "And thus" (wa-kadhalika), is to their being raised up so that they might question one another; that is, just as We raised them, We caused them to be found.

"A'thara" is the causative form of "athara" (to stumble upon), and the root meaning of 'ithar is in the foot. Since the one who stumbles upon a thing resembles it, the term was applied to it, by way of likening the knowledge of a thing that comes to mind and surfaces after being hidden to that stumbling. The pronoun in "li-ya'lamu" (that they might know) may refer to the Muslim community in whose era the People of the Cave were raised; this is the view of al-Tabari. This is because, as it is related, a trial then befell them concerning the matter of the Gathering and the resurrection of bodies from the graves, so some people doubted this and considered it unlikely, saying: only spirits are gathered. This distressed their king, and he remained bewildered, not knowing how to make the matter clear to them, until he put on sackcloth, sat in ashes, and humbly implored God for proof and clarification. So God caused the People of the Cave to be found. When God raised them up and the people became clear about their affair, the king rejoiced, and those who had doubted the resurrection of bodies returned to certainty about it. It is to this that the reference in His saying "when they disputed among themselves their affair" points, on this interpretation. It is possible that "idh" (when) is governed, on this interpretation, by "a'tharna" (We caused them to be found), and it is possible that it is governed by "li-ya'lamu" (that they might know).

The pronoun in His saying "li-ya'lamu" may refer to the People of the Cave; that is, God the Exalted makes their affair a sign to them indicating the resurrection of bodies from the graves. His saying "when they disputed" (idh yatanazi'una), on this interpretation, is a fresh report about the people who were raised in their era, and the governing element of "idh" is an implied verb whose estimate is: "and remember" (wa-dhkur). It is possible that "fa-qalu" (then they said) governs it, and the meaning would be: they said, when they disputed: "Build over them." The disputing, on this interpretation, is only about the matter of the building and the place of worship, not about the matter of the Resurrection. "Al-raib" means doubt, and the meaning is that the Hour in itself and in its reality has no doubt about it; and even if doubt has befallen some people, that does not affect it at all. It has been said that the disputing was only about their having been discovered: some said they were dead, and some said they were alive. It is related that some of the people wanted to bury the cave over them and leave them concealed within it, but the party that prevailed in the matter said: "Indeed we will take over them a place of worship," and they took it. Qatada said: "Those who prevailed were the rulers." Al-Hasan and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read "ghuliba" (were overcome) with a damma on the ghayn and a kasra on the lam. The meaning is that the party that called for the building intended to build a church or a place of worship for their unbelief, and the believers opposed them and said: "Indeed we will take over them a place of worship." It is related from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr that God obscured their affair from the people at that time and veiled it from them, and for this reason he called for the building of a structure so that it would be a landmark for them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verse 22–24:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿They will say, "They were three, the fourth of them their dog," and they will say, "They were five, the sixth of them their dog," guessing at the unseen. And they will say, "They were seven, and the eighth of them their dog." Say, "My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few. So do not argue concerning them except with an apparent argument, and do not consult any of them about them."﴾ ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,"﴾ ﴿unless [you add], "If God wills." And remember your Lord when you forget, and say, "I hope that my Lord will guide me to what is nearer to right guidance than this."﴾

The pronoun in His saying, "They will say," refers to the People of the Book among the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ), because they disagreed about the number of the People of the Cave with this explicitly reported disagreement.

Al-Jumhur read "thalathatun" (thalāthatun), and Ibn Muhaysin read "thalathun" with the assimilation of the tā' into the thā'. Shibl, from Ibn Kathir, read "khamsata" with a fatha on the mīm, following "'ashara" (ʿashara). Ibn Muhaysin read "khimisah" with a kasra on the khā' and the mīm.

His saying, ﴿rajman bil-ghayb﴾ (rajman bil-ghayb), its meaning is: conjecture. It is a metaphor derived from *rajm* (stoning, casting), as if a person throws at the problematic, unknown place in his understanding with his conjecture, time after time, casting at it, hoping to hit it. From this comes *al-turjuman* (the interpreter/translator), and *tarjamat al-kitab* (the translation of a book). And from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

> And war is nothing but what you have known and tasted,
> and it is not by the speech of conjecture concerning it.

Al-Tabari and others said: Ibn 'Abbas only meant that it benefits in making the swearer in the rank of those who made the exception after a year from his oath, but the expiation does not fall from him. Al-Tabari said: I do not know anyone who says (the exception benefits after a period) and says the expiation falls. He said: this is refuted by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever swears an oath, then sees something better than it, let him expiate and let him do that which is better." So if the exception cancelled the expiation, it would be lighter upon the community, and mention of the expiation would have no benefit.

Al-Zahrawi said: Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, only spoke of the exception after a year for one who said "I will do such and such," not for a swearer who wanted to dissolve his oath.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

A group of jurists went to the view that the position of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, is the falling of the expiation, and they obliged everyone who says (the exception benefits after a period) to hold that the expiation falls, and they refuted the view on the basis of this obligation. The exception is only in an oath by God; it does not occur in divorce or the like, nor in walking to Mecca. This is the view of Malik and a group.

Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, and the companions of opinion (ahl al-ra'y), and Tawus and Hammad said: the exception in that is permissible, and there is no exception that benefits in the perjurous oath (al-yamin al-ghamus), and the exception is not by the heart, but must be speech and utterance.

His saying, ﴿And say, "I hope that my Lord will guide me"﴾ and so on. Muhammad al-Kufi, the exegete, said: these words are among what every one who did not make the exception was commanded to say, and it is an expiation for forgetting the exception. The majority said: it is a supplication commanded without this specification.

al-Jumhur read "yahdinī" with the yā' affirmed, and this is the reading of Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu 'Amr. Talhah ibn Musarrif read "yahdin" without a yā' in pausal/connected reading, and this is the reading of Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i.

The indication by "hadha" (this) is to the correction that occurs to one who forgot the exception. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "perhaps God will facilitate, from the proofs of my prophethood, something nearer than the proof of the People of the Cave."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

What I have put forward is more correct, that is: perhaps He will guide me in what lies ahead of my affair. This verse addresses the Prophet (ﷺ), and it further encompasses his whole community, because it is a ruling that people often encounter. And God is the Granter of success.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verse 25–27:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine.﴾ ﴿Say, "Allah is most knowing of how long they remained. To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. How clearly He sees and hears. They have no protector other than Him, and He does not share His command with anyone."﴾ ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord; there is no changer of His words, and you will not find other than Him a refuge.﴾

Qatada, Mutar al-Warraq, and others said: "﴿And they remained in their cave﴾ [up to] the verse is a report about the Children of Israel, that they said that. They argued that the reading of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and in his codex, is: 'And they said, They remained in their cave.' And this, according to Qatada, apart from the reading of 'Abdullah, is a conjunction with ﴿They will say, 'They were three'﴾ [al-Kahf: 22]." This was mentioned by al-Zahrawi.

Then Allah, the Exalted, commanded His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to refer the knowledge of this to Him, as a response to their statement and a refutation of them. Al-Tabari said: "Some of them said: If that were a report from Allah, there would be no comprehensible meaning to His saying: ﴿Say, 'Allah is most knowing of how long they remained.'﴾"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Where has this speaker gone? What is the clear and comprehensible meaning, other than that the verse is a report about their remaining, and then it was said to Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿Say, "Allah is most knowing of how long they remained,"⁠﴾ by His information? This is the truth from the realm of the unseen, so let your disagreement cease, you conjecturers.

The verifiers (al-Muhaqqiqun) said: Rather, His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And they remained in their cave﴾ [up to] the verse is a report from Allah, the Exalted, about the duration of their remaining. Then they differed concerning the meaning of His saying after the report: ﴿Say, "Allah is most knowing of how long they remained."⁠﴾ Al-Tabari said: The Children of Israel differed about the period that passed for them after they were discovered, up to the time of the Prophet ﷺ. Some of them said: They remained three hundred and nine years, and Allah, the Exalted, informed His Prophet that this period was their being asleep, and that what came after that is unknown to humans, so Allah, the Exalted, commanded him to refer the knowledge of that to Him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So His saying, the Exalted, on this interpretation: "they remained" the first means: in the sleep of the cave; and "they remained" the second means: after being discovered, dead, up to the period of Muhammad ﷺ, or up to the time of their being worn away by decay, according to the difference that we will mention later. Some said: When He said: ﴿and added nine﴾, people did not know whether they were hours, or days, or weeks, or months, or years, and the Children of Israel differed according to that. So Allah, the Exalted, commanded him to refer the knowledge of it to Him, meaning: regarding the nine, so these, according to this, are unspecified.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent sense of Arabic speech, and what is understood from it, is that they are years. The apparent indication of their situation is that they stood up and entered the cave shortly after 'Isa, peace be upon him, and some of the disciples (al-Hawariyyun) still remained. Al-Naqqash related what means that they remained three hundred solar years according to the reckoning of the nations, so when the information here is for the Arab Prophet ﷺ, the nine were mentioned, since what is understood by him of years is lunar years; so this addition is the difference between the two reckonings.

The majority read: "thalatha mi'atin sinin" with tanwin on "mi'atin" and the accusative on "sinin," as a substitute (badal) for "thalatha mi'atin" or as an explanatory apposition ('atf al-bayan); it was said: as a specification (tafsir) and a tamyiz. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Yahya, Talha, and al-A'mash read with the "mi'at" put in genitive construction with "sinin" and without tanwin, and it is as if they treated "sinin" as equivalent to "sanatin," since the meaning of both is one. Abu 'Ali said: these numbers, in which the hundreds are attached to singulars, such as "thalathu mi'at rajul" or "thawb," are sometimes attached to plurals. Abu Hatim criticised this reading. In the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "thalathi mi'at sanah." Al-Dahhak read: "thalathi mi'at sunun," with a waw. Abu 'Amr, with a variant, read: "tis'an" with a fatha on the ta', and the majority read: "tis'an" with a kasra on the ta'.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿How clearly He sees and hears﴾, that is: how seeing and hearing He is. Qatada said: no one sees more than Allah, the Exalted, nor hears more.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These are expressions for perception. It is possible that the meaning is: ﴿How clearly He sees﴾, that is: by His revelation and His guidance, your guidance and your proofs and the truth of matters, and "hears" by it the world; so these two would be two commands, not in the form of exclamation. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿They have no protector other than Him﴾ may have the pronoun in "lahum" refer to the People of the Cave, meaning: this is His power alone; no one else has befriended them with kindness, nor has anyone shared with Him in this judgment. It is also possible that the pronoun in "lahum" refers to the disbelieving contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his opponents, and the verse would be a parenthetical threat.

The majority read: "wa la yushraku fi hukmihi ahadan" with the ya' below, as a report about Allah, blessed and exalted. Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatada, and al-Jahdari read: "wa la tushrik" with the ta' above, as a prohibition to the Prophet ﷺ, and his saying "wa la tushrik" would be conjoined with His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿How clearly He sees and hears﴾. Mujahid read: "wa la yushrik" with the ya' below and jussive, Ya'qub said: I do not know its justification.

Al-Tabari related from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim that he said: this verse was revealed: ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred﴾ only. The people said: are they months or days or years? Then it was revealed: ﴿years and they added nine﴾.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As for whether the People of the Cave lasted and their bodies remained preserved after death, the reports differ on this. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he passed through al-Sham on one of his campaigns with people, by the site of the cave and its mountain, and the people walked to it and found bones. They said: these are the bones of the People of the Cave. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said to them: No, those are people who perished and were destroyed a long time ago. A monk heard him and said: I did not think that any of the Arabs knew this. He was told: this is the cousin of our Prophet ﷺ. A group said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "'Isa ibn Maryam will certainly perform Hajj, and with him the People of the Cave, for they have not yet performed Hajj."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In al-Sham, according to what I have heard from many people, there is a cave in which there are dead bodies, which its residents claim are the People of the Cave, and over them is a mosque and a building called al-Raqim, and with them is a dog, a mere skeleton. In al-Andalus, in the direction of Gharnata near a village called Lushah, there is a cave in which there are dead bodies, and with them is a dog, a mere skeleton, and most of them have had their flesh stripped away, and some are still held together. The former generations have passed and we have found no knowledge of their matter to excite us. Some people claim that they are the People of the Cave. I entered to them and saw them in the year five hundred and four, in this state, and over them is a mosque, and near them is a Roman building called al-Raqim on the side of the qiblah, and traces of an ancient Roman city called the city of Diqnayus, in whose remains we found wonders in graves and the like.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I have only ventured to mention this despite its remoteness because it is a wonder whose mention will endure, if Allah, Mighty and Majestic, wills.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you﴾ [up to] the verse. Whoever read: "wa la tushrik" as a prohibition conjoined "wa-tlu" to it, and whoever read: "wa la yushriku" made this a command with which another speech begins, not part of the first. It is as if this verse carries the sense of a rebuke to the Prophet ﷺ, following the rebuke concerning his leaving out the exception, as if He were saying: these are the answers to the questions, so recite the revelation of Allah to you, that is: follow it in your deeds. It was also said: recite, by your recitation, what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord; there is no deficiency in His word, and no changer of His words, and you have no other side that you can incline to and lean upon.

"Al-multahad" is the side to which one inclines; from it comes "al-lahd" (the niche in a grave), as if it were the inclination in one of the two sides of the grave; and from it comes "al-ilhad fi al-haqq" (deviation regarding the truth), which is deviation from the truth. The matter of abrogation (naskh) does not undermine His saying: ﴿there is no changer of His words﴾, because the meaning is either: there is no changer other than Him, so the words remain in their absoluteness; or He intended by "words" the report and the like, which abrogation does not enter. The consensus is that what is not changed is the speech subsisting in His essence, according to which decree proceeds. As for revealed books, the position of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is that they are not changed except through interpretation (ta'wil). Among the scholars there are those who say that the Children of Israel altered the wording of the Torah.

Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatada, and al-Jahdari read: "wa la tushrik" with the ta' above, as a prohibition to the Prophet ﷺ, and his saying "wa la tushrik" would be conjoined with His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿How clearly He sees and hears﴾. Mujahid read: "wa la yushrik" with the ya' below and jussive, Ya'qub said: I do not know its justification.

Al-Tabari related from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim that he said: this verse was revealed: ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred﴾ only. The people said: are they months or days or years? Then it was revealed: ﴿years and they added nine﴾.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As for whether the People of the Cave lasted and their bodies remained preserved after death, the reports differ on this. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he passed through al-Sham on one of his campaigns with people, by the site of the cave and its mountain, and the people walked to it and found bones. They said: these are the bones of the People of the Cave. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said to them: No, those are people who perished and were destroyed a long time ago. A monk heard him and said: I did not think that any of the Arabs knew this. He was told: this is the cousin of our Prophet ﷺ. A group said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "'Isa ibn Maryam will certainly perform Hajj, and with him the People of the Cave, for they have not yet performed Hajj."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In al-Sham, according to what I have heard from many people, there is a cave in which there are dead bodies, which its residents claim are the People of the Cave, and over them is a mosque and a building called al-Raqim, and with them is a dog, a mere skeleton. In al-Andalus, in the direction of Gharnata near a village called Lushah, there is a cave in which there are dead bodies, and with them is a dog, a mere skeleton, and most of them have had their flesh stripped away, and some are still held together. The former generations have passed and we have found no knowledge of their matter to excite us. Some people claim that they are the People of the Cave. I entered to them and saw them in the year five hundred and four, in this state, and over them is a mosque, and near them is a Roman building called al-Raqim on the side of the qiblah, and traces of an ancient Roman city called the city of Diqnayus, in whose remains we found wonders in graves and the like.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I have only ventured to mention this despite its remoteness because it is a wonder whose mention will endure, if Allah, Mighty and Majestic, wills.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you﴾ [up to] the verse. Whoever read: "wa la tushrik" as a prohibition conjoined "wa-tlu" to it, and whoever read: "wa la yushriku" made this a command with which another speech begins, not part of the first. It is as if this verse carries the sense of a rebuke to the Prophet ﷺ, following the rebuke concerning his leaving out the exception, as if He were saying: these are the answers to the questions, so recite the revelation of Allah to you, that is: follow it in your deeds. It was also said: recite, by your recitation, what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord; there is no deficiency in His word, and no changer of His words, and you have no other side that you can incline to and lean upon.

"Al-multahad" is the side to which one inclines; from it comes "al-lahd" (the niche in a grave), as if it were the inclination in one of the two sides of the grave; and from it comes "al-ilhad fi al-haqq" (deviation regarding the truth), which is deviation from the truth. The matter of abrogation (naskh) does not undermine His saying: ﴿there is no changer of His words﴾, because the meaning is either: there is no changer other than Him, so the words remain in their absoluteness; or He intended by "words" the report and the like, which abrogation does not enter. The consensus is that what is not changed is the speech subsisting in His essence, according to which decree proceeds. As for revealed books, the position of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is that they are not changed except through interpretation (ta'wil). Among the scholars there are those who say that the Children of Israel altered the wording of the Torah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verses 28–29:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance; and let not your eyes overlook them, desiring the adornment of the worldly life; and do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, and who follows his own desire, and whose affair has become excess.﴾ ﴿And say: The truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills let him believe, and whoever wills let him disbelieve. Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose enclosure surrounds them. And if they ask for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten brass, which scalds the faces. Wretched is the drink, and evil is the resting place.﴾

The occasion of revelation of this verse: the great men among the disbelievers – it was said, from among the people of Makkah; and it was said, 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn and his companions. The first is more correct, because the surah is Makkan. They said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "If you were to push these away from yourself, we would sit with you and keep your company." They meant 'Ammar ibn Yasir, Suhayb ibn Sinan, Salman al-Farisi, 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and others from among the poor such as Bilal and the like. And they said: "The smell of their woolen cloaks harms us." So the verse was revealed on account of that. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to them, sat among them, and said: "Praise be to Allah, who has placed among my community those whom I was commanded to keep myself patient with." And it is narrated that he said to them: "Welcome to those for whom my Lord rebuked me." Salman narrated that the "those whose hearts are to be reconciled" – 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn, al-Aqra' and their kin – said what was mentioned, and so the verse was revealed.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

According to this, the verse is Madani, though it is likely that the verse is Makkan, and the reconcilable ones did the deed of Quraysh, so it was answered against them with the verse.

"Isbir" (اصْبِرْ) means: restrain yourself. From it comes "al-masbura" (المَصْبُورَةُ), concerning which the hadith says: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade the restraining (sabr) of animals," meaning confining them for shooting at and the like.

Al-Jumhur read "bil-ghadah" (بِالغَداةِ), and Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) read "bil-ghadwah" (بِالغَدْوَةِ), which is the reading of Nasr ibn 'Asim, Malik ibn Dinar, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, and al-Hasan. In the script, both readings are written with a waw, so whoever reads "bil-ghadah" writes it as "al-salah" and "al-zakwah" are written. In the reading of whoever reads "bil-ghadwah" there is weakness, because "ghadwah" is a definite noun, so its right is that the alif and lam not be prefixed to it. The basis for reading it thus is that they attached to it a kind of indefiniteness, when they said "I came ghadwah" meaning "one of the mornings," so the prefixing of the alif and lam became acceptable, as in their saying "al-faynah," while "faynah" is a definite noun.

The indication in His saying, ﴿calling upon their Lord morning and evening﴾, is to the five prayers, said by Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid, and Ibrahim. Qatadah said: what is meant is the Fajr prayer and the 'Asr prayer.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Included in the verse is one who supplicates outside of prayer, and one who gathers for the study of knowledge. 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The remembrance of Allah morning and evening is better than smashing swords in the way of Allah, and than giving wealth generously."

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read "bil-ghuduw" (بِالغُدُوِّ) without the ha', and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "bil-ghadawat wal-'ashiyyat" (بِالغَدَواتِ والعَشِيّاتِ) in the plural.

His saying, ﴿and let not your eyes overlook them﴾, means: do not go beyond them to the people of the world and the affluent among the disbelievers. Al-Hasan read "wa la tu'addi" (وَلا تُعَدِّ) with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the 'ayn and a shadda on the dal with a kasra, meaning: do not let yourself pass beyond them. It was narrated from him: "wa la tu'di" (وَلا تُعْدِ) with a damma on the ta' and a sukun on the 'ayn.

His saying, ﴿whose heart We have made heedless﴾: it was said that by this he intended a specific person, namely 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn and al-Aqra', as Khabbab said. It was also said that he intended only those described by this attribute, and that what is primarily meant is the disbelievers of Quraysh, because the verse is Makkan. Al-Jumhur read "aghfalna qalbahu" (أغْفَلْنا قَلْبَهُ) with a fatha on the ba', in the sense: We made him heedless. 'Amr ibn Fa'id and Musa al-Aswari read "aghfala-na qalbuhu" (أغْفَلَنا قَلْبُهُ), in the sense: his heart neglected Our remembrance and abandoned it. Ibn Jinni said the meaning is: he considered us heedless of him. Abu 'Amr al-Dani mentioned that it is the reading of 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd.

"Al-farut" (الفَرْطُ) may mean neglect and waste, i.e., his affair which must be adhered to; and it may mean excess and extravagance, i.e., his affair and his desire which he pursues. The commentators have explained it with both expressions, namely waste and excess. Khabbab expressed it as ruin, Dawud as regret, and Ibn Zayd as opposition to the truth. All of this is explanation by meaning.

His saying, ﴿And say: The truth is from your Lord﴾ and what follows. The meaning: say to them, O Muhammad: this is the truth from your Lord, that is, this Qur'an, or this turning away from you, and leaving obedience to you, and keeping yourself patient with the believers. Qu'nab and Abu al-Sammal read "wa qula" (وَقُلَ) with a fatha on the lam; Abu Hatim said: that is weak in Arabic. His saying, ﴿so whoever wills let him believe﴾ and what follows, is a threat and warning, meaning: let each person choose for himself what he will find tomorrow with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. A group interpreted it as: whoever Allah wills to believe, let him believe, and whoever Allah wills to disbelieve, let him disbelieve.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is well-founded, i.e., its due is belief and its due is disbelief; then He expressed that in the form of a command, as obligation and exhortation, since for the human being in that there is acquisition (kasb), by which the reward of belief and the punishment of disbelief are connected. Al-Hasan and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read "fa-li-yu'min... wa-li-yakfur" (فَلِيُؤْمِن.. ولِيَكْفُرْ) with a kasra on both lams.

"A'tadna" (أعْتَدْنا) is derived from "al-'atad," which is the thing prepared and present.

"Al-suradiq" (السُرادِقُ) is the enclosing wall, like the stones that encircle and surround the tent, and it may be of the same kind as the tent, a hide or a cloth or the like. From it is the saying of Ru'bah:

O Hakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jarud, the canopy of glory is extended over you.

And from it is the saying of Salamah ibn Jandal:

He is the one who brings the Nu'man into a house whose roof... the bellies of elephants after a canopied house.

Al-Zajjaj said: "al-suradiq" is everything that surrounds a thing.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This, in my view, is more specific than what al-Zajjaj said.

It has been disputed concerning the canopy of the Fire. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: its canopy is a wall of fire. A group said: its canopy is smoke that surrounds the disbelievers, and His saying, ﴿Proceed to a shadow with three branches﴾ [al-Mursalat: 30]. A group said: the encompassing is in this world, and the canopy is the sea. This meaning has been narrated through Ya'la ibn Umayyah from the Prophet (ﷺ), and then His saying, ﴿encompassed them﴾ refers to the humans. Al-Tabari mentioned the hadith from Ya'la, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The sea is Jahannam," and he recited this verse, then said: "By Allah, I will never enter it, or as long as I am alive." It was also narrated from him, peace and blessings be upon him, through Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he said: "The canopy of the Fire has four walls, thick, the width of each wall is a forty years' journey."

His saying, ﴿they will be relieved﴾: that is, there will be for them a station of relief, similar to the saying of the poet:

A greeting among them is a painful blow.

That is: that which stands in place of a greeting.

"Al-muhl" (المُهْلُ): Abu Sa'id narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that it is the dregs of oil when its heat has reached its end. A group said: it is every liquid heated until its heat has reached its end. Ibn Mas'ud and others said: everything melted from gold, silver, lead, or the like of this metal, until it becomes liquid. It was narrated that a water-vessel of gold or silver was presented as a gift to 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, so he ordered it melted until it became liquid and took various colors; then he called those at his door from the people of Kufah and said: I have seen nothing in this world more similar to al-muhl than this, meaning: most similar to the drink of the people of the Fire. A group said: "al-muhl" is pus and blood when they are mixed, and from it is the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) concerning the shroud: "It is only for the muhlah," meaning what flows from the dead person in his grave. This is strengthened by His saying, ﴿of water of pus﴾ [Ibrahim: 16].

His saying, ﴿scalding the faces﴾: concerning its meaning, it was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The drink is brought near to the disbeliever; when it draws close to him he dislikes it, and when it comes closer still it scorches his face and the skin of his face falls off into it; and when he drinks, his intestines are cut to pieces."

"Al-murtafaq" (المُرْتَفَقُ): the thing by which one seeks ease (rifq), that is, one seeks its comfort. "Al-murtafaq" in the sense of the couch on which one reclines is more specific than what is in the verse, since it is one aspect of the meaning of comfort. However, al-Tabari has interpreted the verse with it. The more apparent view in my opinion is that "al-murtafaq" means the thing whose comfort is sought by reclining or otherwise. Mujahid said: "al-murtafaq" is the gathering place.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is as if he took it to the place of gathering (al-rifaqah), and from it comes "al-rifqah" (the company), and all of this returns to the meaning of comfort. Al-Tabari denied that Mujahid's saying has any recognizable meaning, but the statement is clear in its aspect, and Allah is the Helper.

[p. 603] Allah the Mighty and Majestic said:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—indeed, We do not waste the reward of one who does good in deed.﴾ ﴿For them are Gardens of Eternity, beneath which rivers flow. Excellent is the reward, and beautiful is the resting place.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verse 32–34:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And strike for them a parable: two men, for one of whom We had made two gardens of grapevines, and We surrounded them with date palms, and placed between them cultivated land.﴾ ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short therein at all, and We caused a river to gush forth within them.﴾ ﴿And he had fruit, so he said to his companion while he was conversing with him: "I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men."﴾

The pronoun in "lahum" (for them) refers to the bewildered group who wanted the Prophet ﷺ to drive away the poor believers who call upon their Lord morning and evening, and also to those callers themselves. The parable is thus struck for both groups: the disbelieving man owning the two gardens stands in the place of the arrogant tyrants of Quraysh, or of Banu Tamim, according to the disagreement mentioned earlier, and the believing man who acknowledges the Lordship stands in the place of Bilal, 'Ammar, Suhayb and their peers.

"Hafafnahuma" (We surrounded them) means: We made that (the palms) for them on every side. One says: "Hafaka Allah bi-khayr," meaning: He enveloped you with it from your sides. And al-hifaf is the side of a couch and the like.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of this parable is that it concerns an event that actually occurred and existed, and on this basis most of the people of this interpretation explained it. It is possible, however, that the parable is struck for someone with this description even if such a thing never actually happened at any time. The first is more apparent.

It is narrated concerning this that they were two brothers from the Children of Israel who inherited four thousand dinars. One of them did with his wealth what was mentioned: he bought slaves, married, and prospered; the other spent his wealth in obedience to Allah the Exalted until he became poor. They met, the wealthy one boasted and rebuked the believer, and this dialogue took place between them. It is also narrated that they were two partners, blacksmiths, who earned much wealth and did something similar to what was narrated concerning the two brothers, so their affair was what Allah related in His Book. Ibrahim ibn al-Qasim al-Katib mentioned in his book (Fi 'Aja'ib al-Bilad) that the lake of Tinnis was between the two gardens and belonged to the two brothers; one of them sold his share to the other and spent in obedience to Allah, until the other reproached him, and this dialogue took place between them. He said: Then Allah drowned it in a night, and it is this that the verse refers to.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Expounding their stories is lengthy, so I have abridged them and limited myself to their meaning, due to the weakness of their authenticity, and because what is given suffices for understanding the verse.

Reflect upon this scene that Allah the Exalted described, for a person can hardly imagine anything more beautiful among people's means of livelihood: two gardens of grapevines surrounded by date palms, with a space between them that is cultivated land for all kinds of grain, and flowing water irrigating all of that from the river, which beautified this sight, magnified the benefit, brought the labour near, and made one independent of water-carrying camels and other such things.

(p-606) The majority read "kilta" (both). In the Codex of 'Abd Allah it is "kila." The "ta'" in "kilta" is, according to Sibawayh, converted from a waw. It, with the ta' or without it, is a singular noun applied to a dual referent, not a dual noun, and its meaning is: each one of the two. "Al-ukul" is its fruit that is eaten from it. Al-Farra' said: In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "Kull al-jannatayn atat ukulahu" (each of the two gardens brought forth its produce). Allah's saying "wa lam tazlim minhu shay'an" means: it did not fall short of the customary yield. From this is the poet's saying:

"Tazallamani mali kadha wa lawa yadi / lawa yadahu Allahu alladhi huwa ghalibu"

The majority read "wa fajjarna" with a shadda on the jim. Salam, Ya'qub and Isa ibn 'Umar read "wa fajarna" with a fatha on the jim and no shadda. The majority read "nahran" with a fatha on the ha'. Abu al-Sammal, al-Fayyad ibn Ghazwan and Talha ibn Sulayman read "nahran" with a sukun on the ha'. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and the community of the readers of Madina and Makka read "thumurun" and "wa uhita bi-thumurihi" with a damma on the tha' and the mim, the plural of thimar. Abu 'Amr, al-A'mash and Abu Raja' read both with a sukun on the mim for lightness, and it is in meaning like the first. It is plausible that it is the plural of thamara, like badana and budn. 'Asim read "thamarun" and "wa uhita bi-thamarihi" with a fatha on the mim and the tha' in both; this is the reading of Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, Jabir ibn Zayd and al-Hajjaj.

The interpreters differed concerning "al-thumur" with a damma on the tha' and the mim. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: "al-thumur" (p-607) is all wealth of gold, silver and other than that, and they cite for this view the verse of al-Nabigha:

"Wa ma uthammiru min malin wa min walad"

Mujahid said: it refers specifically to gold and silver. Ibn Zayd said: "al-thumur" are the roots in which the fruit is.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is as if they are thimar and thumur, like kuttab and kutub. As for the one who reads with a fatha on the tha' and the mim, there is no difficulty that the meaning is the produce on the tops of the trees. But the eloquence of speech requires that it express concisely the destruction of the fruit and the roots by the destruction of the fruit alone; it singled it out for mention since it is the aim of the one who profits, and since the destruction of the roots only grieves one because of the destruction of the fruit that was hoped for in the future. Just as His saying "inna lahu thamaran" (indeed he had fruit) implies that he had roots, so the all-encompassing surrounding (of the fruit) implies that the roots too had perished. In the codex of Ubayy: "wa atayna-hu thamaran kathiran" (and We gave him abundant fruit). Abu Raja' read "wa kana lahu thamarun" with a fatha on the tha' and a sukun on the mim. "Al-muhawara" is the exchange of speech, and it is from hara, yahuru.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Some people deduced from His, the Glorified's, saying "wa a'azzu nafaran" (and mightier in men) that he was not his brother. The opponent said: he meant by "nafar" the slaves and servants, since they are those who come forth (yanfirun) in his desires. In this speech is such arrogance, vainglory and delusion that its clarification makes further comment on it unnecessary. This statement corresponds to the words of 'Uyayna and al-Aqra' to the Prophet ﷺ: "We are the masters of the Arabs and the people of wool and clay, so push away from us Salman and his companions."

Just as His saying "inna lahu thamaran" (indeed he had fruit) implies that he had roots, so the all-encompassing surrounding (of the fruit) implies that the roots too had perished. "Al-muhawara" is the exchange of speech, and it is from hara, yahuru.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Some people deduced from His, the Glorified's, saying "wa a'azzu nafaran" (and mightier in men) that he was not his brother. The opponent said: he meant by "nafar" the slaves and servants, since they are those who come forth (yanfirun) in his desires. In this speech is such arrogance, vainglory and delusion that its clarification makes further comment on it unnecessary. This statement corresponds to the words of 'Uyayna and al-Aqra' to the Prophet ﷺ: "We are the masters of the Arabs and the people of wool and clay, so push away from us Salman and his companions."

(p-608) The words of the Exalted: ﴿And he entered his garden while he was wronging himself. He said, "I do not think that this will ever perish."﴾ ﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established. And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than it as a destination.﴾ ﴿His companion said to him while he was arguing with him, "Have you disbelieved in He who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then proportioned you into a man?"﴾ ﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I associate no one with my Lord.﴾ ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, "What Allah wills [will be]. There is no power except through Allah"? If you see me as less than you in wealth and children.﴾

[His wronging himself also consisted of] his doubt about the origination of the world, if his reference with "this" (hadhihi) was to the form of the heavens and the earth and the kinds of created beings. If his reference was only to his garden, then his speech contains foolishness, delusion and little understanding. It seems that, from his excessive amazement at it and his joy, he went to extremes in describing it with this statement. Then he also analogized the Hereafter to this world, and thought that he had only been granted respite in his worldly life because of a dignity he deserved in himself. He said: "If there is a return, as you claim, then my situation will be such and such." The statement of al-'As ibn Wa'il to Khabbab was not on this same level; rather, al-'As intended belittlement, out of determination to deny [the truth].

His saying ﴿from dust﴾ is a reference to Adam (ﷺ). His saying ﴿proportioned you into a man﴾ is like your saying "he made you a person" or "a living being," or similar emphases. It is possible that he intended to specify manhood, by way of enumerating the blessing that you were not a female or a hermaphrodite. Al-Tabari mentioned something similar to this.

Harun narrated from Abu 'Amr "lakinnahu huwa Allahu rabbi" with a pronoun attached to "lakin." The rest of the verse is clear.

It may also be the predicate of an omitted subject, its implied sense being: "It is what Allah willed," or "The matter is what Allah willed." He said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "There is no power except through Allah. When the servant says it, Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: My servant has submitted and surrendered."

And in the hadith of Abu Musa, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "O 'Abdullah ibn Qays, shall I not guide you to a treasure from the treasures of Paradise?" He said: "Do so, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "There is no power and no strength except through Allah, the Most High, the Mighty."

Nafi' and Abu 'Amr retained it only in connected speech. The majority read "aqalla" in the accusative as the second object, and his saying "ana" is a superfluous separator. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "aqillu" in the nominative, so that "ana" is the subject and "aqallu" its predicate, and the clause is in the position of the second object. The seeing here is seeing by the heart in this verse.

(p-608) The words of the Exalted: ﴿And he entered his garden while he was wronging himself. He said, "I do not think that this will ever perish."﴾ ﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established. And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than it as a destination.﴾ ﴿His companion said to him while he was arguing with him, "Have you disbelieved in He who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then proportioned you into a man?"﴾ ﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I associate no one with my Lord.﴾ ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, "What Allah wills [will be]. There is no power except through Allah"? If you see me as less than you in wealth and children.﴾

He used the singular "al-Jannah" (the garden) with respect to existence, and likewise, because he would not enter both [gardens] at the same time. His wronging himself was his disbelief and his corrupt beliefs in doubting the Resurrection, and Qatadah and Ibn Zayd explicitly stated this. [His wronging himself also consisted of] his doubt about the origination of the world, if his reference with "this" (hadhihi) was to the form of the heavens and the earth and the kinds of created beings. If his reference was only to his garden, then his speech contains foolishness, delusion and little understanding. It seems that, from his excessive amazement at it and his joy, he went to extremes in describing it with this statement. Then he also analogized the Hereafter to this world, and thought that he had only been granted respite in his worldly life because of a dignity he deserved in himself. He said: "If there is a return, as you claim, then my situation will be such and such." The statement of al-'As ibn Wa'il to Khabbab was not on this same level; rather, al-'As intended belittlement, out of determination to deny [the truth].

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Ibn al-Zubayr, and [the reading] found in the codices of Madinah is "minhuma" (from both of them), meaning the two gardens mentioned first. Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and the majority, and so it is in the codex of the people of Basra, read "minha" (from it), meaning the garden that was entered.

His saying ﴿His companion said to him﴾ is a report that the believer of the two men, when he heard the disbeliever's speech, rebuked him, by way of reproach, for his disbelief in Allah the Exalted. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "wa-huwa yukhasimuhu" (while he was disputing with him). Thabit al-Banani read "waylaka a-kafarta" (woe to you, have you disbelieved). Then he began to magnify Allah the Exalted in his presence with attributes that included the blessings and the proofs of the possibility of resurrection from the graves. His saying ﴿from dust﴾ is a reference to Adam (ﷺ). His saying ﴿proportioned you into a man﴾ is like your saying "he made you a person" or "a living being," or similar emphases. It is possible that he intended to specify manhood, by way of enumerating the blessing that you were not a female or a hermaphrodite. Al-Tabari mentioned something similar to this.

(p-609) The reading differed concerning his saying "lakinna." Ibn 'Amir and Nafi', in the narration of al-Masili, read "lakinna" both in connected speech and in pause. As for this last one, it is clear as [introducing] the matter and the affair. As for the one before it, it means: "But what I say is..." As for one who read "lakinna," its origin in his view is "lakin ana," the hamzah was dropped contrary to analogy, and the nun was assimilated into the nun. Some grammarians have said: the vowel of the hamzah was transferred to the nun, so it became "lakinnana," then it was assimilated after that, so it became "lakinna." Some readers thought that by the assimilation the final alif was dispensed with, so some dropped it in connected speech, and others kept it both in connected speech and in pause, to indicate the original form of the word. In "lakinna" it is also possible that "lakin" was joined by the plural nun found in "kharajna" and "darabna," and assimilation occurred because of the meeting of two identical letters. Then he used the singular in "rabbi" according to the meaning; had he followed the wording, he would have said "rabbuna." Abu 'Ali mentioned this. This explanation makes the view of those who kept the alif in both connected speech and pause preferable. It is also possible that in "lakinna" it is the well-known one of the sisters of "inna," and the meaning is: "But my statement is: He is Allah, my Lord," except that I do not know anyone who reads it that way in both connected speech and pause, and that obliges the one who gives this interpretation. Harun narrated from Abu 'Amr "lakinnahu huwa Allahu rabbi" with a pronoun attached to "lakin." The rest of the verse is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verses 40–44:

His Most Exalted, Majestic saying:

﴿Perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden and will send upon it a calamity from the sky, so that it becomes a barren ground, slippery.﴾ ﴿Or its water will sink away, and you will not be able to seek it.﴾ ﴿And his fruit was encompassed (by ruin), and he began wringing his hands over what he had spent on it, while it lay fallen upon its trellises, and he said: "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord."﴾ ﴿And he had no company to help him besides Allah, nor was he able to defend himself.﴾ ﴿There, guardianship belongs to Allah, the True. He is best in reward and best in outcome.﴾

This expectation with "'asā" (perhaps) may be intended to refer to this world, and it may be intended to refer to the Hereafter. Wishing for that in the Hereafter is a more noble conclusion and more conducive to good and righteousness. And it may be that this refers to this world, which is more effective in afflicting this addressee and more painful to his soul.

"Al-ḥusbān" (the calamity): punishment such as hail, cold wind and the like. The singular of ḥusbān is ḥusbānah, which means the projectiles of these kinds mentioned, that is, arrows shot all at once by an instrument made for that purpose. "Al-ṣaʿīd" (the ground): the surface of the earth. "Al-zalaq" (slippery): that in which no foot can be firm, meaning that its trees and plants are gone, and it remains as earth whose benefits have departed, even the benefit of walking upon it, so it is mud that produces nothing and in which no foot can stand.

(p-611) "Al-ghawr" is a verbal noun used as a description of water, whether singular or plural water, as in your saying: "a just man" and "a just woman" and the like. Its meaning: going down into the earth, so that it cannot be reached. A group read "ghūran" with a ḍammah on the ghayn, and a group read "ghu'ūran" with a ḍammah on the ghayn and a hamza on the waw. "Ghawr" is like "nawḥ" (a wailing), used to describe the singular and the plural, the masculine and the feminine. From it is the saying of the poet:

؎ Her steeds remain wailing over him, / their reins hung with their standing (ṣufūn) horses.

This is common, and the rest of the verse is clear.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed﴾, the verse. This is a report from Allah, Exalted is He, about the encompassing of punishment upon the state of this one who is used as an example. The discussion of "fruit" has already preceded, but "encompassing" is a metaphor for the generality of punishment and corruption. "﴿He began wringing his hands﴾" means: he places the back of one of them upon the back of the other, and that is the act of one who is distressed and regretful over a loss, a deficiency, or the like. Whoever expresses it as "clapping" has not been precise. His saying: ﴿while it lay fallen upon its trellises﴾ means that the roofs collapsed, which are the trellises, and then the walls collapsed upon them, so it lies fallen while the walls are upon the trellises. ﴿And he said: "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord"﴾. Some exegetes said: this is a report of the disbelieving man's words in the Hereafter. It may be intended that he said it in this world, in the manner of repentance after the calamity befell him, and in it there is a warning to the disbelievers of Quraysh or others, lest a state come upon them in which they believe after vengeance descends upon them.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and Shayba read ﴿wa-lam takun﴾ with a *tā'* according to the wording of "fi'ah" (group). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Mujahid and Ibn Wthhab read ﴿wa-lam yakun﴾ with a *yā'* according to the meaning. "Al-fi'ah": the group to whose support one takes refuge. Mujahid said: it is the clan.

(p-612) The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view it derives from *fā'a yafī'u*; its pattern is *fi'latun* (*fī'ah*), and the 'ayn was dropped for lightness. Abu 'Ali and others said it derives from *fa'awtu* and not from *fā'a*. What they said is more involved in morphology, while the first is sounder in meaning. Ibn Abi 'Abla read: *fi'atun tansuruhu* (a group that supports him).

His saying, Exalted is He: "*hunālika*" (there) may be a adverbial complement to His saying "*muntaṣiran*" (one who defends himself), and it may be that "*al-walāyah*" (guardianship) is the subject and "*hunālika*" its predicate. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash and Yahya ibn Wthhab read *al-wilāyah* with a kasrah on the waw, meaning leadership, command and the like. The rest read *al-walāyah* with a fatḥah on the waw, meaning allegiance, association and the like. It is reported from Abu 'Amr and al-Asma'i that kasrah on the waw here is a solecism, because *fi'ālah* comes only for a craft or a rank undertaken, and there is no assumption of a matter here.

Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read *al-ḥaqq* with a ḍammah (*al-ḥaqqu*) as a description of *al-walāyah*, and the rest read *al-ḥaqqi* with a kasrah as a description of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Abu Haywa read *lillāhi al-ḥaqqa* with a fatḥah. The majority read *'uquban* with a ḍammah on the 'ayn and the qāf; 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Hasan read *'uqban* with a ḍammah on the 'ayn, sukūn on the qāf and tanwīn on the bā'; 'Asim also read *'uqbā* with the feminine *yā'*. *Al-'uqb* and *al-'uqub* have the same meaning: consequence, recompense.

Its meaning: going down into the earth, so that it cannot be reached. A group read "ghūran" with a ḍammah on the ghayn, and a group read "ghu'ūran" with a ḍammah on the ghayn and a hamza on the waw. This is common, and the rest of the verse is clear.

[(p-613)] Allah, the Exalted, says:

﴿And set forth for them the parable of the life of this world: it is like water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it, then it becomes dry stubble which the winds scatter. And Allah is ever Able over all things.﴾ ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world; but the enduring good deeds are better in the sight of your Lord for reward and better for hope.﴾ ﴿And the day We will set the mountains in motion, and you will see the earth laid bare, and We will gather them and leave out none of them.﴾ ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in rows: "You have come to Us just as We created you the first time. But you claimed that We would not appoint for you an appointment."﴾

Allah's words, ﴿the life of this world﴾, mean the life of a person with what is connected to it of blessings and wealth. His words, ﴿like water which We sent down﴾, mean: "it is like water." His words, ﴿so the vegetation mingled with it﴾, mean: the plants mingled with one another because of the water. The "bi" in "bihi" (with it) is the "bi" of causation. "Asbaha" (it became) expresses its transformation into that state, and it does not mean a restriction to the time of morning. This is like the saying of al-Rabi' ibn Dab'

> I have become one who no longer bears a weapon,
> nor holds the reins of a camel if it bolts.

"Al-hashim" is the crumbled dry herbage, and from it comes Allah's words, ﴿like the crumbled fodder of the one who builds a pen﴾ [al-Qamar: 31], and from it comes the phrase "hashshama al-thareed" (he crumbled the bread). "Tadhruhu" means "scatters it." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, recited it as "tudhrihi" (uproots it), and the meaning is: it uproots it and throws it away. Al-Hasan recited "tadhruhu al-rih" with the singular "al-rih" (wind), and this is the recitation (qira'a) of Talha, al-Nakha'i and al-A'mash.

Allah's words, ﴿and Allah was﴾, are an expression for the human being that the matter before the existence of humanity was thus, when it was. For his own self, being in a state of heedlessness, judges by this. This is the statement of Sibawayh, and it is a sound meaning. Al-Hasan said: "kana" (was) is a report about the state before the existence of created things, meaning that power was. This too is good. His words, ﴿over every thing﴾, mean: among the things that are determined (possible).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Impossibilities and others of the things to which Allah, blessed and exalted, is not described as having power or as being unable are not included. This is based on calling the impossible a "thing" insofar as it is conceived, not actual. And it has been reported that the earthquake of the Hour is a "thing."

The meaning of this parable is the comparison of a person's state in his life, his wealth, his honour, his pride and his arrogance with a plant that has greenness and freshness from falling rain, then after that it returns to dry stubble and passes into non-existence. Whoever has a righteous deed that remains in the Hereafter is the one who succeeds. So life is like the water, and the greenness and freshness are like the bounty, honour and the like.

Allah's words, ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾, are in the form of a report, but with it is an indicator of the lowliness of wealth and children, because in the parable before this, He belittled the matter of this world and made it clear. So it is as if He says in this: "Wealth and children are only the adornment of this belittled life, so do not follow yourselves in it." His word "zinah" (adornment) is a verbal noun (masdar), and it has been reported about persons. Either it is according to a deleted supposition, its estimate being: "the place of the adornment of the life," or he places wealth and children in the status of abundance and multiplicity.

People differed regarding "the enduring good deeds." Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Abu Maysara 'Amr ibn Shurahbil said: they are the five prayers.

The majority said: they are the words whose virtue has been reported: subhan Allah (Glory be to Allah), al-hamdu lillah (Praise be to Allah), la ilaha illa Allah (There is no god but Allah), Allah akbar (Allah is greatest), and la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah al-'Aliyy al-'Azim (There is no power nor might except with Allah, the Most High, the Most Great).

A hadith has been reported on this: "Increase in the enduring good deeds," and Ibn 'Abbas also said it. It has been reported from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, through the route of Abu Hurayrah and others, that these words are the enduring good deeds.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said: "The enduring good deeds are every righteous deed, of speech or action, that remains for the Hereafter." Al-Tabari preferred this view, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "It is a proof for all people that his statement is general."

Allah's words, ﴿better in the sight of your Lord for reward and better for hope﴾, mean: the one who does them awaits the reward, and his hope is extended to something better than the state of the one who has wealth and children without a righteous deed.

Allah's words, ﴿And the day We will set the mountains in motion﴾, to the end of the verse: the estimate is "remember the day," and this is the most eloquent interpretation of this here. Nafi', al-A'raj, Shayba, 'Asim, Ibn Misraf and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman recited "nusayyiru" with the first person plural of majesty (nun of greatness). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Hasan, Shibl, Qatada and 'Isa recited "tusayyiru" with a ta', and the yaʼ of the doubled form open, "al-jibal" (the mountains) in the nominative. Al-Hasan recited "yusayyiru" with a damma on the yaʼ and the second letter open and doubled, "al-jibal" in the nominative. Ibn Muhaysin recited "tasiru" with an open ta' and a kasra on the sin, the verb being attributed to "al-jibal." Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited "wa yawma suyyirat al-jibal" (and the day the mountains were set in motion).

Allah's words, "bariza" (laid bare), either mean that the earth, because the mountains, hills and trees have gone, became bare and exposed, or they mean the emergence of its people and those gathered from the inhabitants of its interior. "And We gathered them," that is, We raised them from their graves and assembled them for the gathering of the Resurrection. The majority recited "nughadiru" with the nun of majesty, and Qatada recited "tughadiru" as attributed to the power or to the earth. Aban ibn Yazid reported from 'Asim: "yughadiru" with a damma on the yaʼ and an open dal, "ahadun" (anyone) in the nominative.

Al-Dahhak recited "fa lam nughdir" with a damma on the nun, a kasra on the dal and a sukun on the ghayn.

Al-mughadarah means leaving behind, and from it comes "ghadir al-ma'" (a pool of water), which is what the flood leaves behind.

Allah's words, "saffan" (in rows), are a singular noun treated as a plural, meaning "rows." In the sound hadith: "Allah will gather the first and the last in one plain, in rows, the caller will make them hear, and sight will reach them" (the hadith). In another hadith: "The people of Paradise on the day of Resurrection are a hundred and twenty rows, of which you are eighty rows."

Allah's words, ﴿You have come to Us﴾ to the end of the verse, are a address to the disbelievers who denied the resurrection, and its implication is reproach and rebuke. The believers, who in the world believed that they would be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection, are not addressed in this manner in any way. In the speech there is an omission required by the statement and made good by the brevity, its estimate being: it will be said to the disbelievers among them. ﴿Just as We created you the first time﴾ is explained by the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Indeed you will be gathered to Allah barefoot, naked and uncircumcised," ﴿as We began the first creation, We will repeat it﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104].

Impossibilities and others of the things to which Allah, blessed and exalted, is not described as having power or as being unable are not included.
