Al-mughadarah means leaving behind, and from it comes "ghadir al-ma'" (a pool of water), which is what the flood leaves behind.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verse 49–50:

His the Mighty and Majestic's saying:

﴿And the Book will be set down, and you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it, and they will say, "Woe to us! What is this Book that leaves nothing small or great except that it has enumerated it?" And they will find what they did present, and your Lord does not wrong anyone.﴾ ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord. Will you then take him and his descendants as allies other than Me while they are enemies to you? Wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers.﴾

"Al-Kitab" (the Book) is a collective noun, by which is meant the books of the people, which the guardian angels have enumerated for each individual. It is also possible that "the Book" refers to one single book that is present. The "fear of the criminals" (ishfaq al-mujrimin) means their terror of its disclosure and exposure to them. The complaint of the criminals is only from the enumeration, not from any wrong or injustice.

[p-617] He mentioned "small" (al-saghira) first, giving it attention so as to alert [the reader] to it, and it indicates that if the small is enumerated, the great is more deserving of that. The Arabs always mention the lesser first in any pair, and similar to this is their saying: "al-qamarani" (the two moons) and "al-'umaran" (the two 'Umars), where they named the lesser by its name as an alert. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, said:

"The small" (al-saghira): laughter.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an example, and the rest of the verse is clear.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾ — this verse's content is a reproach to the disbelievers and a questioning of them regarding their taking as allies the enemy instead of the One who bestowed upon them all His blessings in general, small and great. The sense of the sentence is: "And mention when We said..." This phrase is repeated wherever this story is repeated, since it is a preface to the event. As for mentioning the event here, it is an introduction to the reproach; and mentioning it in al-Baqara is an announcement of the beginnings of matters.

The interpreters differed concerning prostration to Adam. One group said: it is the well-known prostration, the placing of the face on the ground, which Allah, the Exalted, made for the angels as worship of Him and honor for Adam; so this is like prayer toward the Ka'ba. Another group said: rather, it was a gesture from them toward the ground, and this is called prostration, because prostration in Arabic speech is an expression for the utmost humility. From it is the poet's saying:

"You see the hillocks in it prostrate before the hooves."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is permissible that the Creator should impose it upon the superior for the inferior, and it is permissible that the superior should voluntarily perform it for the superior. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Stand up for your master (sayyid)." And from it is Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's kissing of the hand of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, when he met him on a journey to al-Sham; Sa'id ibn Mansur mentioned it in his Musannaf.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿except Iblis﴾, one group said: it is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), because Iblis is not of the angels, but is of the jinn, who are the devils created from a smokeless fire, while all the angels were created from light. This group differed: some of them said: Iblis is of the jinn, and he is their first and originator, just as Adam is of mankind. Another group said: rather, Iblis and his kind were jinn, but all the devils today are from his descendants, so he is like Noah among mankind. They argued with this verse, and the rebuke of Iblis for his disobedience requires that he had been commanded along with the angels.

Another group said: the exception is connected (istithna' muttasil), and Iblis is from the kind of the angels, who were created from fire; so Iblis is of the angels, and He expressed the angels by "jinn" from the standpoint that they are hidden. So it is an attribute that encompasses the angels and the devils. Some of this group said: there was among the angels a category called the jinn, and they were in the lowest heaven and on earth, and Iblis was their manager.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no disagreement that Iblis was of the angels in meaning, since he was disposing of command and prohibition as an envoy; and the angel (malak) is derived from al-ma'laka, which is message. So he is in the reckoning of the angels, and the saying "Prostrate" encompasses him. In Surat al-Baqara and Surat al-A'raf the comprehensive treatment of these matters is found.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying "fa-fasaqa" (so he defied): its meaning is: he went out and departed. Ru'ba said:

"They descend in a plain and a deep valley, / Deviating from their aim, straying."

From this one says: "fasaqat al-rutba" (the date slipped) when it came out of its skin, and "fasaqat al-fa'ra" (the mouse came out) when it came out of its hole. All this coming out used in these examples is in corruption. And the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Five fawasiq (vermin) kill in the sacred and the non-sacred areas" — they are indeed corrupters.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿'an amri rabbihi﴾ (from the command of his Lord), it may mean: he went out from the command of his Lord, i.e., he separated from it, as one who goes out from a single path, meaning from it. It may also mean: he went out from obedience after his Lord's command to it. The particle "'an" may come in the sense of "after" in many places, as when you say: "I fed him after hunger," and similar; so the meaning is as if: he defied because of the command of his Lord to obey. It may also mean: he went out by the command of his Lord, i.e., by His will that it be so for him; and will is expressed by "command," since it is one of the matters; and this is like your saying: "I did that by your command," meaning by your effort and according to your intent.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said regarding the narrative of this verse: Iblis was of the most noble category, and he had the sovereignty of the heaven and the sovereignty of the earth; when he disobeyed, his state came to what you hear. Some scholars said: if a person's sin is from error, then let him hope for mercy like Adam; and if it is from disbelief, then let him not hope like Iblis.

Then the Mighty and Majestic halted the disbelievers, by way of reproach, with His saying: ﴿Will you then take...﴾, meaning: will you take Iblis? His saying: ﴿and his descendants﴾: the apparent wording requires the whisperers among the devils, who command the reprehensible and drive to falsehood. al-Tabari mentioned that Mujahid said: the descendants of Iblis are the devils, and he enumerated them: "Zalanbur," the lord of the markets, who places his banner in every market; "Tubun," the lord of calamities; "al-A'war," the lord of showing off; "Misut," the lord of news, who brings it and throws it into people's mouths, and they find no basis for it; and "Dasim," who, when a man enters his house without greeting or mentioning the name of Allah, makes him see of the goods what he has not raised.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As for this and what resembles it of what no sound report has come with, I have therefore abridged it. Al-Naqqash lengthened on this meaning and brought narratives that are far from soundness, so I left them for brevity. No sound report has come to me on this except what is in the Book of Muslim, that for ablution and whisperings there is a devil called "Khinzab"; and al-Tirmidhi mentioned that for ablution there is a devil called "al-Walhan." And Allah knows best the details of these matters; there is no lord but Him.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿and they are to you an enemy﴾, meaning: enemies; it is the collective noun.

As for His saying: ﴿Wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: they exchanged the guardianship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for the guardianship of Iblis and his descendants; and that is the taking in exchange of the jinn for falsehood. This is the very essence of wrongdoing, because it placed a thing in other than its proper place.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿'an amri rabbihi﴾ (from the command of his Lord), it may mean: he went out from the command of his Lord, i.e., he separated from it, as one who goes out from a single path, meaning from it. It may also mean: he went out from obedience after his Lord's command to it. The particle "'an" may come in the sense of "after" in many places, as when you say: "I fed him after hunger," and similar; so the meaning is as if: he defied because of the command of his Lord to obey. It may also mean: he went out by the command of his Lord, i.e., by His will that it be so for him; and will is expressed by "command," since it is one of the matters; and this is like your saying: "I did that by your command," meaning by your effort and according to your intent.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said regarding the narrative of this verse: Iblis was of the most noble category, and he had the sovereignty of the heaven and the sovereignty of the earth; when he disobeyed, his state came to what you hear. Some scholars said: if a person's sin is from error, then let him hope for mercy like Adam; and if it is from disbelief, then let him not hope like Iblis.

Then the Mighty and Majestic halted the disbelievers, by way of reproach, with His saying: ﴿Will you then take...﴾, meaning: will you take Iblis? His saying: ﴿and his descendants﴾: the apparent wording requires the whisperers among the devils, who command the reprehensible and drive to falsehood. al-Tabari mentioned that Mujahid said: the descendants of Iblis are the devils, and he enumerated them: "Zalanbur," the lord of the markets, who places his banner in every market; "Tubun," the lord of calamities; "al-A'war," the lord of showing off; "Misut," the lord of news, who brings it and throws it into people's mouths, and they find no basis for it; and "Dasim," who, when a man enters his house without greeting or mentioning the name of Allah, makes him see of the goods what he has not raised.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As for this and what resembles it of what no sound report has come with, I have therefore abridged it. Al-Naqqash lengthened on this meaning and brought narratives that are far from soundness, so I left them for brevity. No sound report has come to me on this except what is in the Book of Muslim, that for ablution and whisperings there is a devil called "Khinzab"; and al-Tirmidhi mentioned that for ablution there is a devil called "al-Walhan." And Allah knows best the details of these matters; there is no lord but Him.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿and they are to you an enemy﴾, meaning: enemies; it is the collective noun.

As for His saying: ﴿Wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: they exchanged the guardianship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for the guardianship of Iblis and his descendants; and that is the taking in exchange of the jinn for falsehood. This is the very essence of wrongdoing, because it placed a thing in other than its proper place.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verses 51–54:

The Almighty said:

﴿I did not make them witnesses to the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor to the creation of themselves, nor was I one to take misleaders as helpers.﴾ ﴿And on the Day He will say, "Call upon My partners whom you claimed," so they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them, and We will place between them a barrier of destruction.﴾ ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and realize that they are going to fall into it, and they will find no escape from it.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an for the people from every example, but man has been most contentious of things.﴾

The pronoun in "ashhadtuhum" (I made them witness) refers to the disbelievers, and to people in general. Thus the verse contains a refutation of groups of astrologers (al-munajjimun), those who adhere to the doctrine of natures (ahl al-taba'i'), the arrogant physicians (al-mutahakkimun min al-atibba'), and others, every fabricator (mutakharris) concerning these matters. My father, may Allah be pleased with him, related to me, saying: I heard the jurist Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Mu'adh al-Mahdawi in al-Mahdiyya say: I heard 'Abd al-Haqq al-Saqqali say this statement, and interpret this verse in this interpretation (p-621), and that it refutes these groups.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Some of the usuliyyun (scholars of the principles of jurisprudence) mentioned this. It has also been said: the pronoun in "ashhadtuhum" refers to the offspring of Iblis, so this verse, according to this view, contains their belittlement. The first opinion is greater in benefit. I say: the primary intended purpose of the verse is Iblis and his offspring, and in this sense the refutation of the aforementioned groups is directed, as well as the soothsayers (kuhhan) and the Arabs who believed them and who venerated the jinn when they say, "I seek refuge in the mighty one of this valley," since all of these groups are attached to Iblis and his offspring, and they have misled everyone. They are therefore the primary intended by "al-mudillin" (the misleaders), and these groups fall within their meaning.

Al-Jumhur recited "ashhadtuhum," while Abu Ja'far, 'Awf al-'Aqili, and Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani recited "ashhadnahum." Al-Jumhur recited "wa ma kuntu," while Abu Ja'far, al-Jahdari, and al-Hasan (in one report) recited "wa ma kunta." The description "al-mudillin" applies to the aforementioned groups and to the offspring of Iblis, may Allah curse him. "Al-'adud" (helper) is a metaphor for one who aids and supports, and it is a likeness to the human arm (adud), which a person relies upon. Al-Jumhur recited "'adudan" with a fatha on the 'ayn and a damma on the dad. Abu 'Amr and al-Hasan recited both with a damma. al-Dahhak recited with a kasra on the 'ayn and a fatha on the dad. 'Ikrima recited "'udan" with a damma on the 'ayn and sukun on the dad. 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited "'adadan" with a fatha on both the 'ayn and the dad. There are other dialectal forms besides these that were not recited.

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And on the Day He will say﴾, the verse is a warning, and the meaning is: remember the Day. Talha, Yahya, al-A'mash, and Hamza recited "naqulu" with the plural of majesty (nun al-'azama). Al-Jumhur recited with the ya', i.e., "yaqulu" (He will say), Allah the Exalted, to the disbelievers who associated partners with Him in the world other than Him: ﴿Call upon My partners﴾ in the manner of seeking help from them. His saying "shurakai" (My partners) means: according to your claim, O polytheists, and this is explained by His saying: ﴿whom you claimed﴾. Ibn Kathir and the people of Makkah recited "shurakai" with an open ya', and al-Jumhur recited "shurakai" with a hamza, and among them are those who made it fully articulated and those who lightened it. "Al-za'm" (claim) is only ever used for what is not certain; rather, most of its use is for falsehood, and this verse is among such uses. Its highest usage is when "za'ama" is used with the meaning of "akhbara" (informed), where the responsibility for the report falls upon the reporter, as Sibawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, says: "za'ama al-Khalil." His saying: ﴿so they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them﴾ its apparent meaning is that this actually occurs, and it may be a metaphor, as if the thought and reflection of the disbelievers, that those lifeless things do not avail anything nor benefit, is equivalent to calling and not answering. The first is clearer.

The interpreters differed concerning His saying, the Exalted: "mawbiqan" (a barrier of destruction). 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, Anas ibn Malik, and Mujahid said: it is a valley in Hell that flows with blood and pus. Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it separates the people of the Fire from the believers. Thus His saying, according to this, "baynahum" (between them) is an adverbial phrase of place. al-Hasan said: "mawbiqan" means enmity, and "baynahum," according to this, is an adverbial phrase. Some of this group hold that the pronoun in His saying, the Exalted, "baynahum" refers to the believers and the disbelievers, and it may refer to the polytheists and their deities in the world. As for the first interpretation, the pronoun in it refers to the polytheists and their deities. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "mawbiqan" means: destroying, in the sense of a place, and it derives from your saying: "wabaqa al-rajul," and "awbaqahu ghayruhu" when he destroyed him. His saying, the Exalted, "baynahum," according to this interpretation, may be an adverbial phrase, and the more apparent view is that it is a noun, meaning: We made their association a destructive matter for them, and "baynahum" is the first object of "ja'alna." Some expressed "al-mawbiq" as the threat, and this is weak.

Then the Almighty informed concerning the seeing of the criminals of the Fire, their witnessing of it, and the knowledge coming to them that they are going to be in direct contact with it. Most people hold that "al-zann" (assumption) here means certainty.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Had the Exalted said, in place of "zannu," "ayqanu" (they were certain), the speech would have been consistent, emphasizing it. But the expression with "al-zann" never comes in a place of complete certainty that has been reached by the senses; rather, its highest level is that it comes in a place of verified knowledge but in which the supposed event did not occur. Otherwise, what occurs and is sensed is hardly ever expressed with "al-zann" in Arabic speech. Reflect on this verse, and reflect on the words of Durayd:

"So I said to them: assume (zunnu) with two thousand armored men."

(p-623) Al-A'mash recited "fa-zannu annahum mulaquha," and likewise in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud. Abu 'Amr al-Dani relates from 'Alqama that he recited "mullaffuha" with a doubled fa', from "laffaftu." Abu Sa'id al-Khudri related that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed the disbeliever will see Hell and think that it is about to fall upon him from a distance of forty years." "Al-masraf" means the way out (al-ma'dil), and from it is the saying of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali:

"O Zuhayr, is there any escape from Shayba, / or is there no eternity for one who spends and strains?"

It is derived from turning away from one thing to another.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We have certainly diversified﴾, the verse. The meaning: We have warned, given hope, and exceeded in clarification, and all of this through illustration and bringing closer to minds. His saying: ﴿from every example﴾ means: from every example that has benefit regarding the intended purpose for them, which is guidance. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿but man has been most contentious of things﴾ is a summarized statement implying: the diversifying of examples did not benefit them; rather, they are a deviant people who dispute with falsehood. His saying, the Exalted: "al-insan" (man) intends by it the species, and it has been narrated that the cause of this verse is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and it was said: Ibn al-Zib'ara. It is narrated that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered upon 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, when he had slept through the night prayer, so he woke him and rebuked him, and 'Ali said to him: 'Indeed our souls are in the hand of Allah,' and similar words, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out striking his cheek with his hand and saying: ﴿But man has been most contentious of things﴾." Thus he used the verse in its generality over all people. "Al-jadal" (contention) means: (p-624) dispute and argument through speech. So man is more contentious than anything that disputes, from angels, jinn, and other things, if such is supposed. In His saying, the Exalted: ﴿but man has been most contentious of things﴾ there is an instruction, a kind of lamentation over people, which will become clear later on.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verses 51–54:

The Almighty said:

﴿I did not make them witnesses to the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor to the creation of themselves, nor was I one to take misleaders as helpers.﴾ ﴿And on the Day He will say, "Call upon My partners whom you claimed," so they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them, and We will place between them a barrier of destruction.﴾ ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and realize that they are going to fall into it, and they will find no escape from it.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an for the people from every example, but man has been most contentious of things.﴾

The pronoun in "ashhadtuhum" (I made them witness) refers to the disbelievers, and to people in general. Thus the verse contains a refutation of groups of astrologers (al-munajjimun), those who adhere to the doctrine of natures (ahl al-taba'i'), the arrogant physicians (al-mutahakkimun min al-atibba'), and others, every fabricator (mutakharris) concerning these matters. My father, may Allah be pleased with him, related to me, saying: I heard the jurist Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Mu'adh al-Mahdawi in al-Mahdiyya say: I heard 'Abd al-Haqq al-Saqqali say this statement, and interpret this verse in this interpretation (p-621), and that it refutes these groups.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Some of the usuliyyun (scholars of the principles of jurisprudence) mentioned this. It has also been said: the pronoun in "ashhadtuhum" refers to the offspring of Iblis, so this verse, according to this view, contains their belittlement. The first opinion is greater in benefit. I say: the primary intended purpose of the verse is Iblis and his offspring, and in this sense the refutation of the aforementioned groups is directed, as well as the soothsayers (kuhhan) and the Arabs who believed them and who venerated the jinn when they say, "I seek refuge in the mighty one of this valley," since all of these groups are attached to Iblis and his offspring, and they have misled everyone. They are therefore the primary intended by "al-mudillin" (the misleaders), and these groups fall within their meaning.

Al-Jumhur recited "ashhadtuhum," while Abu Ja'far, 'Awf al-'Aqili, and Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani recited "ashhadnahum." Al-Jumhur recited "wa ma kuntu," while Abu Ja'far, al-Jahdari, and al-Hasan (in one report) recited "wa ma kunta." The description "al-mudillin" applies to the aforementioned groups and to the offspring of Iblis, may Allah curse him. "Al-'adud" (helper) is a metaphor for one who aids and supports, and it is a likeness to the human arm (adud), which a person relies upon. Al-Jumhur recited "'adudan" with a fatha on the 'ayn and a damma on the dad. Abu 'Amr and al-Hasan recited both with a damma. al-Dahhak recited with a kasra on the 'ayn and a fatha on the dad. 'Ikrima recited "'udan" with a damma on the 'ayn and sukun on the dad. 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited "'adadan" with a fatha on both the 'ayn and the dad. There are other dialectal forms besides these that were not recited.

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And on the Day He will say﴾, the verse is a warning, and the meaning is: remember the Day. Talha, Yahya, al-A'mash, and Hamza recited "naqulu" with the plural of majesty (nun al-'azama). Al-Jumhur recited with the ya', i.e., "yaqulu" (He will say), Allah the Exalted, to the disbelievers who associated partners with Him in the world other than Him: ﴿Call upon My partners﴾ in the manner of seeking help from them. His saying "shurakai" (My partners) means: according to your claim, O polytheists, and this is explained by His saying: ﴿whom you claimed﴾. Ibn Kathir and the people of Makkah recited "shurakai" with an open ya', and al-Jumhur recited "shurakai" with a hamza, and among them are those who made it fully articulated and those who lightened it. "Al-za'm" (claim) is only ever used for what is not certain; rather, most of its use is for falsehood, and this verse is among such uses. Its highest usage is when "za'ama" is used with the meaning of "akhbara" (informed), where the responsibility for the report falls upon the reporter, as Sibawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, says: "za'ama al-Khalil." His saying: ﴿so they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them﴾ its apparent meaning is that this actually occurs, and it may be a metaphor, as if the thought and reflection of the disbelievers, that those lifeless things do not avail anything nor benefit, is equivalent to calling and not answering. The first is clearer.

The interpreters differed concerning His saying, the Exalted: "mawbiqan" (a barrier of destruction). 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, Anas ibn Malik, and Mujahid said: it is a valley in Hell that flows with blood and pus. Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it separates the people of the Fire from the believers. Thus His saying, according to this, "baynahum" (between them) is an adverbial phrase of place. al-Hasan said: "mawbiqan" means enmity, and "baynahum," according to this, is an adverbial phrase. Some of this group hold that the pronoun in His saying, the Exalted, "baynahum" refers to the believers and the disbelievers, and it may refer to the polytheists and their deities in the world. As for the first interpretation, the pronoun in it refers to the polytheists and their deities. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "mawbiqan" means: destroying, in the sense of a place, and it derives from your saying: "wabaqa al-rajul," and "awbaqahu ghayruhu" when he destroyed him. His saying, the Exalted, "baynahum," according to this interpretation, may be an adverbial phrase, and the more apparent view is that it is a noun, meaning: We made their association a destructive matter for them, and "baynahum" is the first object of "ja'alna." Some expressed "al-mawbiq" as the threat, and this is weak.

Then the Almighty informed concerning the seeing of the criminals of the Fire, their witnessing of it, and the knowledge coming to them that they are going to be in direct contact with it. Most people hold that "al-zann" (assumption) here means certainty.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Had the Exalted said, in place of "zannu," "ayqanu" (they were certain), the speech would have been consistent, emphasizing it. But the expression with "al-zann" never comes in a place of complete certainty that has been reached by the senses; rather, its highest level is that it comes in a place of verified knowledge but in which the supposed event did not occur. Otherwise, what occurs and is sensed is hardly ever expressed with "al-zann" in Arabic speech. Reflect on this verse, and reflect on the words of Durayd:

"So I said to them: assume (zunnu) with two thousand armored men."

﴿Nothing prevented the people from believing when the guidance came to them, and from asking their Lord for forgiveness, except that the way of the earlier peoples should come upon them, or that the punishment should come before them face to face.﴾ ﴿We send the messengers only as bringers of good news and warners. Those who disbelieve argue with falsehood in order to overturn the truth with it, and they take My signs and what they were warned of as a mockery.﴾ ﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord, then turns away from them and forgets what his hands have sent forward? Indeed, We have placed coverings over their hearts so that they do not understand it, and deafness in their ears. And if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided, ever.﴾

This is a verse expressing regret over them and an admonition about the corruption of their state. This refusal was not, on their part, a deliberate choice to hold back so that the punishment would come upon them. Rather, they refused while believing themselves to be correct, but the matter in itself leads them to this. Thus their condition calls for regret over them. "The people" (al-nās) refers to the disbelievers of the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who undertook to repel the Sharia and to deny it. "Guidance" (al-Hudā) is the Sharia of Allah the Exalted and the clarification that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. "Seeking forgiveness" (al-istighfār) here means asking for forgiveness for a past sin, disbelief or otherwise. ﴿The way of the earlier peoples﴾ is the punishment of the nations mentioned, such as drowning, the shout, the overshadowing cloud, the wind, and other things.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or that the punishment should come before them face to face﴾, i.e., directly in front of them, visibly. The meaning is a punishment unlike the customary one, so the purpose of the division becomes clear. And this threat was indeed fulfilled at Badr. Mujahid said: "qubulan" means "suddenly."

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Mujahid and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "qibalan" with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba'. 'Asim, al-Kisa'i, Hamza, al-Hasan and al-A'raj read "qubulan" with a damma on both the qaf and the ba'. This reading can carry two meanings. One is that it means "qibal" (in front of), since Abu 'Isa related both with the same meaning in the sense of facing. The other is that it is the plural of "qubayl," meaning that the punishment comes to them in kinds and varieties. Abu Raja' and al-Hasan also read "qubulan" with a damma on the qaf and a sukun on the ba'.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We send the messengers only...﴾ the verse. It is as if, when He lamented over them, over their misguidance, and over their destination toward ruin by their own opinions, He said: the matter is not as they supposed. The messengers were not sent to argue, nor so that their whims should be imposed upon them as demands. Rather, We sent them as bringers of good news to whoever believes in Paradise, and as warners to whoever disbelieves in the Fire. "Yudhḥiḍū" means "to be annihilated" (yazhaqū). The "daḥḍ" is the mud in which one slips. From this is the saying of the poet:

"I perished, while the Yashkurī's wall saved him, and he swerved as a camel swerves from the slippery mud."

In His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and they took...﴾ to the end of the verse, there is a threat. "Āyāt" (signs) includes the verses of the Qur'an and the proofs that appeared upon the tongue of Muhammad (ﷺ). His saying: ﴿and what they were warned of as a mockery﴾ means: of the punishment of the Hereafter. The construction implies: "and what they were warned of," so the pronoun was omitted. "Al-huzʾ" is ridicule and belittling, like their saying: "fables of the ancients," and their saying: "If we wished, we would say the like of this."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And who is more unjust﴾ is an interrogation in the sense of affirmation (taqrīr). This is one of the most eloquent forms of affirmation: a person is confronted with something for which he has no answer except what his opponent wants. So the meaning is: no one is more unjust than one who has this description, who turns away from the signs after being made aware of them through admonition, forgets, and discards the grave sins he committed in the past. This is the extreme of neglect. The attribution of the evil deeds to the two hands is because the two hands are the instrument of acquisition in criminal affairs, so it is made like this in meanings as a metaphor (isti'āra).

Then Allah the Exalted informed about them and about His action toward them, as a recompense for their opposition and their acquisition of the ugly, that Allah the Exalted placed over their hearts coverings (akinna). These are the plural of kinān, which is the protecting sheath.

One is that this general expression is meant in a specific sense, referring to those for whom Allah has decreed that they will never believe nor be guided, ever, and whoever Allah has decreed guidance for at a later stage is excluded from the generality. The other is that it means: even if you call them all to guidance, they will never all believe, ever; that is, some individuals among them may believe. The words of the Exalted:

When the Exalted informed about the people whom He had sealed in their disbelief, that they would never be guided, He followed that with (p-627) the statement that He is, for the believers, the Forgiving, the Possessor of mercy. Al-Ṭabarī said: it is the Day of Badr and the Gathering. And "al-maw'il" means the refuge, a place of escape; it is said: "wa'ila al-rajulu ya'ilu" when a man escaped. From this is the saying of the poet:

﴿Never let your soul perish; you released it to the ʿĀmirites and it was not wounded.﴾

And from it is the saying of al-Aʿshā:

﴿So I may steal from the lord of the house his heedlessness, and though he guards against me, yet he does not escape.﴾

Then the Exalted followed their threat with the mention of examples from the cities upon which had descended what He threatened these [people] with the like of. In the Exalted's saying "And those are the cities," a noun has been omitted; its estimate is: "And those are the people of the cities." "Al-qurā" means the towns. This indication refers to ʿĀd, Thamūd, Madyan and others. "Tilka" is the subject (mubtada'), (p-628) "al-qurā" is a qualifier (ṣifa), and "ahlaknāhum" is the predicate (khabar). It is also permissible for "tilka" to be in the accusative, governed by a verb indicated by "ahlaknāhum."

The majority read "li-muhlakihim" with a damma on the mim and a fatḥa on the lam, from "ahlaka." Muf'il in such a form may denote the time or place of the thing, and may be a verbal noun; the verbal noun, on this reading, is in the genitive construction with its object. ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Abū Bakr, read "li-mahlakihim" with fatḥa on the mim and the lam; and in the transmission of Ḥafṣ he read "li-mahlikihim" with fatḥa on the mim and kasra on the lam, which is a verbal noun from "halaka," and it is, in the well-known usage of the language, intransitive. On this reading the verbal noun is in the genitive construction with the agent, since it means: "and We made for them, because they perished, an appointed time." A group said that "halaka" is transitive; you say "ahlaktu al-rajul" and "halaktuhu" with one meaning, and Abū ʿAlī cited in support:

﴿And a deadly desert whoever crosses it...﴾

On this view the verbal noun in every respect is in the genitive construction with the object.

The Exalted's saying "And when Moses said" is the verse... It is the beginning of a narrative not part of the first discourse, and the meaning is: "Remember," or "recite." "Mūsā" is Moses son of ʿImrān according to the ḥadīths and the histories, and according to the apparent sense of the Qurʾān, since there is no Moses in the Qurʾān other than this one, the son of ʿImrān, and had there been another in this verse, it would have specified him. A group, among them Nawf al-Bakkālī, said that he is not the son of ʿImrān, but Moses son of Mathnā; it is also said: Moses son of Manshā. As for his servant, according to the view that he is Moses son of ʿImrān, he is Yūshaʿ son of Nūn son of Afrāyīm son of Yūsuf son of Yaʿqūb. As for the one who said he is Moses son of Mathnā, the youth is not Yūshaʿ son of Nūn; but this is an incorrect view, rejected by Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others. This is an encouragement to humility. "Al-fatā" in the verse is the servant, and Yūshaʿ son of Nūn is said to be the son of the sister of Moses, peace be upon him.

The occasion of this narrative, as related from the Prophet ﷺ, is that Moses sat one day in an assembly of the Children of Israel and delivered a sermon, and he was asked: "Do you know anyone more knowledgeable than you?" He said: "No." So Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "Yes, Our servant al-Khiḍr." He said: "My Lord, guide me to the way of meeting him." Allah the Exalted revealed to him that he should travel along the shore of the sea until he reaches the junction of the two seas; "when you lose the fish, he is there." He was commanded to take provisions and to watch for its disappearance. Moses did so, and he said to his servant, by way of resolving the determination: "I will not cease," that is, "I will not stop" (lā uzāl); and he said this statement while he was travelling. From this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

﴿So they did not cease until their women were carried along in litters at Baṭḥāʾ Dhī Qār, the fine perfumed garments swaying.﴾

Al-Ṭabarī mentions from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: When Moses, peace be upon him, and his people prevailed over Egypt, he settled his people in Egypt; then when the situation was settled, he delivered a sermon one day, reminding them of the blessings of Allah and His days among the Children of Israel, then he mentioned much of what has preceded.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I have never come across the report that Moses, peace be upon him, settled his people in Egypt except in this speech, and I do not think it is sound. Rather, what is apparent is that Moses, peace be upon him, died in the wilderness of the Tīh before the conquest of the land of the giants. Al-Jumhūr read "majma'" with fatḥa on both mims, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read "majmiʿi" with kasra on the second mim.

People differed about "majma' al-baḥrayn," where it is. Mujāhid and Qatāda said: it is the junction of the Sea of Persia and the Sea of Rome.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an inlet that comes out of the Encompassing Sea from north to south in the land of Persia, beyond Azerbaijan. So the corner where the two seas meet, on the side facing the land of al-Shām, is "majma' al-baḥrayn" according to this view. A group, among them Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, said: the junction of the two seas is at Tangier, where the Encompassing Sea meets the sea that comes out of it, running from the south-west wind to the east wind. It is narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that he said: "majma' al-baḥrayn" is in Ifrīqiyya, and this is close to the previous one. Some scholars said: it is the sea of al-Andalus from the Encompassing Sea.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is one (location), related by al-Naqqāsh, and this is much mentioned. It is mentioned that the town which refused to host them is al-Jazīra al-Khaḍrā'. A group said: "majma' al-baḥrayn" means a salt sea and a sweet sea.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this view, al-Khiḍr was only at the spot where a great river meets the sea. A group said: the two seas are only a metaphor for Moses, peace be upon him, and al-Khiḍr, since they are two seas of knowledge.

All of this is one (location), related by al-Naqqāsh, and this is much mentioned. It is mentioned that the town which refused to host them is al-Jazīra al-Khaḍrā'. A group said: "majma' al-baḥrayn" means a salt sea and a sweet sea.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this view, al-Khiḍr was only at the spot where a great river meets the sea. A group said: the two seas are only a metaphor for Moses, peace be upon him, and al-Khiḍr, since they are two seas of knowledge.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a weak view, and the matter is clear from the ḥadīths that he was only directed to a particular sea. As for His saying: ﴿or I will continue for a long period﴾ its meaning is: "or I will continue on my way for a period of time." The reciters differed: al-Ḥasan, al-Aʿmash and ʿĀṣim read "ḥuqban" with a sukūn on the qāf; the majority read "ḥuqubān" with a damma, which is (p-631) the heavier form of "ḥuqb," and the plural of "ḥuqb" is "aḥqāb." The meaning of "ḥuqb" has been disputed: ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr said: eighty years; Mujāhid said: seventy years; al-Farrāʾ said: "ḥuqb" is one year; Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda said: "ḥuqb" is indefinite periods of time; and a group said: "ḥuqb" is the plural of "ḥiqba," which is a year.

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿So when they reached the junction of the two seas, they forgot their fish, and it took its way into the sea, a tunnel.﴾ ﴿Then when they had passed beyond, he said to his young man, "Bring us our morning meal; indeed we have suffered fatigue from this journey of ours."﴾ ﴿He said, "Did you see when we took refuge at the rock? Indeed I forgot the fish, and none but Satan made me forget it, that I should mention it. And it took its way into the sea in an amazing manner."﴾ ﴿He said, "That is what we were seeking." So they went back, retracing their footsteps.﴾ ﴿And they found a servant from among Our servants, whom We had given mercy from Us and taught knowledge from Us.﴾

The pronoun in His saying "baynihima" (between them) refers to the two seas. This is the view of Mujahid. It was also said that it refers to Musa and al-Khidr, but the first view is more correct. 'Ubayd Allah ibn Muslim read "majma'" with a kasra on the second mim, and read "nasiya" (both forgot). The forgetting was from the young man alone: he forgot to inform Musa, peace be upon him, of what he had seen of the fish's condition, since it was their provision, and the cause was from him. So the act of one of them is attributed to both, as one says, "The sons of so-and-so did such-and-such," when only some of them did it. It is related in a hadith that Yusha' saw the fish had been released from the basket into the sea, and saw that it had made a tunnel for itself. Musa, peace be upon him, was sleeping, so he felt compassion and did not want to wake him, and said, "I will wait until he awakens." When he awoke, Yusha' forgot to inform him, and they set off until they had passed beyond. "Al-sabil" means the path, and "al-sarab" means a passage in the depths of the earth. The passage of the fish in the water, when the water did not close again behind it, was likened to a tunnel (ṭāq). This is what is reported in the hadith from the Prophet ﷺ, and what the majority of the exegetes said: that the fish's passage remained as water that had solidified. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: the place of its passage became a hard rock (p-632). Ibn Zayd said: it took its path as a tunnel on land until it reached the sea, then it swam in its usual manner.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These scholars interpret "sarab" to mean moving freely and roaming, from their saying "fahl sarib," meaning an unrestrained stallion that grazes wherever it wishes. From this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿and one who goes freely by day﴾ [al-Ra'd: 10], meaning one who moves about. Another group said: it made a tunnel in the earth from the basket to the sea, and along its path it encountered a rock and bored through it.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning is that the tunnel was in the water. Among the strange reports in al-Bukhari from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, concerning the narrative of this verse, is that the fish came back to life only because it was touched by the water of a spring there called the Spring of Life, which never touches anything without it coming to life. Also among its strange features is that some exegetes mentioned that the place of the fish's passage turned back into a paved rock path, and that Musa, peace be upon him, walked along it following the fish until that path led him to an island in the sea, where he found al-Khidr, peace be upon him.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of the Book and the narrations is that he found al-Khidr on the bank of the sea. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿so they went back, retracing their footsteps﴾. It is related concerning His saying: ﴿Then when they had passed beyond﴾ that Musa, peace be upon him, alighted near a great tree on the bank of the sea, and Yusha' forgot the fish there. Then Musa awoke, and they journeyed the remainder of the night and the early part of their day. Musa became hungry and was overtaken by the weariness of the road, so he asked for the morning meal.

My father, may Allah be pleased with him, said to me: I heard Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari say in his sermon: Musa went to the place of intimate conversation and remained forty days without needing food, but when he went to a human being, hunger overtook him on part of a day. "Al-nasb" means fatigue and hardship. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read "nisban" with a damma on the nun and the sad, and it seems to be the plural of "nasb," which is a lightened form of "nasab."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "Did you see when we took refuge"﴾ — the verse. Al-Tabari related from a group that they said: "the rock" ...

(p-633)

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The dispute concerning the location of this story has already been mentioned.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿I forgot the fish﴾ means: I forgot the mention of what happened to it concerning you. As for al-Kisa'i alone, he read "ansanihi." Ibn Kathir in continuous recitation read "ansanihi-ī" with a yā' after the hā'. In the codex of 'Abd Allah it reads: "wa-ma ansanihu an adhkurahu lahu illa al-shaytan." His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And it took its way into the sea in an amazing manner﴾ may be from the words of Yusha' to Musa, peace be upon him, meaning: the fish took its way, an amazing thing for people. It may also be that His saying "wa-ittakhadha sabilahu fi al-bahr" completes the report, and then he began an expression of wonder, saying on his own account: "amazing" at this matter. The point of wonder is that the fish had died and its left side had been eaten, and then it came back to life after that. Abu Shuja' said in the book of al-Tabari: "I saw it; it was brought to us, and behold, one side of it was fish and one eye, and the other side had nothing in it."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I too have seen it: the side that had something had a thin skin beneath which its spine and its other side could be seen.

It may also be that His saying: ﴿and it took its way into the sea in an amazing manner﴾ is an report from Allah, the Exalted, and this has two aspects: either He reports about Musa that he took the fish's path into the sea as an amazing thing, meaning he marvelled at it, or He reports about the fish that it took its path as an amazing thing for people. The meaning: Musa said to his young man, "The matter of the fish and its loss is what we were seeking, for the man we came for is ..." then they returned, tracing back their steps, lest they miss their way. The majority read "nabghi" with the yā' affirmed; 'Asim and a group read "nabgha" without a yā'; al-Hasan affirmed it in pausal pronunciation when connected and omitted it when pausing. "Qass al-athar" means following it and seeking it in a place of concealment.

(p-634)

"The servant" is al-Khidr according to the majority, in accordance with the hadiths. Whoever is not taken into account in opinion opposed this and said: the companion of Musa is not al-Khidr, but another scholar. Al-Khidr is a prophet according to the majority, and it was said he is a righteous servant who is not a prophet.

The verse testifies to his prophethood, since were not the inner dimensions of his actions only by revelation from Allah? It is related in a hadith that Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon them both, found him wrapped in his garment, lying on his back on the ground. He said to him, "Peace be upon you." Al-Khidr raised his head and said, "And how is there peace in your land?" Then he said to him, "Who are you?" He said, "I am Musa." He said, "Musa of the Children of Israel?" He said, "Yes." He said to him, "Did you not have among the Children of Israel what occupied you from travelling here?" He said, "Indeed, but I loved to meet you and to learn from you." He said to him, "Indeed I am upon a knowledge from the knowledge of Allah which He taught me that you do not know, and you are upon a knowledge from the knowledge of Allah which He taught you that I do not know."

He said, "The one who seeks the knowledge of people to his knowledge, perhaps he will obtain a word of guidance that leads him." He said, "O Lord, is there anyone on earth?" He said, "Yes," so he asked the way to meet him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verse 66–73:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Moses said to him, "May I follow you on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, [that of] guidance?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me."﴾ ﴿"And how can you have patience over that which you do not encompass in knowledge?"﴾ ﴿He said, "You will find me, if Allah wills, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter."﴾ ﴿He said, "If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you."﴾ ﴿So they set out until, when they boarded the ship, he tore it open. [Moses] said, "Have you torn it open to drown its people? You have certainly done a terrible thing."﴾ ﴿He said, "Did I not say that you would not be able to have patience with me?"﴾ ﴿[Moses] said, "Do not blame me for what I forgot and do not impose upon me difficulty for my affair."﴾

This is an address of one who seeks to be humbled, exaggerating in good manners. The meaning: "Will it be possible for you [to show me], and will it be hidden from you?" This is like what is in the hadith: "Are you able to show me how the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to perform ablution?" And according to some interpretations, His saying, Exalted is He, also comes in this sense: ﴿Is your Lord able to send down to us a table [spread with food] from the heaven?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 112].

Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and 'Asim read "rushdan" with the shin lightened (rushdan), and it is the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. Ibn 'Amir read "rushudan," and Abu 'Amr read "rashadan" with the ra' and shin both fatha. It is in the accusative on two grounds: one is that it is a second object of "tu'allimani" (teach me), and the other is that it is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun in His saying "attabi'uka" (follow you).

Then al-Khidr said: ﴿Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me﴾, meaning: Indeed you, O Moses, cannot endure to be patient over what you see of my actions, because the outward appearances of which you have been taught do not give it [i.e., the inner reality]. ﴿And how can you have patience over (p-636) that which you see as wrong, while you have not been informed of the wisdom in it nor the correct aspect?﴾ So Moses brought the matter near to him by his promise that he would find him patient. Then he made an exception when he passed judgment upon himself with a matter, so al-Khidr reinforced his admonition and ordered him to refrain from questioning and from holding back [his objection] concerning what he sees, until al-Khidr himself begins to explain what must be explained.

Nafi' read "fala tas'alanniyy" with the lam fatha, shaddah on the nun, and the ya' affirmed. Ibn 'Amir likewise, except that he omitted the ya', saying "fala tas'alann." Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "fala tas'alni" with the lam sukun and the ya' affirmed. The majority read "khubran" with the ba' sukun, while al-A'raj read "khubura" with it vowelled.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, "fa-ntalaqa" (so they set out): it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that they set out walking along the shore of the sea until a ship passed by them, and al-Khidr was recognized, so they were carried without a fare to the destination of the people of al-Khidr. The word "safinah" (ship) is defined with the alif and lam as a definition of the genus, not referring to a specific ship. When they boarded, al-Khidr deliberately went to a peg and began striking at the side of the ship until he reached, according to what is narrated, two of its planks; that is the meaning of "kharaqahā" (he tore it open). When Moses (peace be upon him) saw this, the apparent gravity of the matter overcame his speech, since he saw an act that would lead to the drowning of everyone on the ship, so he halted him with his words: "Have you torn it open?" Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read "li-tughriqa ahlahā" with the ta', while Abu Raja' read "li-tugharriqa ahlahā" with the ra' shaddah and the ghayn fatha. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "li-yaghraqa ahluhā" with the ahl in the nominative, attributing the verb to them.

"Al-imr" means the monstrous among matters, like the calamity and the grave matter and the like. From it comes "amira amru Ibn Abi Kabshah," and from it: "amira al-qawm" when they became numerous.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Al-imr" is more specific than "al-munkar" (the reprehensible).

Then al-Khidr replied to Moses: ﴿Did I not say that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾, so Moses became alert to what he had brought with him, and he excused himself by forgetfulness, because he had forgotten the covenant that was between them. This is the statement of the majority. In the Book of Tafsir of the Sahih of al-Bukhari, it is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The first [of Moses' objections] was forgetfulness." (p-637) And in it, from Mujahid, that he said: "The first was forgetfulness, the second was a condition, and the third was deliberate."

For the saying of His, Exalted is He, ﴿Do not blame me for what I forgot﴾ is a fine statement of request, and it contains no mention of the covenant, whether he forgot it or not, and it contains an allusion that he had forgotten the covenant. Thus in this word he combined excuse and truthfulness, and nothing spoils this statement except that what he said, and Ubayy related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The first was forgetfulness."

And "turhiqni" means: burden me and constrain me.

Among what is recounted of their affair: when they boarded the ship and it moved, a sparrow alighted on the side of the ship and pecked once into the water. Al-Khidr said to Moses: "What do you see this sparrow has diminished from the water of the sea?" Moses said: "A little." He said: "O Moses, my knowledge and your knowledge have not diminished from the knowledge of Allah except as much as this sparrow has diminished from the water of the sea."

(p-638) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It has been said: the meaning of this statement is the placing of knowledge in the position of the things known; otherwise the knowledge of Allah, blessed and exalted, cannot be likened to what is finite, since it is not finite, and the sea, even if sparrows were assumed to be in number equal to its drops, would be exhausted. In my view, the objection may intend: from the knowledge of Allah which He gave to the scholars before them both and after them until the Day of Resurrection, so the proportion of His knowledge to the knowledge of mankind is the proportion of that drop to the sea.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a good statement, were it not that in some chains of the hadith there is: "My knowledge and your knowledge and the knowledge of all creation, in the knowledge of Allah, are nothing but like the pecking of this sparrow." So with this, there remains only that the comparison is by way of figurative speech, since among sensible things there is nothing more minute in smallness than a drop in relation to the sea, so it is as if it were nothing, since it has no known proportion to the sea.

**Ibn 'Atiyya, *al-Muharrar al-Wajiz*, on Surah al-Kahf, verses 74–78**

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said:

﴿So they set out until, when they met a boy, he killed him. [Moses] said, "Have you killed an innocent soul, other than for a soul? You have certainly done a terrible thing."﴾ ﴿[Al-Khidr] said, "Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?"﴾ ﴿[Moses] said, "If I ask you about anything after this, then do not keep me as a companion. You have已经 reached an excuse from my side."﴾ ﴿So they set out until, when they came to the people of a town and asked its people for food, they refused to host them. And they found in it a wall about to collapse, so he set it upright. [Moses] said, "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it."﴾ ﴿[Al-Khidr] said, "This is the parting between me and you. I will inform you of the interpretation of that about which you could not have patience."﴾

"Set out" refers to their departure from the place where they had disembarked from the ship. They passed by boys playing, and al-Khidr deliberately targeted a boy of fine appearance and beautiful form and tore off his head. It is said that he crushed him with a stone. It is also said that he slaughtered him. Some people said that the boy had not reached puberty, and for this reason Moses said "innocent" (*zakiyyah*), meaning that he had committed no sin. Another group said that he was in fact a young man, and the Arabs still apply the term "boy" (*ghulam*) to a young man. From this is the saying of Layla al-Akhyaliyyah:

*A boy who, when he shakes the spear, gives it drink*

This is said in describing al-Hajjaj. In a report it is mentioned that this boy used to spread corruption on the earth and would swear to his parents about what he had done, and they would confirm his oath and protect him from anyone seeking him.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Nafi' and the majority read *zakiyyah* as *zakiyyatan* (with an alif, "zaakiyah"), while al-Hasan, 'Asim and al-Jahdari read *zakiyyatan* (without the alif). The meaning is the same, though some have held that there is a distinction, which is not clear. His saying *bi-ghayri nafs* ("other than for a soul") implies that if he had killed in retaliation for a soul, there would have been no fault. This indicates that the boy was grown; otherwise, if he had not reached puberty, his killing would not be obligatory either for a soul or for no soul.

The majority read *nukran* (a terrible thing). Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far and Shayba read *nukuran* with a damma on the kaf, while the reading from Nafi' varies. Its meaning is: something that is denounced.

People differed as to which of the two is more forceful: his saying *imran* or his saying *nukran*. One group said: this is a clear killing, and beyond it lies something anticipated, and *nukran* is more forceful. Another group said: this is the killing of one person, whereas *imran* is the killing of a group, so *imran* is more forceful.

The author (Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him) said:

In my view, they are for two different meanings: his saying *imran* is more dreadful and more terrifying, in that it is an expected great matter, while *nukran* is clearer in corruption, because its harm has already occurred.

"Half of the Qur'an comes after the letter *nun*, or it ends at the *nun* in His saying *nukran*."

His saying ﴿Did I not tell you﴾ contains rebuke and harshness not found in his earlier saying ﴿Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾ (al-Kahf: 72). His saying *ba'daha* ("after this") means: after this story. He returned the pronoun to it although it had no explicit prior mention, because it was implied within the speech.

The majority read *fa-la tusahibunni* ("do not keep me as a companion"), which Ubayy related from the Prophet (ﷺ). 'Isa and Ya'qub read *fa-la tasbahni*. 'Isa also read *fa-la tushbihni* with a damma on the ta and a kasra on the ha, and this was related by Sahl from Abu 'Amr. The meaning is: do not make me a companion in your knowledge. Al-A'raj read *fa-la tasbahanni* with a fatha on the ta and the ba and a shadda on the nun.

His saying *qad balaghta min ladunni 'udhran* means: you have indeed given me an excuse, and you have reached the excuse from my side.

The author (Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It seems that this story is the basis for the time-limits in rulings, which are three days, and the periods of waiting (*tallawwum*) are three. So reflect on this.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read *min ladunni* with a fatha on the lam, a damma on the dal and a shadda on the nun. Here *ladun* is joined to the pronoun nun of the first person (as in *darabani*, "he struck me"), so assimilation occurred. This is the reading of the Prophet (ﷺ). Nafi' and 'Asim read *min ladunnī* as in the first reading, except that the nun is light, so it is *ladun* joined to the first-person *ya'* as in *ghulami* ("my boy"), with the letter before the ya' having a kasra as it does in this word. Abu Bakr from 'Asim read *min ladnī* with a fatha on the lam, a sukun on the dal and a light nun. This is a lightened form of *ladunī*, which we mentioned before this. It is related from 'Asim as *min ludnī* with a damma on the lam and a sukun on the dal. Mujahid said: this is a mistake. Abu 'Ali said: this criticism seems to be due to the transmission; but according to the rules of Arabic, it is correct. Al-Hasan read *min ladnī* with a fatha on the lam and a sukun on the dal.

The majority read *'udran*. Abu 'Amr and 'Isa read *'udurran* with a damma on the dal. Al-Dani related that Ubayy reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) *'udhrī* with a kasra on the ra and a ya' after it. Al-Tabari related with an isnad that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whenever he supplicated for someone, began with himself. He said one day: "May the mercy of Allah be upon us and upon Moses. Had he been patient with his companion, he would have seen wonders. But he said: *'So do not keep me as a companion; you have indeed given me an excuse from my side.'*"

In al-Bukhari, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on Moses. We wished he had been patient until he would have related to us the account of the two of them."

It is reported in the exegesis of this verse that Allah the Exalted made these examples that occurred to Moses with al-Khidr a proof against Moses and a source of wonder for him. That is because when he denied the matter of the damaging of the ship, it was said to him: "O Moses, where was your management of this while you were cast into the sea in the chest?" When he denied the matter of the boy, it was said to him: "Where is your denial of this from your hiding of the Copt and your judgment against him?" When he denied the raising of the wall, it was said to him: "Where is this from your lifting of the stone of the well for the daughters of Shu'ayb without a wage?"

His saying *fa-ntalaqa* ("so they set out") means that al-Khidr and Moses walked, seeking out from al-Khidr a matter in which what he possessed of the knowledge of Allah the Exalted would take effect. They passed by a town and asked its people to feed them, but they refused. In a hadith, they were walking past the gatherings of those people, asking them for food.

The author (Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This expression explicitly states the lowliness of this world before Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

People differed about the town. Muhammad ibn Sirin said: it is al-Ubullah, the stingiest town and the farthest from the sky. Another group said: it is Antakya. Another group said: it is Burqa. Another group said: it is in the Island of al-Andalus. This was related from Abu Hurayrah and others, and it is said that it is al-Jazirah al-Khadra'. Another group said: it is Abu Hurran, which is in the region of Adharbayjan.

The author (Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him) said:

All of this is according to the disagreement about which region of the earth the story of Moses, peace be upon him, took place in, and Allah knows best the reality of that.

The majority read *yudayyifuhuma* with a fatha on the dad and a shadda on the ya'. Abu Raja' read *yudayyifuhuma* with a kasra on the dad and a sukun on the ya'. This is the reading of Ibn Muhaysin, al-Zubayr and Abu Razin. *Al-dayf* (the guest) is derived from *dafa ila al-makan*, meaning to incline towards a place, and from it comes *al-idafah* (the annexation), which is the inclining of one thing towards another. Al-A'mash read *fa-aba an yut'imuhuma* ("they refused to feed them").

His saying, Exalted is He, about the wall: ﴿about to collapse﴾ is a metaphor (*isti'arah*). All the verbs whose proper subject is a living, speaking being, when they are attributed to an inanimate object or an animal, are in fact metaphorical; that is, if a human being were in the place of the inanimate object, he would be carrying out that action. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

*Will you cease? And one who forbids the transgressors ... is not like a spear-thrust in which oil and wick go away.*

Here he attributed the forbidding to the spear-thrust. From this is the saying of the poet:

*The spear desires the chest of Abu Baraʾ, and turns away from the blood of the Banu 'Uqayl.*

From this is the saying of 'Antarah:

*And he complained to me with tears and neighing.*

He explained this meaning with his saying:

*If he had known what dialogue is, he would have complained... (the verse).*

From this is the common saying: "My house looks at the house of so-and-so." And from it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Their fires should not see one another." This is very common.

The majority read *yanqadd*, meaning: it falls. It is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) read, as is related from him: *an yunqada* with a damma on the mim and a lightened dad, and this is the reading of Ubayy. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and 'Ikrimah read *an yanqasa* with an unpointed sad, meaning: it splits lengthwise. It is said: *inqasa al-jidar* ("the wall split"), and *inqasa al-bi'r* ("the well split"), and *inqasat al-sinn* ("the tooth split") when it is split lengthwise. It is also said that it means it cracks in any way. From this is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

*A parting like the chipping of a tooth, so patience, for it is a stumbling and a mending for every person.*

It is also related as *'ibrah* and *huburu*, with ba' and ha'. Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash read *yurid li-yanqadda*.

The exegetes differed about his saying *fa-aqamahu* ("so he set it upright"). One group said: he demolished it and sat down to rebuild it. This occurred in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, and this interpretation is supported by Moses, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it﴾, because this is an act that deserves a wage. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: rather, he wiped it with his hand and it stood up.

The author (Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him) said:

A hadith has been related about this, and it is the more likely of the deeds of the prophets, peace be upon them.

Then Moses said to al-Khidr: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it﴾, meaning: food that we could eat. The majority read *la-ittakhadhta*. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *la-takhidhta*, which is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and Qatadah. Some readers assimilated the dhal into the ta and some did not. From the usage of "takhidha" is the saying of the poet:

*And my leg has taken, beside its stirrup, a limping step like the pressed-down footprint of the sandgrouse.*

In the codex of Ubayy: *law shi'ta la-utiyta 'alayhi ajran* ("if you had wished, you would have been given a wage for it").

Then al-Khidr said to Moses, according to their condition: ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾. Al-Khidr had made a condition, and Moses had given his word that he would not ask about anything. Asking is the least of the forms of objection, while denial and calling it an error is greater than it. His saying ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it﴾, although it is not a question, contains within it a denial of his action and an assertion that taking a wage was correct. In that there is a correction of the abandoning of the wage. As for his separating and repeating ﴿between me and you﴾ and his departure from "between us", it is for the sake of emphasis. The *sin* in his saying *sa-unabbi'uka* ("I will inform you") separates between the two dialogues and the two companionships, and indicates that the first has ended.
