﴿So they set out until, when they met a boy, he killed him. [Moses] said, "Have you killed an innocent soul, other than for a soul? You have certainly done a terrible thing."﴾ ﴿[Al-Khidr] said, "Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?"﴾ ﴿[Moses] said, "If I ask you about anything after this, then do not keep me as a companion. You have已经 reached an excuse from my side."﴾ ﴿So they set out until, when they came to the people of a town and asked its people for food, they refused to host them. And they found in it a wall about to collapse, so he set it upright. [Moses] said, "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it."﴾ ﴿[Al-Khidr] said, "This is the parting between me and you. I will inform you of the interpretation of that about which you could not have patience."﴾

"Set out" refers to their departure from the place where they had disembarked from the ship. They passed by boys playing, and al-Khidr deliberately targeted a boy of fine appearance and beautiful form and tore off his head. It is said that he crushed him with a stone. It is also said that he slaughtered him. Some people said that the boy had not reached puberty, and for this reason Moses said "innocent" (*zakiyyah*), meaning that he had committed no sin. Another group said that he was in fact a young man, and the Arabs still apply the term "boy" (*ghulam*) to a young man. From this is the saying of Layla al-Akhyaliyyah:

*A boy who, when he shakes the spear, gives it drink*

This is said in describing al-Hajjaj. In a report it is mentioned that this boy used to spread corruption on the earth and would swear to his parents about what he had done, and they would confirm his oath and protect him from anyone seeking him.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Nafi' and the majority read *zakiyyah* as *zakiyyatan* (with an alif, "zaakiyah"), while al-Hasan, 'Asim and al-Jahdari read *zakiyyatan* (without the alif). The meaning is the same, though some have held that there is a distinction, which is not clear. His saying *bi-ghayri nafs* ("other than for a soul") implies that if he had killed in retaliation for a soul, there would have been no fault. This indicates that the boy was grown; otherwise, if he had not reached puberty, his killing would not be obligatory either for a soul or for no soul.

The majority read *nukran* (a terrible thing). Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far and Shayba read *nukuran* with a damma on the kaf, while the reading from Nafi' varies. Its meaning is: something that is denounced.

People differed as to which of the two is more forceful: his saying *imran* or his saying *nukran*. One group said: this is a clear killing, and beyond it lies something anticipated, and *nukran* is more forceful. Another group said: this is the killing of one person, whereas *imran* is the killing of a group, so *imran* is more forceful.

The author (Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him) said:

In my view, they are for two different meanings: his saying *imran* is more dreadful and more terrifying, in that it is an expected great matter, while *nukran* is clearer in corruption, because its harm has already occurred.

"Half of the Qur'an comes after the letter *nun*, or it ends at the *nun* in His saying *nukran*."

His saying ﴿Did I not tell you﴾ contains rebuke and harshness not found in his earlier saying ﴿Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾ (al-Kahf: 72). His saying *ba'daha* ("after this") means: after this story. He returned the pronoun to it although it had no explicit prior mention, because it was implied within the speech.

The majority read *fa-la tusahibunni* ("do not keep me as a companion"), which Ubayy related from the Prophet (ﷺ). 'Isa and Ya'qub read *fa-la tasbahni*. 'Isa also read *fa-la tushbihni* with a damma on the ta and a kasra on the ha, and this was related by Sahl from Abu 'Amr. The meaning is: do not make me a companion in your knowledge. Al-A'raj read *fa-la tasbahanni* with a fatha on the ta and the ba and a shadda on the nun.

His saying *qad balaghta min ladunni 'udhran* means: you have indeed given me an excuse, and you have reached the excuse from my side.

The author (Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It seems that this story is the basis for the time-limits in rulings, which are three days, and the periods of waiting (*tallawwum*) are three. So reflect on this.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read *min ladunni* with a fatha on the lam, a damma on the dal and a shadda on the nun. Here *ladun* is joined to the pronoun nun of the first person (as in *darabani*, "he struck me"), so assimilation occurred. This is the reading of the Prophet (ﷺ). Nafi' and 'Asim read *min ladunnī* as in the first reading, except that the nun is light, so it is *ladun* joined to the first-person *ya'* as in *ghulami* ("my boy"), with the letter before the ya' having a kasra as it does in this word. Abu Bakr from 'Asim read *min ladnī* with a fatha on the lam, a sukun on the dal and a light nun. This is a lightened form of *ladunī*, which we mentioned before this. It is related from 'Asim as *min ludnī* with a damma on the lam and a sukun on the dal. Mujahid said: this is a mistake. Abu 'Ali said: this criticism seems to be due to the transmission; but according to the rules of Arabic, it is correct. Al-Hasan read *min ladnī* with a fatha on the lam and a sukun on the dal.

The majority read *'udran*. Abu 'Amr and 'Isa read *'udurran* with a damma on the dal. Al-Dani related that Ubayy reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) *'udhrī* with a kasra on the ra and a ya' after it. Al-Tabari related with an isnad that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whenever he supplicated for someone, began with himself. He said one day: "May the mercy of Allah be upon us and upon Moses. Had he been patient with his companion, he would have seen wonders. But he said: *'So do not keep me as a companion; you have indeed given me an excuse from my side.'*"

In al-Bukhari, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on Moses. We wished he had been patient until he would have related to us the account of the two of them."

It is reported in the exegesis of this verse that Allah the Exalted made these examples that occurred to Moses with al-Khidr a proof against Moses and a source of wonder for him. That is because when he denied the matter of the damaging of the ship, it was said to him: "O Moses, where was your management of this while you were cast into the sea in the chest?" When he denied the matter of the boy, it was said to him: "Where is your denial of this from your hiding of the Copt and your judgment against him?" When he denied the raising of the wall, it was said to him: "Where is this from your lifting of the stone of the well for the daughters of Shu'ayb without a wage?"

His saying *fa-ntalaqa* ("so they set out") means that al-Khidr and Moses walked, seeking out from al-Khidr a matter in which what he possessed of the knowledge of Allah the Exalted would take effect. They passed by a town and asked its people to feed them, but they refused. In a hadith, they were walking past the gatherings of those people, asking them for food.

The author (Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This expression explicitly states the lowliness of this world before Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

People differed about the town. Muhammad ibn Sirin said: it is al-Ubullah, the stingiest town and the farthest from the sky. Another group said: it is Antakya. Another group said: it is Burqa. Another group said: it is in the Island of al-Andalus. This was related from Abu Hurayrah and others, and it is said that it is al-Jazirah al-Khadra'. Another group said: it is Abu Hurran, which is in the region of Adharbayjan.

The author (Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him) said:

All of this is according to the disagreement about which region of the earth the story of Moses, peace be upon him, took place in, and Allah knows best the reality of that.

The majority read *yudayyifuhuma* with a fatha on the dad and a shadda on the ya'. Abu Raja' read *yudayyifuhuma* with a kasra on the dad and a sukun on the ya'. This is the reading of Ibn Muhaysin, al-Zubayr and Abu Razin. *Al-dayf* (the guest) is derived from *dafa ila al-makan*, meaning to incline towards a place, and from it comes *al-idafah* (the annexation), which is the inclining of one thing towards another. Al-A'mash read *fa-aba an yut'imuhuma* ("they refused to feed them").

His saying, Exalted is He, about the wall: ﴿about to collapse﴾ is a metaphor (*isti'arah*). All the verbs whose proper subject is a living, speaking being, when they are attributed to an inanimate object or an animal, are in fact metaphorical; that is, if a human being were in the place of the inanimate object, he would be carrying out that action. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

*Will you cease? And one who forbids the transgressors ... is not like a spear-thrust in which oil and wick go away.*

Here he attributed the forbidding to the spear-thrust. From this is the saying of the poet:

*The spear desires the chest of Abu Baraʾ, and turns away from the blood of the Banu 'Uqayl.*

From this is the saying of 'Antarah:

*And he complained to me with tears and neighing.*

He explained this meaning with his saying:

*If he had known what dialogue is, he would have complained... (the verse).*

From this is the common saying: "My house looks at the house of so-and-so." And from it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Their fires should not see one another." This is very common.

The majority read *yanqadd*, meaning: it falls. It is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) read, as is related from him: *an yunqada* with a damma on the mim and a lightened dad, and this is the reading of Ubayy. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and 'Ikrimah read *an yanqasa* with an unpointed sad, meaning: it splits lengthwise. It is said: *inqasa al-jidar* ("the wall split"), and *inqasa al-bi'r* ("the well split"), and *inqasat al-sinn* ("the tooth split") when it is split lengthwise. It is also said that it means it cracks in any way. From this is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

*A parting like the chipping of a tooth, so patience, for it is a stumbling and a mending for every person.*

It is also related as *'ibrah* and *huburu*, with ba' and ha'. Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash read *yurid li-yanqadda*.

The exegetes differed about his saying *fa-aqamahu* ("so he set it upright"). One group said: he demolished it and sat down to rebuild it. This occurred in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, and this interpretation is supported by Moses, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it﴾, because this is an act that deserves a wage. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: rather, he wiped it with his hand and it stood up.

The author (Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him) said:

A hadith has been related about this, and it is the more likely of the deeds of the prophets, peace be upon them.

Then Moses said to al-Khidr: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it﴾, meaning: food that we could eat. The majority read *la-ittakhadhta*. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *la-takhidhta*, which is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and Qatadah. Some readers assimilated the dhal into the ta and some did not. From the usage of "takhidha" is the saying of the poet:

*And my leg has taken, beside its stirrup, a limping step like the pressed-down footprint of the sandgrouse.*

In the codex of Ubayy: *law shi'ta la-utiyta 'alayhi ajran* ("if you had wished, you would have been given a wage for it").

Then al-Khidr said to Moses, according to their condition: ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾. Al-Khidr had made a condition, and Moses had given his word that he would not ask about anything. Asking is the least of the forms of objection, while denial and calling it an error is greater than it. His saying ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it﴾, although it is not a question, contains within it a denial of his action and an assertion that taking a wage was correct. In that there is a correction of the abandoning of the wage. As for his separating and repeating ﴿between me and you﴾ and his departure from "between us", it is for the sake of emphasis. The *sin* in his saying *sa-unabbi'uka* ("I will inform you") separates between the two dialogues and the two companionships, and indicates that the first has ended.

The majority read *nukran* (a terrible thing). Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far and Shayba read *nukuran* with a damma on the kaf, while the reading from Nafi' varies. Its meaning is: something that is denounced.

People differed as to which of the two is more forceful: his saying *imran* or his saying *nukran*. One group said: this is a clear killing, and beyond it lies something anticipated, and *nukran* is more forceful. Another group said: this is the killing of one person, whereas *imran* is the killing of a group, so *imran* is more forceful.

The author (Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him) said:

In my view, they are for two different meanings: his saying *imran* is more dreadful and more terrifying, in that it is an expected great matter, while *nukran* is clearer in corruption, because its harm has already occurred.

"Half of the Qur'an comes after the letter *nun*, or it ends at the *nun* in His saying *nukran*."

His saying ﴿Did I not tell you﴾ contains rebuke and harshness not found in his earlier saying ﴿Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾ (al-Kahf: 72). His saying *ba'daha* ("after this") means: after this story. He returned the pronoun to it although it had no explicit prior mention, because it was implied within the speech.

The majority read *fa-la tusahibunni* ("do not keep me as a companion"), which Ubayy related from the Prophet (ﷺ). 'Isa and Ya'qub read *fa-la tasbahni*. 'Isa also read *fa-la tushbihni* with a damma on the ta and a kasra on the ha, and this was related by Sahl from Abu 'Amr. The meaning is: do not make me a companion in your knowledge. Al-A'raj read *fa-la tasbahanni* with a fatha on the ta and the ba and a shadda on the nun.

His saying *qad balaghta min ladunni 'udhran* means: you have indeed given me an excuse, and you have reached the excuse from my side.

The author (Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It seems that this story is the basis for the time-limits in rulings, which are three days, and the periods of waiting (*tallawwum*) are three. So reflect on this.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read *min ladunni* with a fatha on the lam, a damma on the dal and a shadda on the nun. Here *ladun* is joined to the pronoun nun of the first person (as in *darabani*, "he struck me"), so assimilation occurred. This is the reading of the Prophet (ﷺ). Nafi' and 'Asim read *min ladunnī* as in the first reading, except that the nun is light, so it is *ladun* joined to the first-person *ya'* as in *ghulami* ("my boy"), with the letter before the ya' having a kasra as it does in this word. Abu Bakr from 'Asim read *min ladnī* with a fatha on the lam, a sukun on the dal and a light nun. This is a lightened form of *ladunī*, which we mentioned before this. It is related from 'Asim as *min ludnī* with a damma on the lam and a sukun on the dal. Mujahid said: this is a mistake. Abu 'Ali said: this criticism seems to be due to the transmission; but according to the rules of Arabic, it is correct. Al-Hasan read *min ladnī* with a fatha on the lam and a sukun on the dal.

The majority read *'udran*. Abu 'Amr and 'Isa read *'udurran* with a damma on the dal. Al-Dani related that Ubayy reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) *'udhrī* with a kasra on the ra and a ya' after it. Al-Tabari related with an isnad that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whenever he supplicated for someone, began with himself. He said one day: "May the mercy of Allah be upon us and upon Moses. Had he been patient with his companion, he would have seen wonders. But he said: *'So do not keep me as a companion; you have indeed given me an excuse from my side.'*"

In al-Bukhari, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on Moses. We wished he had been patient until he would have related to us the account of the two of them."

It is reported in the exegesis of this verse that Allah the Exalted made these examples that occurred to Moses with al-Khidr a proof against Moses and a source of wonder for him. That is because when he denied the matter of the damaging of the ship, it was said to him: "O Moses, where was your management of this while you were cast into the sea in the chest?" When he denied the matter of the boy, it was said to him: "Where is your denial of this from your hiding of the Copt and your judgment against him?" When he denied the raising of the wall, it was said to him: "Where is this from your lifting of the stone of the well for the daughters of Shu'ayb without a wage?"

His saying *fa-ntalaqa* ("so they set out") means that al-Khidr and Moses walked, seeking out from al-Khidr a matter in which what he possessed of the knowledge of Allah the Exalted would take effect. They passed by a town and asked its people to feed them, but they refused. In a hadith, they were walking past the gatherings of those people, asking them for food.

The author (Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This expression explicitly states the lowliness of this world before Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

People differed about the town. Muhammad ibn Sirin said: it is al-Ubullah, the stingiest town and the farthest from the sky. Another group said: it is Antakya. Another group said: it is Burqa. Another group said: it is in the Island of al-Andalus. This was related from Abu Hurayrah and others, and it is said that it is al-Jazirah al-Khadra'. Another group said: it is Abu Hurran, which is in the region of Adharbayjan.

The author (Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him) said:

All of this is according to the disagreement about which region of the earth the story of Moses, peace be upon him, took place in, and Allah knows best the reality of that.

The majority read *yudayyifuhuma* with a fatha on the dad and a shadda on the ya'. Abu Raja' read *yudayyifuhuma* with a kasra on the dad and a sukun on the ya'. This is the reading of Ibn Muhaysin, al-Zubayr and Abu Razin. *Al-dayf* (the guest) is derived from *dafa ila al-makan*, meaning to incline towards a place, and from it comes *al-idafah* (the annexation), which is the inclining of one thing towards another. Al-A'mash read *fa-aba an yut'imuhuma* ("they refused to feed them").

His saying, Exalted is He, about the wall: ﴿about to collapse﴾ is a metaphor (*isti'arah*). All the verbs whose proper subject is a living, speaking being, when they are attributed to an inanimate object or an animal, are in fact metaphorical; that is, if a human being were in the place of the inanimate object, he would be carrying out that action. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

*Will you cease? And one who forbids the transgressors ... is not like a spear-thrust in which oil and wick go away.*

Here he attributed the forbidding to the spear-thrust. From this is the saying of the poet:

*The spear desires the chest of Abu Baraʾ, and turns away from the blood of the Banu 'Uqayl.*

From this is the saying of 'Antarah:

*And he complained to me with tears and neighing.*

He explained this meaning with his saying:

*If he had known what dialogue is, he would have complained... (the verse).*

From this is the common saying: "My house looks at the house of so-and-so." And from it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Their fires should not see one another." This is very common.

The majority read *yanqadd*, meaning: it falls. It is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) read, as is related from him: *an yunqada* with a damma on the mim and a lightened dad, and this is the reading of Ubayy. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and 'Ikrimah read *an yanqasa* with an unpointed sad, meaning: it splits lengthwise. It is said: *inqasa al-jidar* ("the wall split"), and *inqasa al-bi'r* ("the well split"), and *inqasat al-sinn* ("the tooth split") when it is split lengthwise. It is also said that it means it cracks in any way. From this is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

*A parting like the chipping of a tooth, so patience, for it is a stumbling and a mending for every person.*

It is also related as *'ibrah* and *huburu*, with ba' and ha'. Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash read *yurid li-yanqadda*.

The exegetes differed about his saying *fa-aqamahu* ("so he set it upright"). One group said: he demolished it and sat down to rebuild it. This occurred in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, and this interpretation is supported by Moses, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it﴾, because this is an act that deserves a wage. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: rather, he wiped it with his hand and it stood up.

The author (Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him) said:

A hadith has been related about this, and it is the more likely of the deeds of the prophets, peace be upon them.

Then Moses said to al-Khidr: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it﴾, meaning: food that we could eat. The majority read *la-ittakhadhta*. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *la-takhidhta*, which is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and Qatadah. Some readers assimilated the dhal into the ta and some did not. From the usage of "takhidha" is the saying of the poet:

*And my leg has taken, beside its stirrup, a limping step like the pressed-down footprint of the sandgrouse.*

In the codex of Ubayy: *law shi'ta la-utiyta 'alayhi ajran* ("if you had wished, you would have been given a wage for it").

Then al-Khidr said to Moses, according to their condition: ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾. Al-Khidr had made a condition, and Moses had given his word that he would not ask about anything. Asking is the least of the forms of objection, while denial and calling it an error is greater than it. His saying ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it﴾, although it is not a question, contains within it a denial of his action and an assertion that taking a wage was correct. In that there is a correction of the abandoning of the wage. As for his separating and repeating ﴿between me and you﴾ and his departure from "between us", it is for the sake of emphasis. The *sin* in his saying *sa-unabbi'uka* ("I will inform you") separates between the two dialogues and the two companionships, and indicates that the first has ended.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verse 79:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿As for the boat, it belonged to poor people who worked on the sea. So I wanted to damage it, for behind them was a king who seized every boat by force.﴾

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "li-masakin" with a light sin, the plural of miskin (poor). Their description has been disputed. One group said: it belonged to a people of merchants, but since they were travelling on a small boat, in the middle of a deep sea, and in a state of weakness unable to repel an oppressive usurper, He described them as "masakin", since they were in a condition that warrants compassion for them.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is like when you say of a rich man, when he falls into a slip or stumbles in speech: "miskin". Another group said: they were ten brothers with disabilities, five of whom worked on the boat, and five of whom had no capacity for work.

Another group read "li-massakin" with a doubled sin, and its interpretation has been disputed. One group said: by the masakin he meant the boat's sailors, because the massak is the one who holds the boat's rope (rijl al-markab), and every servant suited to holding it is called so, so all of them were called masakin. Another group said: by the masakin he meant tanners of hides (dabaghat al-musuk), which are skins, whose singular is maskun.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The more apparent reading in this matter is the first reading, and its meaning is that the boat belonged to weak people who deserve compassion. People have used this verse as evidence that the miskin who has the means of subsistence is like the boat for these people, and that he is in a better state than the faqir. Those who hold the opposite view have cited the words of the poet:

"As for the faqir whose milch-camel was
Enough for his dependents, and nothing of pasture was left to him..."

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

My own clarification of this is that both are terms indicating extreme weakness of condition, and with miskana there is exposure and humiliation through asking. For this reason Allah the Exalted made them two categories in the section on charity. As for the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ) which says: "The miskin is not the one who goes around with this tawaf," the masakin in language are people in need who have uncovered their faces. As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿For the poor who are confined in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273], He made the fuqara' those who did not uncover their faces. This matter has been discussed earlier more fully than this.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and behind them was a king﴾. Some people said: its meaning is "in front of them," and they said that "wara'" is one of the words with opposite meanings. Ibn Jubayr and Ibn 'Abbas said: in front of them was a king who seized every sound boat. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him) read: "and in front of them was a king who seized every sound boat."

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

His saying "wara'ahum", in my view, stays on its proper meaning, because these words are used with reference to time: the event that comes first in existence is the imam (in front), and "bayna yadayy" refers to what comes after it in time, while what comes after is the wara', which is what is behind. This is contrary to what appears at first glance. Consider these words in their places where they occur and you will find them consistent. So the meaning of this verse is: these people, their work and their effort, the seizure by the king follows them in time. And whoever reads "amamahum" means in place, that is, they were traveling toward his city. His, the Exalted, saying regarding the Torah and the Gospel that they are "bayna yadayi al-Qur'an" is consistent with what we have said regarding time. His, the Glorified, saying: ﴿from behind them is Hell﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 10] is consistent with what we have said regarding the consideration of time. The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The prayer is amamaka" means in place; otherwise their being at that time was in front of the prayer in time. Consider this statement, for it relieves one of the confusion of these words. It occurred in Qatadah's report in al-Tabari's book: ﴿and behind them was a king﴾, Qatadah said: "amamahum" (in front of them). Do you not see that He says: ﴿from behind them is Hell﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 10], and it is before them?

This view is not sound, and this is the non-Arabic-like error (al-'ujmah) about which al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan used to cry out. This was said by al-Zajjaj. It is possible that their return on their route was against the usurper, so "wara'ahum" was literal. It was said: the name of this usurper was Hadad ibn Budad; it was said: his name was al-Jalandi; all of this is not established. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿every boat﴾ is a general term whose meaning is specific to the good, sound boats passing by it.

﴿And as for the boy, his parents were believers, and We feared that he would overburden them with rebellion and disbelief.﴾ ﴿So We desired that their Lord would replace him for them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion.﴾ ﴿And as for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them; their father had been righteous. So your Lord desired that they reach their maturity and extract their treasure, as a mercy from your Lord. I did not do it on my own accord. That is the interpretation (ta'wil) of what you could not bear with patience.﴾

The matter of the boy has already been discussed, along with the disagreement over whether he was an adult or a child. The hadith states that this boy was sealed (ṭubbiʿa) on the day he was sealed as a disbeliever. This supports the apparent meaning that he was not yet of age, although it is possible that the report concerns him even though he had reached adulthood. It is also said that the boy's name was Jaysur with a rāʾ, and it is said Jaysun with a nūn, but none of this is firmly established.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited: "Then he was a disbeliever, and his parents were believers" (fa-kāna kāfiran wa-kāna abawāhu mu'minīn). Abu Sa'id al-Khudri recited: "His parents were two believers" (fa-kāna abawāhu mu'minān), making the kāna here the kāna of the matter and the situation (kāna al-amr wa-l-sha'n).

As for His words "fa-khashīnā" (so We feared), it is said that it refers to the side of Khidr, so this is a clear resolution. In my view, the pronoun refers to Khidr and his righteous companions, who were concerned with the matter and discussed it. It is also said that it refers to the side of God, the Exalted, and Khidr expressed it in this way. Al-Tabari said: its meaning is "fa-'alimnā" (so We knew). Others said: "fa-karihnā" (so We disliked it).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

In my view, the more evident interpretation of this, although the wording resists it, is that it is a metaphor (isti'āra), meaning: according to the assumption of the created beings and of those addressed, if they knew his condition, fear of overburdening the parents would have arisen in them. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Then your Lord feared" (fa-khāfa rabbuka), and this is clear in its being a metaphor. This is like the "la'alla" and "'asā" that occur in the Qur'an with regard to God, the Exalted, for all of that expression of hope, expectation, fear and apprehension is, in fact, according to your measure, O addressees. "Yurhiqahumā" means: it urges them and burdens them with severity, and the meaning is that their love for him would drive them to follow him.

The majority recited "an yubaddilahumā" with a fatḥa on the bā' and a shadda on the dāl. Ibn Muhaysin, al-Hasan and 'Asim recited "an yubdilahumā" with a sukūn on the bā' and without a shadda on the dāl. "Al-zakāh" is nobility of character, dignity, and tranquility containing goodness. "Al-ruḥm" means mercy. According to one group, the meaning is that the boy would show mercy to them (yarḥamuhumā). It is also said that it means that they would show mercy to him (yarḥamānihi). From this is the verse of Ru'ba ibn al-'Ajjaj:

"O you who sent down kin (al-ruḥum) upon Idris,
And who sent down the curse upon Iblis."

Ibn 'Amir recited "ruḥuman" with a ḍamma on the ḥāʾ, and the rest recited "ruḥman" with a sukūn on it, and there is a difference of report from Abu 'Amr. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, recited: "Rabbuhumā azkā minhu wa-aqrab ruḥman" (their Lord, purer than him and nearer in mercy). It is narrated from Ibn Jurayj that they replaced him with a believing boy. It is also narrated from Ibn Jurayj that they replaced him with a girl. Al-Naqqash related that she and her offspring bore seventy prophets. Al-Mahdawi mentioned this from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, but it is far-fetched, since a multitude of prophets is known only among the Children of Israel, and this woman was not among them. It is narrated from Ibn Jurayj that the mother of the boy, on the day he was killed, was pregnant with a believing boy.

As for His words, exalted is He: "As for the wall, it belonged to two boys." These two boys were young, as indicated by the description of them as orphans. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no orphanhood after reaching maturity." This is the apparent meaning, although it is possible that orphanhood remained for them after maturity, that is, they were orphans, in the sense of showing them compassion. People differed about the treasure. Qatada and 'Ikrima said: it was great wealth. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: it was knowledge in buried scrolls. 'Umar, the mawla of Ghufra, said: it was a tablet of gold on which was written: "Wonder at one who is certain of provision yet toils; wonder at one who is certain of the reckoning yet is heedless; wonder at one who is certain of death yet rejoices." Similar reports with the same meaning have also been related.

As for His words, exalted is He: "And their father had been righteous." The apparent meaning of the wording and what precedes it is that he was their father of the nearest generation. It is also said that he was their seventh forefather, and it is said the tenth, and so they were preserved because of him, even though they were not described as righteous. In a hadith: "Verily God, the Exalted, preserves the righteous man through his descendants."

In the account of Khidr, peace be upon him, in the first episode, there is "fa-aradtu an a'ība-hā" (so I desired to damage it) [al-Kahf: 79]; in the second, "fa-aradnā an yubdilahumā" (so We desired that He replace them); and in the third, "fa-arāda rabbuka an yablughā" (so your Lord desired that they reach). He used the word "desire" alone at first because it is a word of defect, so he showed good manners by attributing the desire in it only to himself. This is like the good manners of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, in his saying: "And when I am ill, it is He who cures me" [al-Shu'ara': 80], where he attributed the act both before and after to God, the Exalted, and attributed the illness to himself, since it signifies deficiency and calamity. This principle is widely applied in the eloquence of the Qur'an. Do you not see the placing of the human act first in His words: "So when they deviated, God made their hearts deviate" [al-Saff: 5], and the placing of God's act first in His words, blessed and exalted is He: "Then He turned to them so that they might turn" [al-Tawba: 118]? Khidr said in the second "fa-aradnā" only because it was a hope that he and his righteous companions had held, and they had discussed it in terms of fear for the parents, and wished for their replacement. He attributed the desire in the third to God, the Exalted, because it concerns a matter that is future in time, long-term, and one of the unseen matters, so it was fitting to single out this place with the mention of God, the Exalted, even though Khidr also desired that which God had informed him He desires. This is the explanation of the eloquence of this expression according to our limited understanding, and God knows best.

"Al-ashudd" is the completeness of character and intellect. People differed about its number of years: it is said thirty-five, it is said thirty-six, it is said forty, and other things have been said that are weak. Khidr's words: "And I did not do it on my own accord" (wa-mā fa'altuhu 'an amrī) imply that Khidr is a prophet. People differed about this: it is said he is a prophet, and it is said he is a righteous servant and not a prophet. Likewise, the majority of people hold that Khidr has died. One group says that he is alive, because he drank from the spring of life, remains on the earth, and performs the pilgrimage to the House and other things. Al-Naqqash expanded greatly on this matter and mentioned in his book many things from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, and others, none of which stand on firm ground. Had Khidr, peace be upon him, been alive and making the pilgrimage, he would have had a manifest presence in the religion of Islam. God, who knows the details of things, is the only Lord. Among what decides that Khidr has died now is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Have you considered this night of yours? No one who is upon the earth today will remain."

His words "dhālika ta'wīl" (that is the ma'āl, the outcome). One group recited "tasta'" (you could bear), and the majority recited "tasi'" (you could bear). Abu Hatim said: "This is how we recite it; we follow the codex (muṣḥaf)."

Al-Tabari drew from the connection of this narrative with His words, blessed and exalted is He: "And your Lord is the Forgiving, the Possessor of mercy. Were He to take them to account for what they earned, He would have hastened punishment for them. But for them there is an appointed time from which they will find no refuge besides Him" [al-Kahf: 58], that this narrative was brought as a parable for the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding his people, meaning: do not concern yourself with God's granting them respite and His providing them with blessings in their outward sense, for the inner realities are heading toward taking vengeance upon them. There is something similar to this which is possible, but with some strained interpretation, so consider it carefully.

﴿And as for the boy, his parents were believers, and We feared that he would overburden them with rebellion and disbelief.﴾ ﴿So We desired that their Lord would replace him for them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion.﴾ ﴿And as for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them; their father had been righteous. So your Lord desired that they reach their maturity and extract their treasure, as a mercy from your Lord. I did not do it on my own accord. And who sent down the curse upon Iblis."

It is narrated from Ibn Jurayj that they replaced him with a believing boy. It is also narrated from Ibn Jurayj that they replaced him with a girl. Al-Naqqash related that she and her offspring bore seventy prophets. Al-Mahdawi mentioned this from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, but it is far-fetched, since a multitude of prophets is known only among the Children of Israel, and this woman was not among them. It is narrated from Ibn Jurayj that the mother of the boy, on the day he was killed, was pregnant with a believing boy.

As for His words, exalted is He: "As for the wall, it belonged to two boys." These two boys were young, as indicated by the description of them as orphans. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no orphanhood after reaching maturity." This is the apparent meaning, although it is possible that orphanhood remained for them after maturity, that is, they were orphans, in the sense of showing them compassion. People differed about the treasure. Qatada and 'Ikrima said: it was great wealth. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: it was knowledge in buried scrolls. 'Umar, the mawla of Ghufra, said: it was a tablet of gold on which was written: "Wonder at one who is certain of provision yet toils; wonder at one who is certain of the reckoning yet is heedless; wonder at one who is certain of death yet rejoices." Similar reports with the same meaning have also been related.

As for His words, exalted is He: "And their father had been righteous." The apparent meaning of the wording and what precedes it is that he was their father of the nearest generation. It is also said that he was their seventh forefather, and it is said the tenth, and so they were preserved because of him, even though they were not described as righteous. In a hadith: "Verily God, the Exalted, preserves the righteous man through his descendants."

In the account of Khidr, peace be upon him, in the first episode, there is "fa-aradtu an a'ība-hā" (so I desired to damage it) [al-Kahf: 79]; in the second, "fa-aradnā an yubdilahumā" (so We desired that He replace them); and in the third, "fa-arāda rabbuka an yablughā" (so your Lord desired that they reach). He used the word "desire" alone at first because it is a word of defect, so he showed good manners by attributing the desire in it only to himself. This is like the good manners of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, in his saying: "And when I am ill, it is He who cures me" [al-Shu'ara': 80], where he attributed the act both before and after to God, the Exalted, and attributed the illness to himself, since it signifies deficiency and calamity. This principle is widely applied in the eloquence of the Qur'an. Do you not see the placing of the human act first in His words: "So when they deviated, God made their hearts deviate" [al-Saff: 5], and the placing of God's act first in His words, blessed and exalted is He: "Then He turned to them so that they might turn" [al-Tawba: 118]? Khidr said in the second "fa-aradnā" only because it was a hope that he and his righteous companions had held, and they had discussed it in terms of fear for the parents, and wished for their replacement. He attributed the desire in the third to God, the Exalted, because it concerns a matter that is future in time, long-term, and one of the unseen matters, so it was fitting to single out this place with the mention of God, the Exalted, even though Khidr also desired that which God had informed him He desires. This is the explanation of the eloquence of this expression according to our limited understanding, and God knows best.

"Al-ashudd" is the completeness of character and intellect. People differed about its number of years: it is said thirty-five, it is said thirty-six, it is said forty, and other things have been said that are weak. Khidr's words: "And I did not do it on my own accord" (wa-mā fa'altuhu 'an amrī) imply that Khidr is a prophet. People differed about this: it is said he is a prophet, and it is said he is a righteous servant and not a prophet. Likewise, the majority of people hold that Khidr has died. One group says that he is alive, because he drank from the spring of life, remains on the earth, and performs the pilgrimage to the House and other things. Al-Naqqash expanded greatly on this matter and mentioned in his book many things from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, and others, none of which stand on firm ground. Had Khidr, peace be upon him, been alive and making the pilgrimage, he would have had a manifest presence in the religion of Islam. God, who knows the details of things, is the only Lord. Among what decides that Khidr has died now is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Have you considered this night of yours? No one who is upon the earth today will remain."

His words "dhālika ta'wīl" (that is the ma'āl, the outcome). One group recited "tasta'" (you could bear), and the majority recited "tasi'" (you could bear). Abu Hatim said: "This is how we recite it; we follow the codex (muṣḥaf)."

Al-Tabari drew from the connection of this narrative with His words, blessed and exalted is He: "And your Lord is the Forgiving, the Possessor of mercy. Were He to take them to account for what they earned, He would have hastened punishment for them. But for them there is an appointed time from which they will find no refuge besides Him" [al-Kahf: 58], that this narrative was brought as a parable for the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding his people, meaning: do not concern yourself with God's granting them respite and His providing them with blessings in their outward sense, for the inner realities are heading toward taking vengeance upon them. There is something similar to this which is possible, but with some strained interpretation, so consider it carefully.

﴿And as for the boy, his parents were believers, and We feared that he would overburden them with rebellion and disbelief.﴾ ﴿So We desired that their Lord would replace him for them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion.﴾ ﴿And as for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them; their father had been righteous. So your Lord desired that they reach their maturity and extract their treasure, as a mercy from your Lord. I did not do it on my own accord. That is the interpretation (ta'wil) of what you could not bear with patience.﴾

The matter of the boy has already been discussed, along with the disagreement over whether he was an adult or a child. The hadith states that this boy was sealed (ṭubbiʿa) on the day he was sealed as a disbeliever. This supports the apparent meaning that he was not yet of age, although it is possible that the report concerns him even though he had reached adulthood. It is also said that the boy's name was Jaysur with a rāʾ, and it is said Jaysun with a nūn, but none of this is firmly established.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited: "Then he was a disbeliever, and his parents were believers" (fa-kāna kāfiran wa-kāna abawāhu mu'minīn). Abu Sa'id al-Khudri recited: "His parents were two believers" (fa-kāna abawāhu mu'minān), making the kāna here the kāna of the matter and the situation (kāna al-amr wa-l-sha'n).

As for His words "fa-khashīnā" (so We feared), it is said that it refers to the side of Khidr, so this is a clear resolution. In my view, the pronoun refers to Khidr and his righteous companions, who were concerned with the matter and discussed it. It is also said that it refers to the side of God, the Exalted, and Khidr expressed it in this way. Al-Tabari said: its meaning is "fa-'alimnā" (so We knew). Others said: "fa-karihnā" (so We disliked it).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

In my view, the more evident interpretation of this, although the wording resists it, is that it is a metaphor (isti'āra), meaning: according to the assumption of the created beings and of those addressed, if they knew his condition, fear of overburdening the parents would have arisen in them. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Then your Lord feared" (fa-khāfa rabbuka), and this is clear in its being a metaphor. This is like the "la'alla" and "'asā" that occur in the Qur'an with regard to God, the Exalted, for all of that expression of hope, expectation, fear and apprehension is, in fact, according to your measure, O addressees. "Yurhiqahumā" means: it urges them and burdens them with severity, and the meaning is that their love for him would drive them to follow him.

The majority recited "an yubaddilahumā" with a fatḥa on the bā' and a shadda on the dāl. Ibn Muhaysin, al-Hasan and 'Asim recited "an yubdilahumā" with a sukūn on the bā' and without a shadda on the dāl. "Al-zakāh" is nobility of character, dignity, and tranquility containing goodness. "Al-ruḥm" means mercy. According to one group, the meaning is that the boy would show mercy to them (yarḥamuhumā). It is also said that it means that they would show mercy to him (yarḥamānihi). From this is the verse of Ru'ba ibn al-'Ajjaj:

"O you who sent down kin (al-ruḥum) upon Idris,
And who sent down the curse upon Iblis."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verse 83–86:

(p-652) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿They ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn. Say: "I will recite to you a mention of him."﴾ ﴿Indeed, We established him on earth and gave him of every thing a means.﴾ ﴿So he followed a means,﴾ ﴿until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun, he found it setting in a spring of black mud, and found near it a people. We said: "O Dhu al-Qarnayn, either you punish them or you take among them a good course."﴾

It has been disputed who asked him about this story. It was said: a group of the People of the Book asked him. 'Uqba ibn 'Amir narrated a hadith on this matter, which al-Tabari mentioned. It was also said: it was the Quraysh, when the Jews guided them to ask him about the Spirit, the wandering man, and the youths who went off in ancient times, so that his testing would occur through this.

Dhu al-Qarnayn is Alexander the Greek, the Macedonian. His qaf may be doubled, so it is said "al-Maqqaduni." Ibn Ishaq, in the book of al-Tabari, mentioned that he was Greek. Wahb ibn Munabbih said he was Roman. Al-Tabari mentioned a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ that Dhu al-Qarnayn was a young man of the Romans, but it is a hadith of weak chain, transmitted from two shaykhs of the Tujib.

People differed about the reason he was named Dhu al-Qarnayn. The best of the sayings is that he had two braids of hair, which were his two horns (qarnan), so he was named by them. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi and others. The dafa'ir (braids) are the horns of the head, and from this is the saying of the poet:

﴿So she kissed her mouth, seizing hold of its horns (braids), drinking like one intoxicated, for the coolness of the water of al-Hashraj.﴾

And from this is the hadith concerning the washing of the daughter of the Prophet ﷺ, where Umm 'Atiyya said: "We braided her head into three horns (qurun)." And it is common for the forelocks to be called horns.

It is narrated that at the beginning of his reign he saw in his sleep that he was grasping the sun and holding two of its horns in his hands. He related this, and it was interpreted that he would prevail over whatever the sun shone upon, and so he was called Dhu al-Qarnayn. A group said: he was called Dhu al-Qarnayn because he reached the west and the east, so it is as if he possessed the two horns of the world. Another group said: he reached the rising place of the sun and uncovered by sight its two horns, or the two horns of the devil with it, and so he was named by that. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: he was so named because the two sides of his head were of copper. Wahb ibn Munabbih also said: he had two horns beneath his turban.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is far-fetched. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: he was only named Dhu al-Qarnayn because he was struck on one horn of his head and died, then was revived, then was struck on the other horn of his head and died, so he was named by that, because he received two great wounds on the two horns of his head on two great days of his battles, and so he was named thereby.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

And this is close.

As for the establishment of him on earth: he ruled the world, and all the kings of the world submitted to him. It is narrated that all the kings of the world were four: two believers and two disbelievers. The two believers were Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon him, and Alexander; the two disbelievers were Nimrod and Bakhtnassar. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and We gave him of every thing a means﴾ means: knowledge in every matter, and analogies through which he reaches knowledge of things. His saying "every thing" is a general term whose meaning is specific to whatever he could know and needed, and there are without doubt things of which he was not given a means by which to know them.

(p-654) Dhu al-Qarnayn has been disputed. It was said: he was a prophet, and this is weak. It was said: he was a angel (malak, with a fatha on the lam). It is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he heard a man calling another: "O Dhu al-Qarnayn!" He said: "Is it not enough for you that you named yourselves after the names of the prophets, until you name yourselves after the names of the angels?" And it is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he was asked about him and said: "An angel who wiped the earth from beneath it with the means." It was also said: he was a servant (malik, with a kasra on the lam), a righteous man who advised Allah and so was aided, said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "Among you today there is one like him," meaning himself. And Allah knows best.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿So he followed a means﴾, the verse. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "fa-ittaba'a sababan" with a doubled ta'. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "fa-atba'a sababan" with a sukun on the ta', on the pattern af'ala. Some of the linguists said: the two have one meaning, and likewise "taba'a." A group said: "atba'a" with a cut alif is an expression for one who is diligent, swift, and eager in pursuit, whereas "ittaba'a" only carries the sense of following without these qualities. This was said by Abu Zayd and others.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This speaker derived this view from the Qur'an, such as His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿So a piercing flame pursued him﴾ [al-Saffat: 10], and His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿So Pharaoh followed them with his soldiers﴾ [Yunus: 90], and His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿So Satan pursued him﴾ [al-A'raf: 175]. This is a view related by al-Naqqash from Yunus ibn Habib. And if you reflect on "ittaba'a" with a doubled ta', this meaning does not necessarily connect for you. The "sabab" in this verse is the path travelled, because it is the means of reaching the destination.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Hafs from 'Asim read "fi 'aynin hami'atin" on the pattern fi'lah, meaning possessing mud (hama'a). 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, and the rest read "fi 'aynin hamiyatin," meaning hot. Mu'awiya and Ibn 'Abbas differed over the reading of this. Ibn 'Abbas said "hami'atin," and Mu'awiya said "hamiyatin." So they both sent to Ka'b al-Ahbar to inform them (p-655) of the matter, how it is in the Torah. He said to them: "As for the Arabic, you two know it better than I do, but I find in the Torah that it sets in a spring of tha'th," and the tha'th is mud. When the two of them departed, a man said to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "I wish, Abu al-'Abbas, that I could help you with a verse of Tubba' in which he says regarding Dhu al-Qarnayn:"

﴿Dhu al-Qarnayn, my grandfather, was a Muslim,
a king to whom kings submit and are gathered.
He reached the east and the west seeking
the means of a matter from a wise, guiding one.
So he saw the sun's setting at its going down
in a spring of murky mud, black and dark.﴾

So the khulub is mud, the tha'th is the sediment, and the hardama is the black. As for the one who reads "hamiyatin," its direction is toward heat. And it is narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked at the sun as it was setting and said: "In the hot fire of Allah. Were it not that Allah restrains it, it would burn what is on the earth." And Abu Dharr narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked at the sun at its setting and said: "Do you know, Abu Dharr, where it sets?" I said: "No." He said: "It sets in a hot spring." This indicates that the spring there is hot. And "hamiyatin" is the reading of Talha ibn 'Abd Allah, 'Amr ibn al-'As and his son, and Ibn 'Umar. Al-Tabari went toward combining the two matters, saying: it is possible that the spring is hot and has mud, so each reading describes it by one of its states. Some of the Baghdadi scholars held that "fi" has the function of "'inda" (at), as if it were facing him from the earth, as the observer sees toward a muddy spring. Some of them said: His saying "fi 'aynin" means that Dhu al-Qarnayn was in it, that is, it was the end of the earth.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of these sayings is open to possibility, and Allah knows best. Abu Hatim said: It is possible that "hami'atin" is with a hamza, meaning possessing mud, so both readings would have one meaning. Some people (p-656) took as evidence that Dhu al-Qarnayn was a prophet His saying: ﴿O Dhu al-Qarnayn﴾; and whoever says he was not a prophet says: this speech was from Allah by inspiration.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿either you punish﴾ means: by killing for disbelief; ﴿or that you take among them a good course﴾ means: by bringing them to faith and following guidance. So it was as if it were said to him: "You will not be given except one of two courses: either they disbelieve and you punish them, or they believe and you treat them well." Al-Tabari went toward the view that "taking a good course" is capture together with their disbelief, so the meaning according to this is that they had disbelieved necessarily, and Allah gave him the choice between killing them or taking them captive.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that "taking" means imposing the jizya. However, the division of Dhu al-Qarnayn after this matter into disbelief or belief refutes this view to some extent, so reflect on it.

We said: "O Dhu al-Qarnayn, either you punish them or you take among them a good course."﴾

It has been disputed who asked him about this story. It was said: a group of the People of the Book asked him. 'Uqba ibn 'Amir narrated a hadith on this matter, which al-Tabari mentioned. It was also said: it was the Quraysh, when the Jews guided them to ask him about the Spirit, the wandering man, and the youths who went off in ancient times, so that his testing would occur through this.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said he was Roman. Al-Tabari mentioned a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ that Dhu al-Qarnayn was a young man of the Romans, but it is a hadith of weak chain, transmitted from two shaykhs of the Tujib.

People differed about the reason he was named Dhu al-Qarnayn. The best of the sayings is that he had two braids of hair, which were his two horns (qarnan), so he was named by them. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi and others. The dafa'ir (braids) are the horns of the head, and from this is the saying of the poet:

﴿So she kissed her mouth, seizing hold of its horns (braids), drinking like one intoxicated, for the coolness of the water of al-Hashraj.﴾

And from this is the hadith concerning the washing of the daughter of the Prophet ﷺ, where Umm 'Atiyya said: "We braided her head into three horns (qurun)." And it is common for the forelocks to be called horns.

All of this is far-fetched. And this is close.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿He said: "As for him who does wrong, we shall punish him; then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment." And as for him who believes and does righteous deeds, he shall have a reward of the best, and we shall speak to him of Our command with ease.﴾ ﴿Then he followed a way.﴾ ﴿Until, when he reached the rising-place of the sun, he found it rising over a people for whom We had made no shelter against it.﴾ ﴿So it was. And We had encompassed with knowledge all that was with him.﴾

"Dhulm" (wrongdoing) in this verse means disbelief (kufr). Then He threatened the disbelievers with Dhu al-Qarnayn's punishment of them before God's punishment, and He followed this with mention of God's punishment, because the punishment by Dhu al-Qarnayn is the one that reaches them first, the one that imprisons them, and the closer in harm. When the promise concerning the believers came, He mentioned God's bounty, which is the more deserving with respect to the believers, while the other (the reward of the disbelievers) is, in comparison with it, insignificant. Then He concluded finally with mention of His kindness in the phrase "with ease," and making it a "saying," since all actions are the creation of God Most High; so it is as if He had counted them as delivered and did not take account of their acquisition (kasb).

One group read "nukuran" with a damma on the kaf, and another group read "nukran" with a sukun on the kaf. Its meaning is "the abhorrent thing which imaginations deny because of its greatness and which bewilders."

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim (in the narration of Abu Bakr), Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "jaza'an al-husna" with the "jaza'" (reward) construct-annexed to "al-husna." This may bear two meanings: first, that by "al-husna" is meant the Garden, and the Garden is the reward, so the noun is annexed to it, as He said: "and the abode of the Hereafter" (Yusuf 109), where "the Hereafter" is the abode. Second, that by "al-husna" is meant their righteous deeds in their faith, so He promised them the reward of righteous deeds. His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Then he followed a way﴾ ﴿until, when he reached between the two barriers, he found beside them a people who could hardly understand any speech﴾ ﴿They said: "O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Ya'juj and Ma'juj are corrupters in the earth. So shall we pay you a tribute on condition that you set up a barrier between us and them?"﴾ ﴿He said: "That in which my Lord has established me is better. So help me with strength, and I will set up between you and them a rampart﴾

One group read "ittaba'a" with a doubled ta' (shaddah), and another group read it with the ta' unstressed, and this has already been mentioned. This implies that when he reached the place where the sun rises, he then followed another way (sababan), i.e., another path; so he, and Allah knows best, went either to the right or to the left from the place where the sun rises. As for "al-saddayn" (the two barriers), according to what the people of tafsir have mentioned, they are two mountains that blocked the passages of that region of the earth, and between the two mountain paths there is an opening, which is the place of the Romans.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The two mountains between which is the barrier are Armenia and Adharbayjan. Another group said: They are behind the lands of the Turks; this was mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is unverified; rather, they are at the far end of the earth in the direction of the east. It appears from the wording of the histories that they are toward the north, but determining a specific location is weak.

Nafi', 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "al-Sudayn" with a dammah on the sin, and likewise "suddan" wherever it occurs. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read all of it with a fathah from all the recitations; this is the reading of Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i. Ibn Kathir read "al-Saddayn" with a fathah on the sin, and "suddan" with a dammah in (Ya-Sin). Then scholars differed: al-Khalil and Sibawayh said the dammah is the noun (ism) and the fathah is the verbal noun (masdar). Al-Kisa'i said the dammah and the fathah are two dialects with one meaning. 'Ikrimah, Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and Abu 'Ubayda said: whatever is of Allah's creation in which no one has participated by work is with a dammah, and whatever is of human making is with a fathah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It follows for the adherents of this view that we should read "bayna al-saddayn" with a dammah, and after that "saddan" with a fathah; and this is the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. Abu Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah the opposite of what Abu 'Ubayda said. Ibn Abi Ishaq said: what your eyes see is "sudd" with a dammah on the sin, and what is not seen is "sadd" with a fathah.

The pronoun in "min duniHima" refers to the two mountains, i.e., he found them in the region that leads toward the west. There is disagreement about "al-qawm" (the people): it was said they are humans, and it was said they are jinn, and the first is more correct on several grounds. His saying: ﴿who could hardly understand any speech﴾ is an expression for the remoteness of their language from the languages of people; yet they understood or grasped by translation or the like. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yafqahuna" from afqaha, and the rest read "yafqahuna" from faqiha.

The pronoun in "qalu" refers to the people who are beyond the two barriers. Ya'juj and Ma'juj are two tribes of the children of Adam, but they divide into many kinds, the number of which has been disputed, so I have omitted mentioning it for lack of soundness. In their creation there is deformity: among them are those extremely tall, and among them those extremely short, about the size of a span or less or more; and among them is a kind with enormous ears, one ear being furry and the other bare; they use the one for summer and sleep on the other in winter, and it covers him.

(p-661) The Exalted's saying:

﴿"Bring me blocks of iron," until when he had made it level between the two cliffs, he said, "Blow," until when he had made it a fire, he said, "Bring me molten copper to pour over it."﴾ ﴿So they could not scale it, nor could they pierce it.﴾ ﴿He said, "This is a mercy from my Lord. But when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level, and the promise of my Lord is ever true."﴾ ﴿And We left some of them that day surging against one another, and the Trumpet was blown, and We gathered them together in one gathering.﴾ ﴿And We presented Hell that day to the disbelievers, displayed.﴾

Ibn 'Asim and Hamza read "ٱيتُونِي" (ītūnī, "bring me") meaning "come to me with" (jī'ūnī). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read "آتَوْنِي" (ātawnī, "give me") meaning "give me." All of this is close in meaning, because it is only a call to hand over, not a call for a gift or donation. This is because the preceding statement already linked it with His saying that they would not take tribute from them, so only the call to hand over and the exertion of strength remains. "ٱيتُونِي" is more fitting with His saying: ﴿So help me with strength﴾ [al-Kahf: 95]. The accusative of "الزُّبَرَ" (al-zubar, "blocks") is like the line of the poet:

"I commanded you the good."

The preposition was elided, so the verb took the accusative. Most readers read "زُبَرَ" (zubar) with a fatha on the ba', while al-Hasan read it with a damma. Both are plurals of "زُبْرَة" (zubra), which means a large piece of it. The meaning is: he arranged it and built it until, when he had made it level between the two cliffs. The rest is omitted because the apparent sense points to it. Most readers read "ساوى" (sawā, "made level"), while Qatada read "سَوَّى" (sawwā, "leveled"). "الصَّدَفَانِ" (al-ṣadafān, "the two cliffs") are the two facing mountains. One is not called "صَدَف" alone; rather "صَدَفَانِ" is said of two things, one of which faces the other. Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "الصَّدَفَيْنِ" (al-ṣadafayn) with a fatha on the ṣad and a shadda. This is the reading of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz (may Allah be pleased with him). Most of the commentators (mufassirun) said: "al-qiṭr" is molten copper. What supports this is what has been narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): a man came to him and said, "O Messenger of Allah, I have seen the barrier of Gog and Magog." He said, "How did you see it?" He said, "I saw it like a striped cloak, a yellow stripe, a red stripe and a black stripe." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "You have seen it." From this is His saying in the Muwatta': "and the sun in its chamber before it rises (taẓharu)." ﴿Nor could they pierce it﴾ because of its width and strength. 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "دَكَّاءَ" (dakkā') with a long vowel. This is by comparison with the "ناقة دكاء" (nāqa dakkā', a she-camel with a flat hump), which is one without a hump. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 18, verses 107–110:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them will be the Gardens of Firdaws (the highest paradise) as a lodging,﴾ ﴿abiding therein forever; they will not desire any change from them.﴾ ﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought the like of it as a supplement.﴾ ﴿Say: I am only a human being like you. It is revealed to me that your God is one God. So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord.﴾

When He had finished mentioning the disbelievers and those whose deeds were the greatest losers, He followed it with mention of the state of the believers, so that the contrast would become clear. In this there is an incitement of souls to follow what is good and upright.

The exegetes (mufassirun) differed concerning "Firdaws." Qatadah said: it is the highest part of the Garden and its elevated ground. Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: it is a mountain from which the rivers of the Garden gush forth. Abu Umamah said: it is the navel (center) of the Garden and its middle. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the rivers of the Garden gush forth from it. 'Abdullah ibn al-Harith ibn Ka'b said: it is the gardens of vines and grapes specifically, among the fruits. Ka'b al-Ahbar also said this. Some people cited for this the verse of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt:

"Their dwellings at that time were manifest, / in them were the firadis, the fuman, and the onion."

Al-Zajjaj said: it has been said that Firdaws is Syriac, and it has been said that it is Greek (Rumi). Firdaws is not heard in the speech of the Arabs except in the verse of Hassan ibn Thabit:

"Indeed, the reward of Allah for every monotheist / is a garden of Firdaws in which he will abide forever."

It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you ask Allah, ask Him for Firdaws." Another group said: Firdaws is the orchard in Greek (Rumi). This is a concise statement of what has been said about "Firdaws" and the essential points of what has been said concerning it.

His saying, exalted is He, "nuzulan" (as a lodging), may carry the two meanings we mentioned earlier. "Hiwal" means "change" (tahawwul). Mujahid said: "a place of transfer (mutahawwal)." From this is the saying of the poet:

"For every state there is a term, / then after it there is a change (hiwal)."

It seems to be a collective noun, and its singular seems to be hiwalah, but this is open to question. Al-Zajjaj reported from some people that it means "scheming/stratagem" in the matter of occupation. 

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is weak and forced.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: If the sea were ink...﴾ and the rest of the verse, it is narrated that the occasion of revelation was that the Jews said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "How do you claim that you are the prophet of all nations and are sent to them, and that you have been given what people need of knowledge, while you are deficient? You were asked about the soul and did not answer about it," and similar speech. So the verse was revealed informing them of the vastness of the knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that it is not finite, and that standing short of it is neither strange nor reprehensible. He expressed this by an illustration of what they consider great, which is His saying: ﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord...﴾ The "words" (kalimat) are the meanings subsisting in the self, and they are the known things (ma'lumat). The known things of Allah, glorified is He, are not finite, while the sea is necessarily finite.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read "tanfad" with a ta' at the beginning. 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read "yanfad" with a ya'. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Talhah ibn Musarrif read "qabla an tuqda kalimatu rabbi" (before the words of my Lord are fulfilled).

His saying "midadan" means "an increase." Al-Jumhur read "midadan." Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, al-A'mash, Mujahid, and al-A'raj also read "midadan." The meaning is: if the sea were ink with which the known things of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, were written, it would be exhausted before it had completed them, and likewise however many multiples you wish. "I am only a human being like you; I have not been given except what is revealed to me and uncovered for me."

Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "yanfad" with a ya' below, and the rest read with a ta' above.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: I am only a human being like you...﴾ and the rest of the verse. The meaning is: I am only a human being whose knowledge extends only to where it is revealed to me. What is most important of what is revealed to me is that your God is one God. Their disbelief was in worshipping idols, so this section from what was revealed to him was specified for this reason. Then he began exhortation and clear advice of right guidance.

"Yarju" retains its usual sense of "hope." A group said: "yarju" means "fear." This has already been discussed, since the intent is: whoever believes in the meeting with his Lord. Every believer in the meeting with his Lord is necessarily in a state of both fear and hope. If the verse expressed it with fear, the meaning would be complete in the manner of warning and admonition. When it expresses it with hope, it is in the manner of encouragement and expanding souls toward the goodness of Allah, glorified and exalted is He. That is: whoever hopes for everlasting bliss from his Lord, let him do righteous work. The rest of the verse is clear regarding associating partners with Allah, blessed and exalted is He. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said in its interpretation: he does not show off in his work. A hadith has been narrated that it was revealed concerning showing off, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about someone who fights in jihad and is praised by people. Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan said: this is the last verse revealed of the Qur'an.

The commentary on Surat al-Kahf is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
